He  was  elected  M.P.  for  the  city  of  Dublin  in  1865,  and 
created  a  baronet  of  the  United  Kingdom  by  patent  dated 
15th  April,  1867.  To  the  munificence  and  energetic  and 
patriotic  spirit  of  this  gentleman  his  native  city  of  Dublin 
owes  much ;  especially  the  restoration  of  the  venerable 
Catliedral  of  St.  Patrick.  Though  almost  in  ruins  when  he 
commenced  the  great  work,  which  he  carried  out  at  his  own 
sole  cost,  and  under  his  own  personal  direction,  the  Cathedral 
restored  in  exact  conformity  witli  its  original  style,  is  now 
the  finest  specimen  of  church  architecture  in  Ireland.  In 
commemoration  of  this  patriotic  act.  Her  Majesty  granted  to 
the  baronet  and  his  successors  the  right  to  bear  supporters.

Thomas. 

John,  a  secular  priest,  who,  leaving  Scotland  on  account  of 
his  religion,  took  up  his  abode  at  Paris  in  1573,  and  was 
apjiointed  professor  of  philosophy  in  the  college  of  Navarre. 
He  became  tutor  to  the  Cardinal  de  Bourbon,  in  1576;  and 
to  Francis  de  Joyeuse,  afterwards  a  cardinal,  in  1578;  and 
was  chosen  rector  of  the  university  of  Paris,  in  1584.  He 
was  a  zealous  partizan  of  the  League,  and  one  of  the  council 
who  otfered  the  crown  to  Philip  II.  of  Spain,  in  1591.  When 
Henry  IV.  entered  Paris,  in  1594,  Hamilton  was  arrested, 
but  had  liberty  soon  after  to  depart  fi'om  Paris.  He  retired 
to  Brussels,  and  in  1601,  ventured  to  revisit  his  native  coun- 
try, after  an  absence  of  nearly  thirty  years.  He  found  a 
temporary  asylum  at  the  castle  of  Lord  Ogilvie;  but  in  1609 
was  arrested  by  a  party  of  life-guards,  and  committed  to  the 
Tower  of  London,  where  he  died.

The  race  of  Douglas  is  amongst  the  noblest  in  Europe, 
whether  we  consider  a  long  line  of  illustrious  ancestors,  a 
princely  domain,  a  series  of  royal  and  noble  alliances  during 
seven  centuries,  or  a  well-earned  renown  for  indomitable 
wai-like  prowess.  The  origin  of  this  great  house  is  lost 
amid  the  mists  of  antiquity ;  and  we  will  not  here  attempt 
to  weigh  the  conflicting  claims  of  an  indigenous  and  a 
foreign  descent,  both  of  which  havo  been  assigned  to  "  The 
Douglas."  Suffice  it  to  say  that  he  is  found  a  chief  of  baronial 
rank,  possessing  large  estates  in  Lanarkshire,  in  the  days 
of  William  the  Lion  and  the  two  last  Alexanders;  and 
that  he  rapidly  rose  to  eminence  during  the  stirring  times 
of  Edward  I.  and  Robert  Bruce. 

Akohibald  Douglas,  of  Douglas,  lived  in  the  reign  of 
King  Alexander  II.,  and  d.  in  1240.  He  m.  Margaret, 
dau.  and  co-heir  of  Sir  John  Crawford,  of  Crawford,  by 
whom  he  had,  i.  William,  his  successor;  ii.  Andrew, 
ancestor  of  a  very  great  branch  of  the  house  of  Douglas, 
viz.,  Dalkeith.  This  race,  after  existing  for  several  genera- 
tions in  great  splendour  as  Barons  of  Dalkeith,  were  raised 
to  the  dignity  of  Earls  of  Morton.  The  main  line  ended  on 
the  death  of  James,  3rd  Earl  of  Morton,  in  1553.  In  1588, 
Sir  William  Douglas,  of  Lochlevan,  the  descendant  of  a 
remote  branch  of  the  Dalkeith  family,  was  called  to  the 
succession  of  the  earldom,  and  is  ancestor  of  the  present 
Earl  of  Morton.  There  are,  however,  families  of  the 
name  of  Douglas  which  are  more  directly  descended  from 
the  great  house  of  Dalkeith. 

William  Douolas,  of  Douglas,  the  eldest  son,  flourished 
in  the  reigns  of  Alexanders  II.  and  III.,  and  d.  in  1276, 
leaving  two  sons,  Hugh,  his  heir,  who  d.  without  issue  ; 
and 

William  Douglas,  of  Douglas.  He  joined  "Wallaco  in 
1299,  but  was  obliged  to  make  submission  to  King 
Edward  I.,  and  being  sent  to  England,  d.  in  the  castle  of 
York  in  1302.  By  a  dau.  of  William  de  Keith  he  had 
three  sons,  i.  James;  ii.  Hugh,  who  had  no  succession; 
III.  Archibald.    The  eldest  son, 

James  Douglas,  of  Douglas,  is  known  in  history  as  "the 
Good  Sir  James,"  and  in  romance  as  the  flower  of  chivalry. 
His  personal  history  is  that  of  Scotland  during  the  time  in 
which  he  lived.  He  was  the  friend  and  brother  in  arms  of 
King  Robert  Bruce;  and  after  that  monarch's  death,  he 
set  out  on  a   crxisade   with  the  intention    of   depositing

*  A  cadet  branch  of  the  house  of  Hamilton  settled  in  the 
seventeenth  centurv  in  Sweden,  viz.,  that  of 

Hamilton,  Count  Hamilton,  and  Hamilton,  Baron  Hamil- 
ton, oj  t'iweden.  This  family  is  one  of  the  most  widely-spread 
and  powerful  branches  of  the  house  of  Hamilton,  and  during  the 
two  centuries  of  its  establishment  in  Sweden,  it  has  risen  to  the 
highest  lionours,  contracted  the  noblest  alliances,  and  acquired 
immense  wealth.  Many  of  its  members  have  been  field-mar- 
shals, knights  of  the  Seraphim,  and  presidents  of  the  Diet, 
while  others  have  held  distinguished  posts  at  court,  and  in  the 
diplomatic  and  military  service.  The  estates  and  lordships 
belonging  to  the  different  branches  of  the  family  extend  o\er 
many  of  the  provinces  of  Sweden,  and,  taken  altogether,  are 
more  important  than  those  of  any  other  family  in  that  kingdom.

Henry  Hardinge  the  3rd  son  of  the  Rev.  H.  Hardinge, 
rector  of  Stanhope,  was  b.  at  Wrotham,  in  Kent,  30  March, 
1785  ;  he  entered  the  British  army  as  an  ensign  in  1791, 
and  rose,  through  a  long  and  brilliant  career,  to  the  very 
summit  of  his  profession.  He  was  actively  engaged  during 
the  whole  of  the  Peninsular  war.  He  afforded  valuable 
assistance  at  Busaco,  the  Douro,  and  Torres  Vedras,  at 
Badajoz,  and  Ciudad  Rodrigo  ;  he  contributed  not  a  little 
to  the  victory  of  Albuera,  and  we  find  him  again  at  Sala- 
manca and  Vittoria,  at  Nivelle,  Nive,  and  Orthes.  He  was 
vrounded  at  Vittoria;  he  lost  his  hand  under  Blucher  at 
Ligny.  After  the  peace  he  filled  many  high  ministerial 
offices  ;  he  was  clerk  of  the  ordnance  in  1823,  and  secretary- 
at-war  and  P.  C.  in  1S2S  ;  he  was  chief  secretary  of  Ireland, 
with  a  seat  in  the  Cabinet,  in  1 830  and  1834;  he  was  again 
secretary-at-war  in  1841  ;  he  became  govenior-general  of 
India  in  1844,  and  during  his  administration  there,  which 
lasted  to  Jan.  1848,  occurred  the  war  against  the  Sikhs, 
which  ho  rendered  for  ever  famous  by  a  glorious  campaign 
on  the  banks  of  the  Sutlej.  For  that  and  his  other  ser- 
vices in  Intlia  he  was  created  by  patent,  dated  2  May,  1846, 
Viscount  Hardinge,  of  Lahore,  and  of  King's  Newton,  co. 
Derby.  In  Feb.  1852,  Viscount  Hardinge  was  appouited 
master-general  of  the  ordnance,  and  on  28  Dec.  of  the  same 
year,  he  was  made  the  general  commander-in-chief;  he 
was  raised  to  the  rank  of  field-marshal  2  Oct.  1855,  and  he 
retired  from  public  life  on  account  of  ill  health  in  1856  ;  he 
d.  24  Sept.  of  that  year,  at  his  seat,  South  Park.  Viscount 
Hardinge  was  colonel  of  the  57th  regiment  of  foot ;  he  bad 
a  cross  and  five  clasps  for  the  Peninsula,  was  a  G.C.B.,  and 
was  knight  of  four  foreign  orders,  Prussian,  Dutch,  Portu-

The  family  of  Lascelles  has  been  of  importance  in  the  co.  York 
since  the  reign  of  Edward  L,  when  Roger  de  Lascelles  was

the  barony  fell  into  abeyance,  and  has  so  continued  to  the  pre- 
sent day.     (See  Burke's  Extinct  and  Dormant  Peerage.)

Captains  Humphrey  and  William  Hartwell*  served 
in  the  Irish  wars  previous  to  1649.  William  was  mayor  of 
the  city  of  Limerick  in  1659.  In  1606  Humphrey  received, 
in  recompense  of  his  military  services,  a  grant  of  877  acres 
of  land  in  the  co.  Limerick,  and  72  acres  in  the  King's  co. 
He  served  twice  the  office  of  mayor  of  the  city  of  Limerick, 
viz.,  in  1676  and  1677,  and  in  1682  was  appointed  a  justice 
of  peace  for  the  co.  Limerick.  He  was  s.  in  his  estates  by 
(his  son,  we  presume)

The  family  of  Rawdon  deduces  its  pedigi-ee  from  Paulinus

considerable  estates  (part  of  which  the  present  marquess 
enjoys).  This  Pauljai,  or  Paulinus,  commanded  a  V^and 
of  archers  in  the  Norman  invading'  army,  and  derived  his 
smname  of  Rawdon  from  the  lands  of  that  denomination 
near  Leeds,  which  constituted  a  portion  of  the  royal  grant.

Hatherley,  Baron  (Sir  William  Page  Wood,  P.O.), 
of  Dowu  Hatherley,  in  the  co.  of  Gloucester,  lord 
high  chancellor,  6.  29  Nov.  1801  ;  m.  5  Jan.  1830, 
Charlotte,  only  dau.  of  Edward  Moor,  Esq.  of  Great 
Bealings,  Suffolk.  His  lordship,  au  eminent  lawyer, 
who  is  the  second  son  of  Sir  Matthew  Wood,  Bart. 
{i'ee  post,  Wood,  Bt.),  was  called  to  the  Bar  in  1827  ;

1868,  and  on  the  9th  of  December  of  the  same  year 
was  raised  to  the  Peerage  as  Lord  Hatherley.

The  2nd  son, 

Sir  Henry  Havelock,  6.  at  Bishopwearmouth,  co. 
Durham,  5  .4.pril,  1795,  one  of  the  most  eminent  soldiers 
of  his  time,  was  educated  at  tlie  Charterhouse,  and  was 
originally  a  student  of  the  Middle  Temple.  He  became 
an  officer  in  the  British  rifle-brigade  in  1815,  and  went 
first  to  India  in  1823.  He  there  took  an  active  part  in 
the  first  Burmese  w.ar.  He  was  a  captain  in  1838  ;  and 
was  at  the  storming  of  Ghuzneo,  and  the  occupation  of 
Cabul :  he  was  also  at  the  forcing  of  the  Cabul  Pass  and  the 
battle  of  Tezeen  ;  and  he  commanded  the  right  column  in 
the  sortie  from  Jellalabad  and  final  victorious  attack  on 
Akbar  the  7th  April,  1842,  for  which  he  was  made  a  major 
and  a  C.B.  After  various  other  services,  he  became  a  lieut.- 
col.  in  1844,  and  went  through  the  Sikh  war,  being  present 
at  the  victories  of  Moodkee,  Ferozeshah,  and  Sobraon.  In 
the  late  Persian  war  he  was  appointed  to  head  the  second 
division,  and  commanded  at  the  battle  of  Mohammerah. 
On  his  return  to  Calcutta,  he  was  sent  as  brig.adier-general 
to  relieve  Cawnpore  and  succour  Lucknow,  then  sorely 
pressed  by  the  savage  and  mutinous  Sepoys.  He  conse- 
quently commenced,  on  the  7th  July,  1857,  that  memorable 
march,  unp.aralleled  in  history,  wherewith  only  1,400  British 
bayonets  and  eight  guns,  united  to  a  small  native  force, 
and  opposed  to  a  countless  mass  of  the  enemy,  when  the 
slightest  reverse  would  have  been  fatal,  he  proceeded  vic- 
toriously througli  a  country  deluged  with  rain,  from  the  7th 
July  to  the  16th  Sept.,  hurling  back  the  foe  in  twelve 
severe  eng.agements.  Joined,  on  the  10th  Sept.,  by  Sir 
James  Outr.am  and  a  few  more  troops,  he  stormed  Luck- 
now, and  effected  his  junction  with  and  relief  of  its  gar-

rison.  Then  pent  up  in  the  Residency  and  its  precincts  at

Edward  Hawke  6  1710  (cmly  son  of  Edward  Hawke, 
Esq.  of  Lincoln's  Inn,  barrister-at-law,  by  Elizabeth,  relict 
of  Col.  Ruthven,  and  dau.  of  Nathaniel  Bladen,  Esq.  ot 
Lincoln's  Inn,  barristcr-at-law,  and  sister  of  Col.  Martin 
Bladen,  M.P.  of  Abery  Hutch,  Essex,  comptroller  of  the 
Mint,  and  a  Lord  of  Trade,  and  also  editor  of  a  splendid 
edition  of  Cctsar's  Cominentaries),  having  attained,  by  a 
Berios  of  gallant  services,  high  reputation  as  a  naval  officer, 
was  promoted  to  be  rear-admiral  of  the  White,  in  July, 
1747;  and  on  the  Hth  Oct.  of  the  same  year,  he  achieved 
a  splendid  victory  over  the  French,  taking  at  the  time 
six  large  ships  of  the  enemy's  line.  In  reward,  he  was 
made  a  knight  of  the  Bath.  In  1755,  Sir  Edward  was 
appointed  vice-admiral  of  the  White.  In  1759  he  got  the 
command  of  a  grand  expedition  destined  to  act  against  the 
French  coast,  and  in  the  November  of  that  year,  having 
hotsted  his  flag  on  hoard  the  "  Roj-al  George,"  sailed  with 
his  whole  fleet  in  pursuit  of  the  French  fleet,  under  Admiral 
de  Conflans,  and  signally  defeated  them  oflf  Bellisle  in  an 
engagement  for  ever  memorable  in  our  naval  annals.  For 
this  he  was  honoured  by  the  thanks  of  parliament,  and 
rewarded  with  a  pension  of  £2000  a  year.  In  1765,  Sir 
Edward  was  promoted  to  the  rank  of  vice-admiral  of  Great 
Britain,  and  appointed  first  lord  of  the  Admiralty  ;  and 
20  May,  1770,  created  Baron  Hawke,  of  Towton,  co.  York.

and  certainly  not  advanced  without  serious  personal  risk),

DESCENT  OF  THE  HERRIES'  BARONY. 

It  is  uncertain  at  what  i^recise  period  the  dignity  of 
Lord  Ilerries  was  created. 

Herbbet  Herries,  of  Terregles,  sat  in  the  parhament  of

seizin  of  Bernewell  and  other  lands,  by  a  charter,  dated

Herries  of  Terregles."  The  baronies  of  Terregles  .and  Kirk- 
gunzean,  with  other  lands,  were  erected  in  his  favour  into

"*  During  the  proceedings  in  the  House  of  Lords  upon  the 
claim  of  Lord  Herries,  it  was  alleged  that  the  original 
barony  of  Herries  was  limited  tn  heirs  male,  and  that  Sir 
John  Maxwell  was  created  Lord  Herries,  and  did  not  enjoy 
the  ancient  barony  in  right  of  his  wife.  It  would,  however, 
appear  that,  according  to  the  then  state  of  the  law.  Sir  John 
Maxwell  could  not  have  borne  the  title  of  Herries  if  the  heir 
male  had  been  entitled  to  a  dignity  of  the  same  name.  In 
the  proceedings  in  council  regarding  the  precedency  of  the 
Earl  of  Nithsdale,  on  the  11th  Jan.  1621,  it  was  laid  down 
as  undoubted  law  that  two  peers  could  not  bear  the  same 
title,  and  the  lords  commissioners  for  exercising  the  ofiBce 
of  earl  marshaj,  in  the  case  of  Sarsfield,  created  Viscount 
Kingsale  in  Ireland,  came  to  the  same  decision  on  the  19th 
April,  1627,  and  their  report  was  confirmed  by  the  King. 
This  point  was  not  adverted  to  in  the  judgments  pronounced 
in  the  Herries's  case,  but  it  appears  to  aflford  an  additional 
reason  in  favour  of  the  decision.

Sir  Edward  Seymour,  4th  baronet.  This  gentleman  made  a 
distinguished  figure,  both  in  court  and  parliament,  during  four 
successive  reigns.  He  served  constantly  after  his  first  election 
to  the  time  of  his  death,  and  few  had  more  weight  in  the 
House  of  Commons.  In  i667,  lie  promoted  the  impeachment 
of  Lord  Clarendon ;  was  the  first  that  moved  it,  and  carried  it 
up  to  the  House  of  Lords.  In  Feb.  1672-3,  he  was  unanimously 
chosen  speaker  of  the  Long  Parliament,  on  the  resignation  of 
Sir  Job  Charleton.  In  the  April  following  he  was  sworn  of  the 
privy  coimcil,  and  soon  after  made  treasurer  of  the  navy. 
Burnet  describes  Sir  Edward  as  "the  ablest  man  of  his  party, 
the  first  speaker  of  the  House  of  Commons  that  was  not  bred 
to  the  law ;  a  graceful  man,  bold  and  qiuck,  and  of  high  birth, 
being  the  elder  branch  of  the  Seymour  family."  He  in.  1st, 
Margaret,  dau.  and  co-heir  of  Sir  William  Wall,  Knt.,  an  alder- 
man of  the  city  of  London,  l)y  whom  he  had  two  sons,  and  was 
s.  in  the  baronetcy  by  the  elder  Edward,  whose  eldest  son, 
Edward,  inherited  the  Dukedom  of  Somerset.  Sir  Edward  m.

Eiurage 

The  Heskeths  (like  many  other  great  northern  families) 
owed  their  original  elevation  to  martial  achievement;  and 
they  have  flourished  in  the  coimty  palatine  of  Lancaster  for 
more  than  seven  centuries  up  to  the  present  period,  being 
now  in  the  actual  enjoyment  of  the  greater  part  of  the  landed 
property  acquired  at  the  commencement  of  that  remote  era. 

The   direct  or  authenticated    foimder  of   the    family   was 
Richard  de  Heskayth,  Lord  of  Heskayth,  Ruffourd,  &c.,  in 
the   12th    century,   whose    son,   William  de   Heskayth,   m. 
Anabilla,  dau.  of  Sir  Richard  de  Stafford;  his  grandson,

Sir  AMUiam  A'Court  obtained  the  barony,  by  patent  of  creation, 
dated  23  Jan.  1828.  Lord  Heytesbury,  was  a  privy-councillor 
and  G.C.B.,  and  was  a  distinguished  diplomatist  and  was 
British  envoy  and  ambassador  in  various  countries  ;  his  last 
diplomatic  duties  were  as  ambassador-extraordinary  and  pleni- 
potentiary at  the  court  of  St.  Petersburg,  where  he  remained 
from  1828  to  1832.  He  was  nominated  Governor-General  of 
India  in  1834,  but  the  ministry  broke  up  before  he  went  out. 
He  was  Lord-Lieutenant  of  Ireland  from  1844  to  1846.  He  d. 
31  May,  1860.

Sir  James,  shortly  after  he  was  called  to  the  bar, 
proceeded  to  Calcutta,  where  he  practised  with  great 
success,  and  latterly  held  the  principal  office  in  the 
Supreme  Com't.  He  returned  to  England  in  June, 
1833.  In  1834,  he  was  elected  M.P.  for  the  borough 
of  Beverly,  which  place  he  continued  to  represont 
until  1847,  when  he  was  returned  for  Honiton.  In 
Sept.  1839,  he  became  a  director  of  the  East  India 
Company,  and  was  twice  chairman.  He  is  now  a 
Member  of  the  Indian  Council. 

Sin  James-Weir  Hogg  descends  from  a  branch  of  the  ancient 
Scottish  family  of  that  name :  his  great-grandfather,  William, 
vho  m.  Abigail  Hamilton,  having  emigrated  from  Scotland 
towards  the  latter  end  of  the  seventeenth  century,  and  settled 
in  the  north  of  Ireland.  They  had  issue  (with  one  dau.), 
three  sons,  1  William;  2  Edward;  3  James  of  Lisburn. 
Edward,  the  2nd  son,  ra.  Rose,  dau.  of  John  O'Neill,  Esq. 
of  Largy,  a  branch  of  the  O'Neill  family,  and  had  issue,  two 
sons  and  three  dans.  The  eldest  son,  William,  rn.  Mary,  dau. 
of  James  Dickey,  Esq.  of  Dunmore,  co.  Antrim,  and  had  issue,

in  1846.

The  family  of  Hood  possessed  considerable  landed  property  in

The  Kev.  Samcei,  Hood,  vicar  of  Eutley,  Somersetshire,  and 
afterwards  of  Thomcombe,  co.  Devon  (2nd  son  of  Alexander 
Hood,  Esq.  of  Mosterton,  co.  Dorset),  lu.  Mary,  dau.  of  Richard 
Hoskyns,  Esq.  of  Beaminster,  co.  Dorset,  and  had  issue,  Samuel, 
of  whom  presently;  Alexander,  admiral  of  the  Red,  created 
Lord  Beidport  (see  Bridport,  Viscount)  ;  and  Ehzabeth,  m. 
to  Alderman  Edward  Walker,  of  Exeter.     The  elder  son. 

Admiral  Sir  Samuel  Hood,  K.B.,  a  famous  British  seaman, 
was  b.  at  Thorncombc,  in  1724,  and  entered  the  royal  navy  iu 
1740.  His  first  exploit  was  in  1759,  when  he  took  the  "Bellona." 
Lord  Anson  presented  the  victor  to  George  II.,  who  gave  him 
the  command  of  the  "Africa."  Hood,  early  in  1782,  made  the 
first  attack  on  the  Coimt  de  Grasse's  fleet,  and  he  commanded 
the  van  division  under  Sir  George  Rodney,  on  the  12th  Aug. 
1782,  when  the  Count  de  Grasse  and  his  fleet  were  so  memorably 
defeated.  In  1793,  Hood,  commanding  the  Mediterranean  fleet, 
signalized  himself  by  his  victorious  attack  on  Toulon,  and  his 
capture  of  the  island  of  Corsica.  He  was  made  governor  of 
Greenwich  Hospital  in  1796,  and  in  1799  became  admiral  of  the 
Red  and  a  G.C.B.  He  had  long  previously  been  created  a  Baro- 
net, as  a  reward  for  achievements,  19  May,  1778,  and  elevated 
to  the  peerage  of  Ireland,  12  Sept.  1782,  as  Earon  Hood,  oj 
Catheriixjton.  His  lordship  was  enrolled  among  the  peers  of 
Great  Britain  1  June,  1796,  by  the  title  of  Viscount  Hood,  of 
Whitley,  to.  Waricick:  He  ni  in  1749,  Susamiah,  dau.  of 
Eilward  Linzee,  Esq.  of  Portsmouth  (which  lady  was  elevated

The  founder  of  the  family  of  Hope  of  Craighall  appears  to 
have  been 

John  de  Hope,  who  is  said  to  have  come  from  France  in  the 
train  of  Magdalene,  Queen  of  King  James  1.  He  m.  Elizabeth 
Cummin,  and  left  a  son, 

Edward  Hope,  whose  son, 

Henry  Hope,  a  very  eminent  merchant,  vi.  Jaqueline  de 
Tott,  a  French  lady,  and  left  two  sons,  Thomas,  of  whom 
presently;  and  Henry,  ancestor  of  the  Hopes  of  Amsterdam, 
now  represented  by  Adrian-Elias  Hope,  Esq.,  nephew  of 
Alexander-J.-B.  Beresford-Hope,  Esq.  of  Bedgebury  Park, 
Kent,  M.P.  for  the  University  of  Cambridge. 

I.  Sir  Thomas  Hope,  Knt.  (the  elder  son)  of  Craighall,  co. 
Fife,  having  been  bred  to  the  bar,  attained  great  eminence  in 
his  profession.  In  1626,  he  was  appointed  joint  lord-advocate 
along  with  Sir  Wilham  Oliphant ;  and  his  colleague  dying  in 
two  years  afterwards,  he  enjoyed  the  office  alone.  Sir  Thomas 
obtained  many  substantial  favours  from  the  crown,  and  was 
created  a.  Baronet  of  Nova  Scotia,  19  Feb.  1628.  In  1643,  he 
was  appointed  commissioner  to  the  General  Assembly  of  the 
church  of  Scotland,  a  dignity  which,  it  is  said  no  commoner  has 
since  enjoyed.  "  He  took  the  place  proudly  upon  him,  for 
the  honours  (crown,  sword,  and  sceptre)  were  daily  carried 
when  he  went  out  and  into  this  assembly  before  him;  and 
at  preaching  he  sat  in  the  King's  loft.  Sir  Thomas  m.  Eliza- 
beth, dau.  of  John  Binning,  of  Wal'yford,  by  whom  he  had 
fourteen  children ;  three  of  whom  were  upon  the  bench  when 
he  pleaded  as  lord-advocate  before  them ;  and  to  this  circum- 
stance ti'adition  assigns  the  privilege,  which  that  officer  of  the 
crown  enjoys,  of  pleading  covered  in  the  supreme  court  of 
judicature,  it  being  deemed  indecorous  that  a  father  should 
stand  uncovered  before  his  sons.  He  d.  in  Nov.  1646,  and  was 
s.  by  his  eldest  son, 

II.  Sir  John,  who  was  appointed  a  lord  of  session  in

I.  EstellaMary, 

The  surname  of  Hope  is  one  of  great  antiquity  in  Scotland ; 
and  the  ancestor  of  the  present  family, 

John  de  Hope,  is  said  to  have  come  from  France  in  the 
retinue  of  Magdalene,  Queen  of  James  V.,  in  1537,  and  settling 
in  Scotland,  left  a  son, 

Edward  Hope,  who  was  one  of  the  most  considerable  inhabit- 
ants of  Edinburgh  in  the  reign  of  Queen  Mart,  and  being  a 
great  promoter  of  the  Reformation,  was  chosen  one  of  the  com- 
missioners for  the  metropolis  to  the  parUanient  in  1560.  He 
left  a  son, 

Henry  Hope,  a  very  eminent  merchant,  who  m.  a  French 
lady,  Jaqueline  de  Tott,  and  had  two  sons,  Tliomas  and  Henry.* 
The  elder, 

Thomas  Hope,  being  bred  to  the  Scottish  bar,  first  attained 
eminence,  in  1606,  by  his  defence  of  the  six  ministers  (clergy- 
men) tried  for  high  treason,  for  denying  that  the  king  possessed 
authority  in  matters  ecclesiastical ;  and  acquired,  eventually, 
the  largest  fortime  ever  accumulated  by  a  member  of  the  legal 
profession  in  Scotland.  He  was  subsequently  appointed  king's 
advocate,  and  created  a  Baronet  of  Nova  Scotia  11  Feb.  162S. 
(See  lineage  of  Sir  Archibald  Hope,  Bart.,  the  chief  of  the 
house  of  Hope,  for  a  further  account  of  this  learned  person.)  Sir 
Thomas  left  a  very  large  family,  from  the  eldest  son  of  which 
descend  the  Hopes  of  Craighall.    The  6th  son, 

Sir  John  Hope,  of  Hopetoun,  a  member  of  the  Scottish  bar, 
marrying  Anne,  only  dau.  and  heir  of  Robert  Foules,  of  Lead-  ' 
hills,  CO.  Lanark,  acquired  the  valuable  mines  there ;  and  apply- 
ing himself  to  nimeralogy,  brought  the  art  of  mining  to  the 
highest  perfection  ever  before  known  in  Scotland.  Sir  John 
was  appointed  in  1641  governor  of  the  Blint,  and  constituted  a 
lord  of  Session  in  1649.  He  m.  2ndly,  Lady  Mary  Keith,  eldest 
dau.  and  one  of  the  co-heirs  of  William,  7th  Earl  Marischal.  By 
the  1st  marriage  he  had  several  children;  by  tlie  2nd,  an  only 
surviving  son,  William,  of  Balcoraie,  who  was  created  a  Baronet 
in  1698  (having  had  previously  the  honour  of  knighthood),  a 
dignity  that  expired  with  his  grandson,  Sir  William  Hope,  3rd 
baronet,  a  captain  in  the  East  India  Company's  service,  who  was 
killed  in  Bengal  in  1763.  Sir  John  d.  in  1661,  and  was  s.  by  his 
eldest  surviving  son, 

John  Hope,  Esq.  of  Hopetoun,  who  took  up  his  residence  at 
the  castle  of  Niddry,  the  Barony  of  which  he  pm-chased  from

(1678)  the  Barony  of  Abercoi-n,  with  the  office  of  heritable  sheriff 
of  the  CO.  of  Linlithgow,  from  Sir  AValter  Seton.  Mr.  Hope 
represented  the  shire  of  Linlithgow  in  parliament  in  1684.  He 
■III.  Slargaret,  eldest  dau.  of  John,  4tli  Earl  of  Haddington,  by

Sir  John  de  Trehouse,  for  the  good  services  he  had  rendered 
to  the  Conqueror  at  the  battle  of  flastings,  obtained  a  grant  of 
the  castle  and  manors  of  Colleyweston,  in  Northamptonshire, 
and  of  Hotham,  in  Yorkshire.     His  great-great-grandson, 

Peter  de  Trehouse,  assumed  the  surname  of  Hotham,  from 
the  place  of  his  residence,  which  has  ever  since  been  that  of  his 
descendants.  This  Peter  was  living  in  1188,  and  was  great- 
grandfather of 

John  de  Hotham,  bishop  of  Ely,  treasurer  of  the  Exchequer ; 
and  Lord  High  Chancellor  of  England.  The  elder  brother 
of  this  distinguished  prelate,

to  1863,  is  author  of  The  Memorial  of  a  tour  in

The  family  of  Milnes,  formerly  seated  in  the  romantic  village 
of  Ashford-in-the-Water,  were  considerable  proprietors  of 
estates  in  the  county  of  Derby,  in  the  reign  of  Queen 
Elizabeth.  William  Milnes,  residing  at  Ashford,  within  the 
hundred  of  High  Peak,  at  that  period  had  a  numerous  family ; 
from  his  eldest  son,  Richard,  descended  the  Milnes  of  Dunstone 
Hall,  and  Aldecar  Park,  co.  Derby,  represented  by  Philip  Gell, 
Esq.,  of  Hopton,  in  that  shire.

The  original  surname  of  this  very  ancient  family  was 
Tristram,  and  it  is  said  to  have  been  exchanged  for  the 
present  one  of  St.  Lawrence,  under  the  following  circum- 
stances : — A  member  of  the  house  of  Tristram,  having  the 
command  of  an  ai-my  against  the  invaders  of  his  native 
soil,  attacked  and  totally  routed  them  on  St.  Laurence's 
day,  near  Clontarf,  and  assumed,  in  consequence  of  a  vow 
made  previously  to  the  battle,  the  name  of  the  saint,  which 
his  descendants  have  ever  since  borne.  The  sword  with 
which  this  warrior  fought  and  vanquished  still  hangs  in 
the  hall  of  Howth,  where  the  family  has  resided  since  its 
first  arrival  in  Ireland,  a  period  of  six  centuries  at  least. 

Sir  Amoricus  Tristram,  the  brother-in-law  and  com- 
panion in  arms  of  Sir  John  Courcy,  having  in  the  year 
1177,  effected  a  landing  at  Howth,  defeated  the  Irish  in 
a  pitched  battle  at  the  bridge  of  Ivora,  and  obtained  the 
lands  and  barony  (by  tenure)  of  Howth,  as  a  reward  for 
his  distinguished  valour  during  the  conflict.  After  this 
successful  commencement,  Sir  Amoricus,  with  his  brothcr-

in-law.  Sir  John  Courcy,  reduced  the  whole  proviuc  of 
Ulster  ;  but  in  1189,  when  Sir  John  was  removed  from  tba 
government  of  Ireland  by  Richard  I.,  Sir  Amoricus,  who 
was  then  in  Counaught,  being  attacked  by  O'Connor,  the 
kins'  of  that  province,  and  overwhelmed  by  numbers,  him- 
self and  his  whole  party,  consisting  of  thirty  knights  and

Although  there  are  numerous  histories  of  this  illustrious 
family  extant,  yet  the  historians  do  not  coincide  as  to  its 
origin  and  first  settlement  in  Great  Britain.  Some  bring 
the  Gordons  from  Greece  to  Gaul,  and  thence  into  Scot- 
land, at  least  a  thousand  years  ago  ;  while  others  convey 
thern  Irom  Spain,  Flanders,  &c.  The  more  probable  con- 
ecture,  however,  is,  that  some  of  these  Gordons  came  into 
England  with  William,  Duke  of  Normandy,  and  into 
Scotland  with  Khig  Malcolm  Canmore.  Indeed,  there  is 
a  tradition  in  North  Britain  that  the  first  of  the  name  who 
609 


crossed  the  Tweed  was  a  valiant  kniglit,  a  favourite  of 
Malcolm's,  who,  having  killed  a  wild  boar  that  greatly 
infested  the  borders,  obtained  a  grant  of  lands  in  the  Merse, 
or  Berwickshire,  which  he  called  Gordon,  after  his  own 
Rurn.ame,  .and  setthng  there,  assumed  the  boar's  head  for 
his  armorial  bearing,  in  commemoration  of  the  exploit.  Be 
the  early  origin,  however,  what  it  may  (and  there  is  no 
doubt  that  it  was  distinguished),  the  noble  family  of  which 
we  are  about  to  treat  deduces  its  direct  maternal  descent  from 
Sir  John  de  Gordon,  Kut.,  who  obtained  in  the  28th 
year  of  David  II.  a  charter,  dated  20th  March,  1357-8,  con- 
firming the  donation  which  Robert  I.  had  made  to  his 
gi-andfather.  Sir  Adam  de  Gordon,  of  the  lands  of  Strath- 
bogie,  and  was  s.  by  his  son. 

Sir  John  de  Gordon,  who  obtained  a  confinnatory  char- 
ter of  the  same  lands  from  Robert  II.,  dated  16  Jmie,  1376. 
In  the  next  year,  the  Earl  of  March  having  attacked  and 
bunied  the  town  of  Roxburgh,  the  English  borderers 
retaliated  on  the  lands  of  Sir  John  Gordon,  who,  passing 
the  border,  encountered  Sir  John  de  Lilburn,  and  after 
a  desperate  affray,  defeated  him  at  Carbarn.  Sir  John 
Gordon  had  also  a  chief  hand  in  the  defeat  and  capture 
of  Sir  Thomas  de  Musgrave,  governor  of  Berwick,  in  1378, 
after  a  severe  conflict.  Sir  John  fell,  eventually,  at  the 
battle  of  Otterburn,  in  Aug.  13SS,  leaving  a  son, 

Sir  Adam  Gordon,  Knt.  of  Huntley,  who  was  slain  in 
1402,  at  the  battle  of  Homildon,  and  wass.  in  his  estates  by 
his  only  dau.  (by  his  wife,  Elizabeth,  dau.  of  Sir  William 
de  Keith,  great-marischal  of  Scotland), 

Elizabeth  Gordon,  who  m.  Alexander  Seton  (2nd  son 
of  Sir  William  Seton,  of  Seton),  and  obtained,  in  conjunc- 
tion with  her  husband,  from  Robert  Duke  of  Albany,  a 
charter,  dated  20  July,  1408,  to  their  joint  heirs,  and  in 
default,  to  the  heirs  of  the  said  Ehzabeth,  of  the  baronies  of 
Gourdoun  and  Hun  tie,  and  thenceforward  the  said  Alexander 
was  styled  Lord  of  Gordon  and  Huntly.  Of  this  marriage

*  Mr.  O'Donoughue,  in  his  able  Historical  Memoir  of  the 
O'Br'u'int,  tlms  introduces  the  subject  in  his  opening  chapter: — 
"  It  has  been  the  fortune  of  the  race  of  O'Brien  to  form  an 
exception  to  those  instances  in  which  families  once  occupying  a 
regal  station  have,  after  their  declension,  sunk  into  obscurity. 
A  reader  of  Irish  history  will  find  the  names  of  the  O'Briens  so 
often  mentioned  in  the  pages  of  its  annals,  that  he  cannot 
hesitate  to  conclude,  that  whether  as  Idngs  of  the  whole  island, 
or  later,  of  the  southern  half,  or  again,  after  the  arrival  of  the 
Annlo-Normans,  ruling  their  restricted  principality  of  Thomond 
witli  independent  authority,  as  a.sserted  by  Sir  John  Davis  of 
them  and  others,  the  descendants  of  Brian  Eoriomhehave  written 
their  names  in  indelible  characters  in  the  history  of  their 
country.  In  no  part  of  the  kingdom  can  so  many  memorials  of 
the  energy  and  power  of  the  native  princes  be  found  at  this  day, 
as  in  the  territory  of  Thomond,  before  it  was  restricted  to  the 
present  county  of  Clare.  The  erection  of  the  monasteries  of 
Manister-nenagh,  Holycross,  the  cathedral  of  Limerick,  the 
abbey  of  Ennis,  and  many  others,  too  numerous  to  mention, 
devoted  to  the  promotion  of  learning  and  piety,  exhibit  to  the 
modern  traveller  proofs  of  the  genius  and  vigour  of  the  de- 
scendants of  Brian.  And  notwithstanding  the  various  changes 
wliicli  the  state  of  society  has  for  so  many  ages  undergone,  and 
the  downfall  of  so  many  of  the  ancient  families  of  the  country, 
we  find  the  descendants  of  Brian  of  the  Tributes  still  holding 
their  own,  while  we  may  search  in  vain  even  amongst  some 
of  the  ro)-al  houses  on  the  continent  of  Eurojie  for  a  line  of 
greater  antiquity,  or  one  whose  descent  is  more  clearly  traced 
thi'nugh  the  historic  records  of  their  country,  than  that  of 
which  this  work  purports  to  record  the  history."

This  gentleman,  grandson  of  John  James,  Esq.  of

honour  of  knighthood  from  the  Marquis  Wellesley,

a  baronet,  1 9  March,  1 823.  Sir  John  filled  the  civic 
chair  again  in  18i0-l. 

This  family  of  James  came  originally  from  Somersetshire. 
Thomas  James  (who,  according  to  family  tradition,  was  son  of 
a  Captain  Thomas  James,  who  undertook,  by  command  of  King 
Charles  I.,  a  voyage  to  discover  the  north-west  passage),  sold 
his  possessions  in  Somersetshire,  went  into  Ireland  as  an  officer 
in  Cromwell's  army,  and,  settling  in  King's  County,  d.  in  1694.

I.  John  Kennatvat,  Esq.  (descended  from  William  Kenna-

Kennaway  returned  to  Bengal;  was  apiwinted,  in  1786,  aide-de- 
camp to  Marquess  Cornwallis,  and  sent  by  his  lordship,  in  1788,

the  cession  of  the  maritime  province  of  Guntoor,  which,  con- 
trary to  treaty,  had  for  many  years  remained  in  his  highness's 
possession.  Captain  Kennaway  was  in  this  embassy  eminently 
successful,  and  soon  after  concluded  with  the  Nizam  a  treaty  of 
alliance  against  Tippoo  Sultan,  for  which  services  his  majesty 
was  pleased  to  create  him  a  Baronet,  25  Feb.  1791,  and  the  Court 
of  Directors  of  the  East  India  Company  to  take  out  his  patent  at 
the  public  expense.  In  1792,  he  was  appointed,  by  the  Marquess 
Cornwallis,  commissioner  to  adjust,  in  concert  with  agents  of 
the  Nizam  and  the  Mahrattas,  a  preliminary  and  definitive  treaty 
of  peace  with  the  commissioners  of  Tippoo  Stdtan,  by  which  the 
latter  prince  ceded  half  his  dominions,  and  agi-eed  to  the  pay- 
ment of  three  millions  three  hundred  thousand  pounds  to  the 
three  aUied  powers,  for  the  expenses  of  the  war,  and  to  deliver 
up  two  of  his  sons  as  hostages  for  the  due  performance  of  the 
ti-eaty.  He  m.  in  1797,  Charlotte,  2nd  dau.  and  co-heir  of

Lloyd  Kenyon,  Esq.,  the  2nd  son,  b.  at  Gredington,  in  Flint- 
shire, 5  Oct.  1732,  having  received  the  elementary  part  of  his 
education  at  Ruthin,  in  Denbighshire,  was  articled,  at  an  early 
age,  to  Mr.  W.-J.  Tomkinson,  an  eminent  attorney  at  Nantwich, 
in  Cheshire.  At  the  expiration  of  his  articles,  Mr.  Kenyon 
determined  to  pursue  the  higher  walk  of  the  profession,  and 
became,  accordingly,  in  Trinity  Term,  1754,  a  member  of  the 
society  of  Lincoln's  Inn,  by  which  he  was  called  to  the  bar  in 
Hilary  Term,  1761.  His  subsequent  success  was  slow,  but  not 
the  less  certain;  and  about  the  year  1773,  we  find  him  enjoying 
very  considerable  practice  in  the  court  of  Chancery ;  his  reputa- 
tion was,  however,  firmly  established  in  1 780,  by  his  able  defence, 
in  conjunction  with  Mr.  (afterwards  Lord)  Erskine,  of  Lord 
George  Gordon.  In  1782,  soon  after  the  accession  of  the  Rock- 
ingham administration,  Mr.  Kenyon  was  appointed  attorney- 
general,  without  serving  the  intermediate  office  of  solicitor- 
general,  and  was  constituted,  at  the  same  time,  chief-justice  of 
Chester.  In  March,  1784,  he  was  appointed  Master  of  the  Rolls, 
and  created  a  Baronet.  Upon  the  Rolls'  bench  Sir  Lloyd  con- 
tinued until  the  end  of  May,  1788,  when  he  succeeded  Lord 
Mansfield  as  lord-chief-justice  of  the  court  of  King's  Bench,  and 
was  elevated  to  the  peerage  (9  June,  1788)  in  the  dignity  of 
Lord  Kenyon,  Baron  of  Gredington,  co.  Flint.  His  lordship  /,;.

The  Right  Rev.  Edv/ard  King,  a  native  of  Huntingdonshire, 
and  D.D.  in  the  university  of  Dublin,  was  consecrated  Bishop  of 
Elphinin  1611.  He  had  a  family  of  fifteen  children,  and  yet, 
having  found  his  bishopric  the  poorest,  he  left  it  the  richest  in 
all  Ireland.  He  recovered  its  ancient  possessions,  which  had 
been  alienated  by  his  predecessor ;  and  that  income  which  he 
found  reduced  to  200  marks,  he  left  worth  1500^.  a-year.  Having 
thus  reclaimed  the  possessions  of  his  bishopric,  and  permanently 
augmented  its  revenues,  his  lordship  volmitarily  resigned  the 
". quarta  pars  episcopalis"  which  his  predecessors  had  enjoyed. 
For  these  and  other  praiseworthy  actions,  the  lord-lieutenant 
(Strafford)  mentions  him  with  gi-eat  honour  in  a  letter  to  Arch- 
bishop Laud,  and  alluding  to  his  patronymic,  calls  him  "  a  truly 
royal  bishop."  His  lordship  was  twice  married.  His  1st  wife 
was  Anne,  dau.  of  -^  Coxsed,  Esq.,  by  whom  he  had  a  large 
family.  His  lonlship  m.  2ndly,  Grace,  dau.  of  Nathaniel  Samp 
son,  Esq.  of  Leicestershire,  whose  father,  Thomas  Sampson,  was 
a  distinguished  preacher,  prebendary  of  St.  Paul's,  &c.,  and 
whose  mother  was  niece  of  Bishop  Latimer.  By  his  2nd  wife, 
who  survived  him,  his  lordship  had  issue.  His  lordship  adorned 
the  bishopric  of  Elphin  for  twenty-seven  years  and  three 
months,  and  dying  8  March,  1638,  aged  63,  was  buried  in  his 
own  cathedral,  where  his  monument  still  remains.  His  will 
was  nuncupative,  was  attested  by  the  chancellor  of  his  diocese, 
and  proved  on  the  16th  of  March,  1639.     His  eldest  son, 

James  King,  of  Charlestown,  co.  Roscommon,  b.  6  Feb.  1610, 
and  was  probaljly,  therefore,  a  native  of  England,  like  his 
father,  for  the  latter  did  not  receive  the  bishopric  of  Elphin  till 
1611.  He  held  the  rank  of  captain  in  the  army,  and  filled  the 
ofBce  of  high-sheriff  of  Roscommon  in  1673.  He  m.  before  the 
year  1634,  Judith,  dau.  of -^  Rawson,  Esq.  of  Dublin,  by  whom 
he  had  issue,  Edward,  b.  17  July,  1640,  disinherited  by  his 
father;  four  sons  who  d.s.p.;  and  Gilbert,  of  whom  here- 
after, as  heir  of  his  father.  Of  the  daus.,  Anne,  m.  Jasper 
Maguire,  Esq. ;  EUzabeth,  m.  in  March,  1662,  to  Captain  Charles

KINGSALE. 


KiNGSALE,  Lord  (Michael -Com-ad  de  Courcy), 
Baron  Courcy  of  Courcy,  and  Baron  of  Ringrone,  iu 
the  peerage  of  Ireland;  b.  21  Dec.  1828;  s.  his 
brother  as  30th  and  premier  baron,  15  June,  1865. 
Lord  Kingsale  enjoys  the  hereditary  privilege 
(granted  by  King  John  to  De  Courcy,  Earl  of 
Ulster)  of  wearing  his  hat  in  the  royal  presence. 

Et'itcagr. 

The  family  of  Courcy  claims  alliance  withmostof  the  royal 
houses  of  Europe,  paternally  through  the  Dukes  of  Lorrains, 
and  maternally  through  the  ducal  house  of  Normandy,

dau.  of  Henry  I.,  Emperor  of  Germany,  by  whom  he  had 
two  sons,  Lotharius,  who  5.  to  the  French  throne  (and  with 
whose  son,  Louis  V.  the  race  of  monarchs  descended  from 
Charlemagne  ceased)  ;  and

Robert  de  Courcy,  was  Lord  of  Courcy,  in  Normandy, 
in  1006,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son, 

Richard  de  Courcy,  who  accompanied  his  sovereign,

Robert,  Baron  of  Stoke  Courey,  who  temp.  King

This  nobleman  d.  in  1171,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son. 

Sib  John  Codrcy,  who  having  distinguished  himself 
temp.  Henry  II.  in  that  monarch's  wars  in  England  and 
Gascony,  was  sent  into  Ireland,  in  the  year  lli'Y,  as  an 
assistant  to  William  Fitz-Adelm,  in  the  government  of  that 
kingdom.  Sir  John  having  prevailed  upon  some  of  the 
veteran  soldiery  to  accompany  him,  invaded  the  province 
of  Ulster  with  twenty- two  knights,  fifty  esquires,  and  about 
three  hundred  foot-soldiers,  and  after  many  hard  fought 
battles,  succeeded  in  attaching  that  quarter  of  the  kingdom 
to  the  English  monarchy,  for  which  important  service 
he  was  created,  in  1181  (being  the  first  Englishman  dig- 
nified with  an  Irish  title  of  honour),  Earl  of  Ulster. 
Ilis  lordship  continued  in  high  favour  during  tho  remainder 
of  the  reign  of  his  royal  master,  and  performed  prodigies 
of  valour  in  Ireland  ;  but  upon  the  accession  of  King  John, 
his  splendour  and  rank  having  excited  the  envy  of  Hugh 
de  Lacie,  appointed  governor  of  Ireland  by  that  monarch, 
the  Earl  of  Ulster  was  treacherously  seized  while  perform- 
ing penance,  unarmed  and  barefooted,  in  the  churchyard 
of  Downpatrick,  on  Good  Friday,  anno  1203,  and  sent  over 
to  England,  where  the  king  condemned  him  to  perpetual 
impi'isonment  in  the  Tower,  and  granted  to  Laeie,  all  the 
earl's  possessions  in  Ireland.  After  his  lordship  had  been 
in  confinement  about  a  yeai",  a  dispute  happening  to  arise 
between  King  John  and  Philip-Augustus  of  France  con- 
cerning the  Duchy  of  Normandy,  the  decision  of  which 
being  referred  to  single  combat.  King  John,  more  hasty 
than  advised,  appointed  the  day,  against  which  the  King 
of  France  provided  his  champion  ;  but  the  King  of  England, 
less  fortunate,  could  find  no  one  of  his  subjects  willing  to 
take  up  the  gauntlet,  until  his  captive  in  the  Tower,  the 
gallant  Earl  of  Ulstei-,  was  prevailed  upon  to  accept  the 
challenge.  But  when  everything  was  prepared  for  the 
contest,  and  the  champions  had  entered  the  lists,  in  pre- 
sence of  the  monarchs  of  England,  France,  and  Spain,  the 
opponent  of  the  earl  seized  with  a  sudden  panic,  put  spurs 
to  his  horse,  and  fled  the  arena;  whereupon  the  victory 
was  adjudged  by  acclamation  to  the  champion  of  England. 
The  French  king  being  informed,  however,  of  the  earl's 
powerful  strength,  and  wishing  to  witness  some  exhibition 
of  it,  his  lordship,  at  the  desire  of  King  John,  cleft  a 
massive  helmet  in  twain  at  a  single  blow.  The  king  was 
so  well  satisfied  with  this  signal  performance,  that  he  not 
only  restored  the  eai-1  to  hi.s  estates  and  effects,  but  desired 
him  to  ask  anything  within  his  gift,  and  it  should  be 
granted.  To  which  the  earl  replied,  that  having  estates 
and  titles  enough,  he  desired  that  his  successors  might 
have  the  privilege  (their  first  obeisance  being  paid)  to 
remain  covered  in  the  presence  of  his  majesty,  and  all 
future  kings  of  England ;  which  request  was  immediately 
conceded.  This  heroic  warrior  and  able  statesman  d.  in 
France,  about  the  year  1210,  and  was  s.  by  his  only  son.

Sir  Thomas  Larcom  was  created  a  Baronet  in  Dec. 
1868,  on  his  retirement  from  the  office  of  under 
.seci'etary  of  state  for  Ireland,  which  he  had  filled 
for  many  years  with  great  aliility  and  great  public 
advantage.  He  had  previously,  in  1828,  been  given 
the  charge  of  the  ordnance  survey  office,  Dublin, 
and  had  been  appointed,  in  181(3,  a  commissioner  of 
public  works  in  Ireland.  He  entered  the  army,  as 
2nd  lieut.  roy.  engineer.s,  in  1820,  and  attained  the 
rank  of  maj.-gen.  in  1858.  In  1860,  he  was  created 
a  kuight  commander  of  the  Order  of  the  Bath,  and, 
in  1868,  sworn  of  her  Majesty's  privy  council  in 
Ireland. 

Tills  family  was  formerly  settled  at  Whippingham,  in  the  Isle 
of  AVight. 

Thomas  Larcom,  "the  first  who  left  the  island,"  was  born  at 
Whippingham  in  1708,  and  settled  in  the  parish  of  Alverstoke, 
Hants.     He  m.  in  1731;  d.  1784,  and  left  an  only  son, 

Thomas  Larcom,  b.  15  Dec.  1732.  He  m.  Charity  Bantor, 
and  d.  12  Feb.  1768,  leaving  two  sons,  Thomas  and  Joseph,  and 
a  dau.,  Anne,  who  d.  unm.  Both  the  sons  entered  the  royal 
navy  ;  Thomas  served  as  first  lieutenant  to  Lord  Howe  in  the 
action  of  the  1st  June,  1798,  and  received  his  commission  as 
commander,  on  the  quarter-deck  of  the  "  Queen  Charlotte."  on 
the  morning  of  the  victory.  lie  was  afterwards  flag  captain  to 
Admiral  Sir  Thomas  Graves,  in  Newfoundland,  and  com- 
manded a  hne-of-battle  ship  (the  "Russell,"  of  74  guns)  in 
Lord  Bridport's  action  in  the  West  Indies.    He  d.  vnin.  in  1804. 

Joseph  Larcom  (the  second  son),  also  in  the  royal  navy,  was 
likewise  promoted  after  the  action  of  the  1st  June,  1798.  He 
was  distinguished  in  the  suppression  of  the  mutiny  at  the 
Nore ;  and,  becoming  post-captain,  was  appointed  to  the

The  surname  of  Latjdee,  anciently  De  Latedre,  is  of 
Norman  origin,  and  the  Scottish  historians  mention  the 
first  De  Lavedre  as  one  of  those  Anglo-Norman  barons  wbo 
accompanied  Malcolm  Canmore  into  Scotland  in  1056,  to 
assist  that  prince  in  recovering  his  kingdom  from  the 
usurper  Macbeth  ;  for  this  important  service  De  Lavedre 
obtained  from  the  king  grants  of  lands,  particularly  in 
Berwickshire,  to  which  he  gave  his  own  name,  as  other 
knights,  similarly  recompensed,  did,  in  obedience,  accord- 
ing to  Boethius,  of  a  direct  royal  command  to  that  effect. 
De  Lavedre  was  also  invested  with  the  hereditary  bailieship 
of  Lauderdale.  The  next  of  the  family  of  whom  there  is 
particular  notice  is 

Sir  Robert  de  Lawedre  of  the  Bass,  the  brave  assc^- 
ciate  of  Sir  William  Wallace,  who  had  a  charter  from 
"William  de  Lamberton,  bishop  of  St.  Andrew's,  of  that 
fragment  of  the  island  of  Bass  over  which  the  abbey  of  St. 
Andrew's  had  until  then  retained  a  right,  the  Landers 
having  already  possessed  the  larger  part  of  it  for  some 
generations.  This  Sir  Robert  was  ambassador  to  England 
from  Robert  I.  upon  various  occasions.  In  1323,  he  was 
one  of  the  proxies  in  the  oath  of  peace  with  Edward  II., 
on  which  occasion  he  swore  "on  the  soul  of  the  Bruce  " 
for  its  due  maintenance  by  the  Scottish  king.  He  was 
justiciary  of  the  Lothians  and  that  part  of  Scotland  to 
the  south  of  the  Forth,  in  1328 ;  and  in  1333  he  was  present 
at  the  battle  of  Halidon,  though  ho  was  then  too  old  to 
dismount  and  take  a  part  in  the  fight,  which  took  place  on 
foot.     His  son, 

Sir  Robert  de  Lavedre,  fought  at  Halidon  in  1333.

Lauderdale,  Earl  of  (Sir  Thomas  Maitland). 
Viscount  of  Lauderdale  and  Maitland,  and  Bai-on  of 
Thirlestane,  Boltouu,  and  Lauderdale  of  Thirlestane, 
in  the  peerage  of  Scotland ;  a  Knight  Bachelor ;  a 
Baronet  of  Nova  Scotia;  admiral  R.N. ;  principal 
naval  A.D.C.  to  the  Queen;  K.C.B. ;  and  Knight 
of  K.  Charles  III.;  h.  3  Feb.  1803  ;  s.  his  cousin, 
in  his  Scotch  honors,  as  11th  earl,  22  March,  1863  ; 
m.  1828,  Amelia,  3rd  dau.  of  William  Young,  Esq.  of 
Rio  de  Janeiro,  and  has  had  issue, 

I.  Thomas-Mordaunt,  h.  1838 ;  d.  7  Aug.  1844. 

I.  Isabel-Anne,  d.  3  May,  1854. 

II.  Mary-Jane,   m.  7  Jan.  1868,  to  Lord   Brabazon,   only 
son  of  WilUam,  11th  and  present  Earl  of  Meath. 

in.  Alice-Charlotte,  d.  30  Jan.  1833. 
The  Earl  of  Lauderdale  is  heritable  standard-bearer 
and  a  representative  peer  for  Scotland. 

This  veiy  ancient  and  distinguished  family  of  North 
Britain  has  been  seated  at  Thirlestane,  in  Berwickshire, 
for  nearly  six  centuries.  Its  earliest  ancestor  was  Sir 
Richard  de  Mautland  (as  the  name  was  formei'ly  written), 
who  gave  divers  lands  to  the  abbey  of  Dryburgh,  in  the 
reign  of  Alexander  III. 

Sir  Eichaed  Maitland,  12th  feudal  lord  of  Thirlestane, 
was  a  person  of  considerable  importance  in  the  era  in  which 
he  lived.  In  1552  and  1560,  we  find  him  one  of  the  com- 
missioners appointed  to  adjust  the  differences  with  England 
about  the  debatable  lands  on  the  borders.  In  1554,  he  was 
constituted  one  of  the  extraordinary  lords  of  Session ;  in 
1561,  appointed  one  of  the  ordinary  lords,  and  in  the  foUow- 
ing  year,  keeper  of  the  privy  seal,  which  latter  ofSce  he 
resigned  in  1567  in  favour  of  his  2nd  son.  His  lordship 
retired  from  the  bench  in  1584  ;  on  which  occasion  James 
VI.  acknowledged  by  letter  Sir  Richard's  faithful  services 
"to  his  grandsire,  goodsire,  gooddame,  mother,  and  him- 
self;" by  which  it  would  seem  that  this  eminent  person 
was  employed  seventy  years  at  least  in  the  public  service. 
In  the  literary  world  he  was  known  by  his  history  of  the 
family  of  Seton,  and  poems  on  several  subjects.  He  m. 
Mary,  dau.  of  Sir  Thomas  Cranston,  and  had  (with  a  second 
son,  John,  of  whom  presently,  and  other  issue)  an  eldest 
son, 

William,  of  Leigthington,  a  man  of  great  integrity  and 
loyalty,  and  the  devoted  friend  and  ailherent  of  Queen 
Mart  Stuart.  In  1558,  William  Maitland  was  consti- 
tuted principal  secretary  of  state  to  Mary  ;  and  in  1561 
he  was  nominated  one  of  her  privy  council.  He  many 
times  afterwards  came  as  Her  Majesty's  ambassador  to 
the  court  of  England,  where  he  had  the  management  of 
affairs  of  the  utmost  importance  ;  and  though  his  nego- 
tiations were  sometimes  not  attended  with  the  desired 
success,  yet  he  always  acquitted  himself  with  fidelity

Ceylon,  28  June  1806,  and  entered  the  military  service  of  the

paigns in  1843,  and  was  British  resident  at  Nepaul  in  184S, 
after  which  he  was  made  lieut. -colonel  and  militai-y  C.B. 
He  was  appointed,  in  18-16,  resident  at  Lahore  and  governor- 
general's  agent  on  the  north-west  frontier.  He  became  a 
general,  and  was.  for  his  eminent  services,  made  a  civil 
K.C.B.  in  1848.  He  was  named  chief  commissioner  for  the 
government  of  the  Punjaub  on  its  annexation  in  1849,  and,  ' 
in  the  spring  of  1857,  he  went  to  Lucknow,  as  chief  com- 
missioner of  Oude,  after  that  territory  had  been  some  time 
united  to  British  India.  Here  he  was  when  the  hideous 
mutiny  broke  out,  and  here,  within  the  fortified  residency 
of  Luckuow,  he  was  intrenched  with  all  the  Europeans  and 
the  others  who  remained  faithful,  and  he  thus  began  that 
renowned  defence,  which  for  skill,  endurance,  and  heroic 
bravery,  has  little  to  rival  it  in  the  annals  of  war.  He  did 
not,  however,  live  to  share  in  the  glorious  result.  He  was, 
on  the  2nd  July,  1857,  mortally  wounded  by  a  shell,  and  d. 
in  the  i-esidency  two  days  afterwards.  Sir  Henry  Lawrence 
was  known  in  the  literary  world  as  author  of  Tlie 
Adventures  of  an  Officer  in  Runjeet  Singh's  service.  Sir

LAW 


LAW 


This  very  eminent  civil  servant  of  the  East  Indian 
government  was  the  younger  brother  of  the  late 
Sir  Heury-Montgomery  Lawrence  (see  supra,  lineage 
Sir  H.  H.  Lawrence,  Brrt.),  and  was  educated  at 
Haileybnry  College  where  he  obtained  many  prizes. 
He  went  to  India  in  1829,  and  his  career  there  has 
been  of  the  greatest  public  utility.  After  filling 
various  minor  offices,  he  was  appointed  commissioner 
of  the  Sutlej  in  1846,  and  commissioner  of  the  Pun- 
jaub  in  1849.  He  was  made  a  K.C.B.  in  1856.  The 
energy  and  activity  he  displayed  at  Lahore  on  the 
outbreak  of  the  Sepoy  mutiny  has  tended  not  a 
little  to  the  victorious  s\ippressiou  of  the  terrible 
insurrection.  In  reward,  Sir  John  Lawrence  was 
made  a  G.C.B.  (civil)  in  1857,  and  was  created  a 
Baronet,  16  Aug.  1858,  to  hold  to  him  and  the 
heirs  male  of  his  body.  He  was  a  member  or 
the  Indian  Council.  The  court  of  Directors  of  the 
,  East  India  Company  granted  him  a  life  pension  of 
£2,000  a  year,  which,  by  an  act  specially  passed  27 
Vic,  cap.  2,  he  was  empowered  to  hold  with  his  full 
salary  as  Viceroy  of  India,  to  which  high  office  he 
was  appointed  in  1864,  and  from  which  he  retired 
in  1868.

I.  William  Lawrence,  one  of  the  most  distinguished 
surgeons  of  his  time,  was  6.  at  Cirencester,  16  July,  1783,  and 
was  educated  at  Elmore  Court  school,  near  Gloucester.  He 
studied  in  London,  under  the  great  surgeon  Abernethy,  whose 
success  he  afterwards  rivalled.  He  rose  rapidly  in  his  pro- 
fession, and  throughout  his  subsequent  life  had  a  very  exten- 
sive practice.  He  was  Demonstrator  of  Anatomy,  and 
Lecturer  on  Surgery,  at  St.  Bartholomew's  Hospital,  and  was 
twice  President  of  the  College  of  Surgeons.  He  was  in  1857, 
appointed  Serjeant-Surgeon  to  the  Queen,  having  long  been 
j  Her  Majesty's  Surgeon  Extraordinary.  He  was  a  F.R.S.,  and 
a  member  of  the  Institute  of  France,  as  well  as  of  many  of

The  very  ancient  family  of  Lechmere,  originally  from  the 
Low  Countries,  derives  from  Joscelyne  de  Lechmere,  who 
acquired  from  William  the  Conqueror  a  grant  of  lands  in 
Hanley,  co.  Worcester,  and  a  messuage  called,  in  old  deeds, 
Lechmere's  Field,  Leclimere's  Place,  and  Red  Court.  (For 
ddailed  pedigree,  see  Nash's  Worcestershire.)  The  Lcchmeres 
have  intermarried,  and  arc  connected,  with  the  Ruyhales, 
Whitmores,  Hungerfords,  Sandys,  Dyneleys,  Foleys,  Freres, 
Overburys,  Berkcleys,  De  Rupes,  Howards,  &.<:.,  <fcc. 

Sir  Nicholas  Lechmere,  Knt.,  M.P.  for  Bewdley  (repre- 
sentative of  this  distinguished  line,  and  son  of  Edmund 
Lechmere,  Esq.,  by  Margaret  his  wife,  sister  of  Sir  Thomas 
Overbury,  wlio  was  poisoned  in  the  Tower),  was  appointed 
a  Baron  of  the  Exchequer  at  the  Revolution.  He  ;».  Pene-

Et'itragr. 

The  family  of  Osborne  ia  one  of  considerable  antiquity  in 
Kent,  and  was  early  seated  at  Ashford,  in  that  county.  So 
far  back  as  the  12th  of  Henry  VI.  John  Osborne,  of  Can- 
terbury, occurs  on  the  list  of  Kentish  gentry.  Ancient, 
however,  as  is  the  paternal  ancestry  of  the  noble  family  ol 
Osborne,  the  illustrious  houses  of  Conyers,  D'Arcy,  and 
Godolphin,  which  the  present  Duke  of  Leeds  represents, 
and  his  descent  through  various  lines  from  the  royal  house 
of  Plantagenet,  (see  Burke's  Royal  Families. )  add  a  lustre  to 
his  grace's  coronet  of  which  few  other  families  can  boast.

The  family  of  Coke,  from  which  the  Earl  of  Leicester 
derives  through  female  descent,  and  which  he  now  repre- 
sents, is  deduced  by  Camden,  from 

William  Coke,  of  Didlington,  in  the  co.  of  Norfolk, 
mentioned  in  a  deed,  anno  1206,  who  was  father,  by  his 
wife  Felice,  of 

Geoffrey  Coke,  of  Didlington,  from  whom  descended 

Sir  Edward  Coke,  the  celebrated  lawyer.  This  eminent 
person  the  son  of  Robert  Coke,  Esq.  of  Milehim,  in  the  co. 
of  Norfolk,  and  Winifred,  his  wife,  dau.,  and  one  of  the 
heirs  of  William  Kuightley,  of  Morgrave-Knightley,  in  the 
same  shii-e,  was  born  at  the  seat  of  his  father,  in  1549,  and 
was,  at  ten  years  of  age,  sent  to  the  grammar-school  at 
Norwich,  whence  he  removed  to  Trinity  College,  Cambridge, 
where  he  studied  foi-  four  years,  and  where,  in  after  time, 
he  was  chosen  high-steward  of  that  university.  From  Cam- 
bridge ho  removed  to  Clifford 's-Inn,  and,  tbe  year  after, 
1672,  he  was  entered  a  student  in  the  Inner-Temple,  whence 
he  was  called  to  the  bar,  in  1578,  and  being  chosen  reader 
in  Lyon's-Inn,  acquired  so  much  celebrity,  that  he  very 
soon  attained  considerable  practice.  About  this  period  he 
to.  Ist,  Bridget,  dau.  and  co-heir  of  Jobn  Paston,  Esq.  of 
Huutingfield  Hall,  in  the  co.  of  Suffolk,  Srd  son  of  Sir 
William  Paston,  of  Paston,  her  ancestor.  Judge  Paston, 
had  sat  on  the  bench  of  the  Common  Pleas  with  Judge 
Littleton,  whose  renowned  commentator  Coke  was  to 
become.  With  this  lady.  Coke  acquired  a  fortune  of  30,0001. 
His  2ud  wife  was  the  Lady  Elizabeth,  dau.  of  Thomas 
Cecil,  first  Earl  of  Exeter  and  widow  of  Sir  William 
Hatton,  Knt.  Coke's  first  alUauce  brought  him  honours 
and  preferments  as  well  as  wealth.  The  cities  of  Coventry 
and  Norwich  soon  after  elected  him  their  recorder.  The 
county  of  Norfclk  returned  him  to  parliament,  and  the 
House  of  Commons  placed  him  in  the  speaker's  chair.  In 
the  35th  of  Elizabeth  (16  June,  1592),  Mr.  Coke  was  ap- 
pointed Solicitor,  and,  10  April,  the  next  year  Attorney- 
General,  and.  in  that  capacity,  acted  as  state  prosecutor 
with  an  asperity  and  a  roughness  of  manner  tbat  did  little 
credit  to  himself  or  his  oflace.  In  1603,  he  received  the 
honour  of  knighthood  from  King  James  I.  at  Greenwich, 
and  in  three  years  afterwards  was  elevated,  30  June,  1606, 
to  the  bench,  as  chief-justice  of  the  Court  of  Common  Pleas, 
from  which  be  was  advanced,  25  Oct.  1613,  to  bo  chief-justice 
of  the  Court  of  King's  Bench.  His  lordiship  incun-ed  subse- 
quently, however,  the  displeasure  of  his  sovereign ;  but

Between  his  paternal  property,  the  great  marriage  portion 
he  had  with  his  wife,  and  his  valuable  oflBces  and  lucrative

The  FitzGeralds  are  descended  from  "  Dominus  Otho," 
who  is  supposed  to  have  been  of  the  family  of  Gherardini 
of  Florence  ;  and  this  notion  is  confirmed  by  the  Latin  form 
of  name,  Geraldini,  assumed  by  his  descendants.  This 
noble  passed  over  into  Normandy,  and  thence,  in  1057, 
into  England,  where  he  became  so  great  a  favourite  with 
Edward  the  Confessor,  that  he  excited  the  jealousy  of  the 
Saxon  Th.anes.  However  derived,  his  English  possessions 
were  enormous,  which,  at  his  death,  devolved  on  his  son 
Walter,  who.  it  is  somewhat  remarkable,  was  treated  after 
the  Conquest  as  a  fellow-countryman  of  the  Normans. 
This  fortunate  heir  put  the  cope-stone  to  his  prosperity  by 
a  marriage  with  Gladys,  the  daughter  of  Ehiwallon  ap 
Cynfyn,  Prince  of  North  Wales ;  and  his  son,  Gerald 
FiTZWALTER,  Hi.  Ncsta,  the  d.aughter  of  Rhys  ap  Griiffydd, 
Prince  of  South  Wales,  by  whom  he  had  three  sons,  viz., 

I  Maurice,  his  heir.

Geraldines.  In  1168,  Dermot  Mac  Murrough,  King  of 
Leinster,  driven  from  his  territory  b}'  Roderick  O'Connor, 
King  of  Ireland,  sought  assistance  from  the  English,  and 
succeeded  in  enlisting  in  his  cause  the  renowned  Richard 
de  Clare,  Earl  of  Pembroke.  Having  reached  St.  David's, 
on  his  way  back  to  Ireland,  Dermot  was  Ivospitably  received 
by  David  FitzGerald,  bishop  of  the  diocese  ;  and  at  the  pre- 
late's persuasion,  his  younger  brother,  Maurice,  .and  his 
half-brother,  Robert  Fitzstephen,  engaged  to  assist  Mac 
Murrough  with  their  forces.  Soon  after,  Maurice  embarked 
for  Ireland,  with  two  ships  containing  a  small  body  of 
soldiers,  and  after  having  been  invested  with  the  lordship 
of  Wexford,  marched  forward  and  took  Dublin.  But  the 
Irish  king  was  no  idle  or  unconcerned  spectator  of  this 
achievement.  In  1171,  he  had  gathered  such  an  increase  of 
strength  that  though  Maurice  was  by  this  time  joined  by 
StroMgbow,  Roderick  was  able  to  invest  Dublin  with  30,000 
men,  while  at  sea  he  blockaded  it  with  a  fleet  of  thirty 
Manx  vessels.  The  case  of  the  English,  with  only  600 
troops,  seemed  well  nigh  desperate.  In  this  emergency,  by 
Maurice's  advice  and  earnest  and  inspirating  exhortations, 
the  beleaguered  garrison  determined  to  trust  to  their 
superior  warlike  prowess  and  darmg,  .and  regardless  of  the 
disparity  of  numbers,  to  encounter  the  foe.  The  bold 
exploit  was  crowned  with  success  ;  the  Irish  were  com- 
pletely defeated,  and  the  king,  Roderick,  with  difficulty 
escaped.  Maurice  died  at  Wexford  in  1177,  and  waa 
buried  in  the  Abbey,  outside  the  wal's  of  that  town.  "  His 
death,"  says  the  old  chronicler,  "  was  not  without  much 
Borrcw  of  all  his  friends,  and  much  harm  and  loss  to 
the  English  interest  in  Ireland.  He  was  a  man  witty  and 
manfuU ;  a  truer  man,  not  stedfister,  for  constancy, 
fidelity,  and  love,  left  he  none  in  Ireland."  '  In  truth," 
continues  Giraldus  Cambrensis,  "  M.aurice  was  an  honour- 
able and  modest  man  ;  with  a  face  sun-burnt  and  well- 
looking,  of  middle  height;  a  man  well  modelled  in  mind 
and  body  ;  a  man  of  innate  goodness ;  desiring  rather  to  be 
than  to  seem  good ;  a  man  of  few  words,  but  full  of 
weight,  havingmore  of  the  heart  than  of  the  mouth,  more  of 
reason  than  of  volubility,  more  wisdom  than  eloquence  ; 
and  yet  when  it  was  required,  earnest  to  the  purpose.  In 
military  affairs  valiant,  and  second  to  few  in  activity, 
neither  impetuous  nor  rash,  but  circumspect  in  attack  and 
resolute  in  defence  ;  a  sober,  modest,  and  chaste  man  ;  con- 
stant, trusty,  and  f  lithful ;  a  man  not  altogether  without 
fault,  yet  not  spotted  with  any  notorious  or  great  crime." 
By  his  wife,  Alice  de  Montgomery,  he  left  a  son  and  heir,

before  the  council,  that  Elizabeth  menaced  his  life,  and 
would  have  imiwisoned  him,  but  for  the  influence  of  his

of  Lesly  or  Leslie,  Earls  of  Rothes.

Sir  Alexander  Lesley,  one  of  the  most  noted  soldiers  of 
his  time,  remarkable  for  his  coolness  and  courage,  and  his 
great  knowledge  in  the  military  art.  Lesley  first  acted  as  a 
volunteer  in  Lord  Vere's  regiment  in  Holland,  where  he  soon 
rose  to  the  degree  of  a  cajitain.  He  then  went  to  Sweden,  and 
entered  into  the  service  of  Gustavus  Adolphcs,  and  behaved 
so  gallantly,  that  that  warlike  monarch  raised  him  to  the  rank 


LEV 


LEV 


of  a  lieutenant-general,  ana  then  to  that  of  field-marshal  of  his 
armies.  In  lG-23,  when  the  town  of  Stralsund  was  besieged  by 
a  victorious  army,  under  the  command  of  Count  Walsten,  and 
reduced  almost  to  the  last  extremity,  the  King  of  Sweden  sent 
General  Lesly  to  take  upon  him  the  command  of  the  garrison, 
and  he  there  acted  with  such  singular  resolution  and 
conduct,  that  he  obliged  the  coimt  to  raise  the  siege.  The 
burghers  were  so  sensible  of  the  great  service  Lesly  had  done 
them,  that  they  struck  several  medals  in  his  honour,  some  of 
which  have  been  preserved  in  the  family.  In  1630,  Lesly 
drove  the  Imperialists  entirely  out  of  Riigen,  and  continued  in 
tlie  Swedish  service  with  high  distinction  imtil  the  troubles 
in  Scotland  brought  him  home.  He  was  in  1638,  invited  by 
the  Covenanters  to  take  upon  him  the  conmiand  of  their  army, 
which  he  accepted,  and  was  made  governor  of  the  castle  of 
Edinburgh  in  March,  1639.  In  IC40  he  invaded  England  at 
.,he  head  of  the  Scotch  array,  and  defeated  a  party  of  the  king's 
troops  under  the  command  of  Lord  Conway,  at  Newburn,  and 
took  possession  of  Newcastle.  At  the  treaty  with  the  king  at 
Eipon,  General  Lesley  was  one  of  the  parliament's  commis- 
sioners, and  the  king  was  so  well  pleased  with  the  general's 
behaviour,  that  he  created  him  Loed  Balgont,  and  Earl  of 
Leven,  by  patent  dated  1641.  After  going  in  1642  to  Ireland ' 
to  suppress  the  insurrection  there,  Lesly,  Earl  of  Leven,  had 
again  in  1643  the  command  of  the  Scotch  army  that  was  sent  to 
the  assistance  of  the  parliament's  forces  against  the  king;  and 
the  victory  at  Marston  Moor  in  1644  was  chiefly  ascribed  to  him. 
He  was  appointed  in  1647  lord-general  of  Scotland.  Notwith- 
standing his  support  of  the  parliamentarians,  Lesly  showed 
himself  afterwards  more  loyal  than  otherwise,  owing  to  his 
disapproval  of  the  king's  murder.  After  that  event,  none 
appeared  more  forward  than  the  Earl  of  Leven  in  raising  an 
army,  and  restoring  King  Charles  II.  He  served  as  a 
voltmteer  against  Oliver  Cromw'ell  at  the  battle  of  Dunbar, 
and  lieartily  joined  and  concurred  with  the  royalists  in  every 
measure  for  the  restoration ;  but  when  he,  with  others  of  the 
royal  party  had  a  meeting  in  Angus,  to  concert  matters  for 
their  future  conduct,  General  Monk,  who  then  besieged  Dundee, 
having  got  intelligence  of  their  meeting,  sent  a  strong  party 
in  the  night,  sui-prised  and  took  them  prisoners  at  Alyth  in 
Angus,  and  transferred  the  veteran  Earl  of  Leven,  with  several 
others,  prisoners  to  London,  where  they  were  confined  in  the 
Tower.  The  earl  remained  incarcerated  there,  and  suffered 
sequestration  and  many  other  hardships,  till  by  the  mediation 
of  tlie  Queen  of  Siveden  he  obtained  his  liberty,  and  was  so 
sensible  of  the  service  her  majesty  had  done  him,  that  he  went 
over  to  Sweden  in  person  to  make  his  acknowledgments,  and 
was  there  received  and  entertained  with  great  respect,  in 
honour  of  liis  former  services.  He  at  last  returned  to  his  own 
country,  retired  to  his  seat,  Balgony,  in  Fife,  and  d.  there  at  a 
very  advanced  age  in  1G62.  The  Earl  ni.  Agnes,  dau.  of

LiNDSET,  Earl  of  (George-Augustus-Frederick- 
Albemarle  Bertie),  co.  Lincoln  ;  b.  4  Nov.  1814  ;  s.  as 
10th  earl,  upon  the  decease  of  his  father,  17  Sept. 
1818. 

Eincagc. 

This  noble  family,  which  eventually  obtained  the  highest 
degree  of  rank  in  the  British  peerage,  springs  maternally 
from  the  Willouohbys,  original  Barons  Willoughby  de 
Eresby,  and  paternally  from  the  Bertiesof  Bersted  in  Kent. 
The  Borties  were  a  very  ancient  house,  deriving  descent 
from  a  family  of  free  Barons  of  Bertieland  iu  Prussia. 
Their  name,  in  olden  deeds,  is  spelt  Berteghe,  Berteye,  and 
Bertewe,  in  later,  Bertye,  and  Bertie.  TLey  first  landed  in 
England,  in  company  with  the  Saxons,  and  their  descen- 
dant, Leopold  Bertie,  was  constable  of  Dover  Castle  in  the 
reign  of  King  Ethelred,  and  was  also  the  proprietor  of  a 
castle  and  town  named  Bertiested,  now  Bersted,  near 
Maidstone,  in  Kent.  Leopold  having  fallen  into  a  violent 
dispute  with  the  Augustine  Monks  of  Canterbury  about 
tithes,  and  the  monks  endeavouring  to  enforce  their 
demands  by  force  of  arms,  a  fray  ensued,  in  which  Leopold's 
sou  was  slain.  The  king  giving  Leopold  no  satisfaction, 
he  solicited  Sweyn,  King  of  the  Danes,  and  induced  him 
to  invade  England.  The  Danes  joining  Leopold's  forces 
in  Kent,  laid  siege  to  Ca?\terbury,  and  took  the  arch- 
bishop prisoner,  and  slew  the  monks  by  nines,  sparing 
every  tenth.  On  the  death  of  Sweyn,  however,  Ethelred 
returned  to  England,  and  Burbach  Bertie,  only  surviving 
son  of  Leopold,  conscious  of  his  father's  actions,  fled  to 
Robert,  the  French  king,  who  received  him  hunmn-ably,  and 
taking  to  wife  a  Frenchwoman,  he  settled  in  France,  where 
his  posterity  continued  tUl  1154,  when  his  descendant, 
Philip  Bertie  "  de  eadem  familia,"  accompanied  Henry  II. 
to  Engl.and,  and  "  propter  bellandi  peritiam,"  recovered 
from  that  monarch  his  patrimony  of  Bersted.  (See 
Hasted's  m^tori/  of  Kent,  vol.  ii.  p.  488.)  This  Phihp's 
lineal  descendant,  Hierouimus  Bertie  (temp.  Henry  V.)  was 
excommunicated,  and  had  to  make  a  pilgrimage  to  Rome 
for  the  following  oflence.  Hearing  a  monk  in  a  sermon 
utter  assertions  injurious  to  his  ancestor  Leopold,  he  rushed 
violently  upon  the  preacher,  and,  but  for  the  interference  of 
the  bystanders,  would  have  slain  him.  Hieronimus  ap- 
peased the  anger  of  the  Church  by  a  severe  persoxial 
penance,  and  by  the  payment  of  two  thousand  crowns  of 
gold  to  the  monastery  of  the  monk  whom  he  had  as6aultc(c. 
He  further,  in  proof  of  his  repentance,  rebuilt,  at  his  own 
expense,  the  north  part  of  the  temple  belonging  to  the  sams

"  On  the  22ncl  of  September,  1586,  an  interesting  affray  took

convoy  accordingly,  by  the  orders  of  the  Prince  of  Panna,

A  second,  commanded  by  George  Cressiac,  an  Albanois,  was

captive  was  conducted  to  the  tent  of  the  general,  Lord  Leicester 
The  engagement  was  hot,  and  cost  the  enemv  many  lives,  but 
few  of  the  English  were  missing.  Willoughby  was"  extremely 
forward  in  the  combat:  at  one  moment  his  basses  (or  mantle)

ledge himself  prisoner  to  any  but  the  knight  to  whom  he  had 
submitted  on  the  field.  There  is  something  in  this,  and  the 
like  incidents  of  the  period  which  recil  un  very  agreeably  to 
recollections  of  earlier  days  of  chivalry  and  romance.  Ciessiac

tensions to  the  last.  His  lordship  was,  however,  created 
Earl  of  Lindsey,  22  Nov.  1626,  and  elected  in  four  years 
afterwards  a  knight  of  the  Garter.  In  the  11th  of  Charles 
I.,  ho  was  constituted  lord-high-admiral  of  England;  and 
in  1639,  was  appointed  governor  of  Berwick.  J  His  lordship 
fell  at  the  battle  of  Edgehill,  28  Oct.  1642,  at  the  head  of  a 
division  of  the  royal  army,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son 

prisoner.  It  was  in  this  skirmish  that  the  gallant  and  lamented 
Sir  Philip  Sidney,  the  boast  of  his  age,  and  the  hope  of  many 
admiring  friends,  received  the  fatal  wound  which  cut  short  the 
thread  of  a  brief  but  brilliant  existence.  During  the  whole  day 
he  had  been  one  of  the  foremost  in  action,  and  once  rushed  to 
the  assistance  of  his  friend  Lord  Willoughby,  on  obsei-ving  him 
'nearly  surrounded  by  the  enemy' and  in  imminent  peril:  after 
seeing  him  in  safety  he  continued  the  combat  with  great  spirit, 
until  he  received  a  shot  in  the  thigh  as  he  was  remounting  a 
second  horse,  the  first  having  been  kiUed  under  him."

Montagu,  2nd  earl,  K.G.  This  nobleman  being  with  his 
gallant  father  at  Edgehill,  when  his  lordship  received  his 
doath-wound,  voluntarily  surrendered  himself  a  prisoner,  in 
order  to  be  near  and  to  attend  him.  He  was  subsequently 
an  active  commander  during  the  civil  wars,  on  the  same 
side.  "He  was,"  says  Archdeacon  Echard,  "one  of  the 
Quadrumvirate  that  had  been  so  eminently  distinguished 
for  their  unparalleled  loyalty  to  the  late  king,  by  oflfering 
their  lives  as  his  councillors  ;  a  brave  experienced  soldier  ; 
a  great  patron  of  useful  learning  and  ingenuity  ;  and  a 
true  patriot,  and  imitator  of  ancient  nobility.  After 
having  received  wounds  at  Naseby,  and  waded  through  an 
ocean  of  difficulties,  he  died  in  quiet,  peace,  and  honour, 
at  Campden  Hovise,  Kensington,  the  25th  of  July,  16(3ii, 
aged  58,  and  was  buried  at  Edenham,  in  the  vault  with

This  is  one  of  the  very  few  native  families  which  has  been 
dignified  by  the  peerage  of  Ireland.  The  O'Callaghans  were

year.  From  a  junior  branch  of  this  great  Milesian  house

Martin  de  Tours,  a  Noi-man,  who  accompanied  the 
Conqueror  to  England  having  as  one  of  the  Lord-Marchers, 
acquired,  by  conquest,  a  large  district  in  Pembrokeshire, 
called  Cemaes  or  Kemes,  became  Palatine  Baron  thereof. 
He  made  Newport  the  head  of  his  Palatinate,  and  there 
erected  his  castle  (the  ruins  of  which  still  exist).  He  was 
s.  by  his  son,  Robert  Martin,  Lord  Palatine  of  Kemes,  who 
m.  Maud  Peverel,  and  had  a  son  and  successor,

LOCKHART. 


LOCKHA.RT,  Sir  Norman  Macdonald,  of  Lee  and 
Cai-nwath,  co.  Lanark,  D.L.  for  that  co.,  b,  iu  1845  ; 
s.  bis  father,  as  4th  baronet,  1849. 

ILtitcagc. 

This  family  has  an  undoubted  right  to  rank  as  one  of  the 
oldest  in  Scotland,  the  surname  of  Lockhart  being  of  great 
antiquity  and  distinction.  There  is  to  be  found  evidence 
of  this  in  the  reigns  of  David  I.  and  Malcolm  IV.  ;  the 
latter  of  whom  succeeded  to  the  crown  in  the  year  1153  : 
during  whose  time  appears, 

Stbphanus  Lockard,  a  "man  of  rank  and  distinction," 
who  was  s.  by 

Simon  Lockard,  who  had  afterwards  the  honour  of 
knighthood  conferred  upon  him  by  King  William  (who 
ascended  the  throne  in  1166).  But  for  a  particular  account 
of  the  descent  of  the  family,  reference  should  be  made  to 
Douglas's  Baronage  of  Scotland,  p.  323.  Following  the 
descent,  we  come  to 

Sir  Simon  Locard,  of  Lee,  who  accompanied  Lord  James 
Douglas  to  the  Holy  Laud,  with  the  heart  of  the  deceased 
monarch,  for  interment.  From  this  circumstance,  the 
Douglases  bear  in  their  arms  a  crowned  heart ;  and  Sir 
Simon  changed  his  name  to  Lockheart  (as  it  was  until 
lately  spelt),  and  for  part  of  his  arms  got  a  heart  within  a 
lock,  and  the  motto,  "  Corda  serrata  pando."  In  the  pos- 
session of  this  family  is  that  singular  piece  of  antiquity 
ualled  The  Zee  Ptnni/,  upon  which  is  founded  Sir  Walter 
Scott's  romance  of  T/ie  Talisman.  The  account  given  of  it 
is  that  Simon  Locard,  during  his  stay  in  the  Holy  Land, 
took  prisoner  a  Saracen  chief,  whose  wife  came  to  ransom 
him,  and  on  the  counting  out  of  the  money  or  jewels,  this 
(which  is  a  stone  or  composition  of  a  dark  red  colour  and 
triangular  shape,  set  on  a  silver  coin)  fell ;  she  hastily 
snatched  it  up,  which  Simon  observing,  insisted  upon 
having  it,  and  procured  it  before  giving  up  his  prisoner. 
More  of  this  singular  relic,  and  its  alleged  properties  and 
virtues,  may  be  found  in  Sir  Walter  Scott's  preface  to  The 
Talisman. 
Continuing  to  follow  the  destsiit,  we  come  to 
Sir  James  Lockhart,  b.  in  1596,  a  lord  of  the  court  of 
Session  in  Scotland,  and  afterwards  lord-justice-clerk,  as 
Lord  Lee,  in  the  time  of  Charles  I.  He  m.  twice :  by  his 
1st  wife,  Helen,  dau.  of  Alexander  Fairly,  of  Biaid,  he  had 
no  issue  ;  by  his  2ud,  Marth.-i,  dau.  of  Sir  George  Douglas, 
of  Mordington  (brother  of  J  ames.  Lord  Toithorwald),  and 
maid  of  honour  to  Charles  I.'s  queen,  he  had,  with  two 
daus.,  four  sons,  namely,  i.  William  (Sir)  ;  ii.  George  (Sir), 
of  whom  hereafter;  iii.  John  (Sir),  of  Castlehill,  appointed 
by  Charles  II.  one  of  the  senators  of  the  College  of  Justice, 
and  a  Lord  of  Justiciary ;  and  iv.  Robert,  killed  iu  the  civil 
wars.     Sir  James  was  s.  at  his  decease  by  his  eldest  son. 

Sir  William  Lockhart,  b.  in  1621,  an  eminent  states- 
man, and  one  of  the  gi-eatest  politicians  of  his  age,  well 
known  as  Ambassador  Lockhart,  having  been  many  years 
accredited  to  the  court  of  France.  He  afterwards  s.  his

The  clan  Fraser,  of  which  Lord  Lovat  is  the  chief,  are 
of  Norman  descent.    The  uame  of  Frisell,  their  original

designation,  occurs  in  the  roll  of  Battle  Abbey,  and  esta-

Peter  Kino,  son  and  heir  of  Jerome  King,  of  the  city

fession. Mr.  King  accordingly  entered  himself  of  the  Inner
