Edmund,  6.  21  Nov.  1790,  entered  the  royal  navy  in  June, 
1801,  and  after  an  early  and  distinguished  career  during  the 
French  war,  having  been  in  sevei-al  actions,  and  having 
escorted  Louis  XVIII.  to  France,  as  commander  of  the 
"  Rinaldo,"  he  became  a  captain  in  1814,  since  wiiich  ha 
continued  to  do  able  public  service,  both  as  a  naval  officer 
and  a  diplomatist,  and  was  created  a  Baronet  20  May,  1840. 
He  was  appointed  to  the  chief  command  of  the  Mediterra- 
nean Fleet,  in  1855,  and  achieved  the  highest  renown  by  the 
brilliant  and  effective  assistance  he  gave  to  the  Crimean 
expedition,  and  to  the  allied  forces  in  the  late  Russian  war. 
For  these  services  he  was  created,  23  June,  1856,  Baron 
Lyons.  His  lordship  was  also  a  G.C.B.,  G.C.M.G.,  K.C.H., 
vice-admiral  of  the  White,  knight  grand  cross  of  the  Legion 
of  Honour,  and  a  knight  1st  class  of  various  other  foreign 
orders.  He  m.  18  July,  1814,  Augusta-Louisa,  d.iu.  and 
co-heir  of  the  late  Captain  Josias  Rogers,  R.N.,  and  by  her 
(who  d.  10  March,  1852),  had  issue,

Lord  Lytton,  the  distinguished  writer,  novelist,  and 
politician,  was  elected  M.P.  for  Herts  in   1852,  and 
was  constituted,  in  1858,  H.  M.  Principal  Secretary

Sir  Edward  Bulwer-Lytton,  the  3rd  son  of  William- 
Earle  Bolwer,*  of  Heydon  Hall  and  Wood-DaUlng,  Nor- 
folk, Esq.  (brigadier-gen.),  by  Elizabeth-Barbara  his  wife, 
dau.  and  sole  heiress  of  Bichard-Warburton  Lytton, 
Esq.  of  Knebworth  Park,  Herts,  succeeding  to  the  Kneb- 
worth estates  by  the  will  of  his  mother,  19  Dec.  1843,  and 
taking  the  surname  of  Lytton  by  sign-manual,  became  the 
representative  of  his  mother's  famUy,  and  the  head  of  the 
two  ancient  houses  of  Lytton  of  Knebworth,  and  Robinson 
or  Norreys,  of  Gwersylt  and  Monachdy.  The  Ltttons  came 
originally  from  Lytton,  in  Derbyshire.  Sir  Gilbert  de 
Lytton  fought  at  Askalon,  under  Richard  Cceur  de  Lion, 
and  Sir  Alexander  do  Lytton  held,  temp.  Edward  I.,  con- 
siderable estates  in  the  Peak.  In  the  reign  of  Henry  IV., 
Robert  de  Lytton  was  governor  of  Bolsover  Castle,  comp- 
troller of  the  king's  household,  and  Agister  of  the  forests 
in  the  Peak,  to  Queen  Joan.  His  grandson,  Sir  Robert  de 
Lytton,  knight  of  the  Bath,  privy -counciUor.  keeper  of  the

Thomas  Parker,  Gent,  of  Leke,  in  Staffordshire.  2nd  son

chief-justiceship  of  the  court  of  Queeu'.s  Bench  in  1710,  and

A  ngus,  Lord  of  the  Isles,  descended  from  Somerled, 
Thane  of  Argyll,  after  King  Robert  Bruce  was  defeated  by 
the  English  in  1306,  afforded  him  an  asylum  iu  his  castle  of 
Duuavarty.     The  descendant  of  this  Angus, 

Donald,  Lord  of  the  Isles,  entered  into  a  treaty  with 
Richard  II.,  iu  1388,  on  the  footing  of  a  sovereign  prince. 
He  in.  Lady  Margaret  Lesly,  only  dau.  of  Euphemia, 
Countess  of  Ross,  by  Sir  Walter  Lesly,  in  her  right  Earl  of 
Ross,  and  he  subsequently  took  up  arms  to  establish  his 
right  tot  hat  earldom.  He  was  defeated,  however,  or,  more 
correctly  speaking,  weakened,  by  the  Earl  of  Man-,  who 
engaged  him  at  Harlaw,  near  Aberdeen,  24  July,  1411. 
The  battle  was  bloody  and  obstinate,  but  indecisive.  On 
the  side  of  Donald,  the  cliiefs  of  Macintosh  and  Maclean 
fell,  with  about  nine  hundred,  while  Mavr  lost  about  five 
hundred,  amongst  whom  were  some  persons  of  rank.  The 
Lord  of  the  Isles  was  forced  to  retire  ;  and  the  Regent  Duke 
of  Albany  marched  to,  and  took  the  castle  of  Dingwall. 
Eventually  Donald  was  compeUed  to  abandon  his  preten- 
sions to  the  earldom,  to  naake  personal  submission,  and  to 
give  oaths  and  hostages  for  indemnification  and  future 
observance  of  peace.     He  was  s.  by  his  son, 

Alexander,  Lord  of  the  Isles.  This  chief  was  defeated 
by  James  I.,  at  Loohaber,  23  June,  1429,  and  reduced  to 
the  most  abject  submission.  In  absolute  despair,  the  Lord 
of  the  Isles  sent  an  embassy  to  sue  for  peace,  which  being 
refused,  he  resolved  to  throw  liimself  upon  the  king's 
mercy.  For  that  purpose  he  came  privately  to  Edinburgh, 
and  on  the  27  Aug.  1429,  attired  only  in  his  shu-t  and 
drawers,  presented  his  sword  to  the  king  upon  his  knees, 
before  the  high  altar  of  Holyrood  church,  in  presence  of 
the  queen  and  nobles.  He  to.  Elizabeth,  only  dau.  of 
Alexander  Seton,  Lord  of  Gordon  and  Htmtly,  and  was  s. 
by  his  son, 

John,  11th  Earl  of  Ross  and  Lord  of  the  Isles.  This 
nobleman  having  entered  into  a  treaty  with  Edward  IV. 
of  England,  in  1462,  was  deemed  a  traitor  to  his  liege 
sovereign  of  Scotland,  and  was  forced  to  surrender  the 
Earldom  of  Ross,  which  was  inalienably  annexed  to  the 
crown  by  act  of  parliament,  10  July,  1476.  He  d.  in  1498, 
without  legitimate  issue,  when  the  line  was  continued  by 
his  brother, 

Hugh,  or  the  Isles,  whose  great-grandson,

The  clan  Qregor  or  MacGregor  is  said  to  have  sprung 
from  Grcgor,  or  Gregorius,  .3rd  son  of  Alpin  one  of  the 
Scottish  kings  of  the  eighth  century.  From  this  descent 
of  their  founder,  the  sept  deiived  their  original  name  o 
Mac.\lpine,  and  they  still  occasionally  receive  the  appella- 
tion of  Tlie  clan  Alpine.  From  a  very  ancient  period,  they 
.appear  to  have  possessed  a  wide  tract  of  land  on  the 
boundary  lines  of  Argyle  and  Perth  sliires,  around  Loch 
Katrine  and  the  nox-thern  end  of  Loch  Lomond.  While 
the  strong  arm  constituted  the  sole  title  to  property  in 
Scotland,  the  MacGrcgors  man.aged  matters  as  well  as  their 
neighbours,  being  sufficiently  able  and  willing  to  make 
their  hands  keep  their  lands  ;  but  when  territorial  posses- 
sions were  legally  secured  by  written  tenures,  the  clan 
imprudentlv  continued  to  trust  o  the  right  of  the  sword, 
and  thus  paved  the  way  for  the  long  train  of  misfortunes 
which  fell  upon  them.  While  they  pursued  their  simple 
and  retired  mode  of  life,  the  gi'eat  barons  in  their  vicinity 
used  their  court  influence  to  obtam  charters  over  the  old 
MacGregor  possessions,  and  followed  up  the  acquisition  of 
such  dociimentary  rights  by  driving  out  the  true  proprie- 
tors. The  MacGregors  h.abitually  and  obstinately  resisted 
such  encroachments,  and  their  bravery  often  gained  them 
advantages  over  their  adversaries.  But  the  latter  parties 
had  always  possession  of  the  royal  ear,  and  what  was  sim- 
ply self-defence  on  the  part  of  the  devoted  sept,  was  uni- 
formly misrepresented  at  court  as  a  headstrong  defiance  of 
all  proper  rule  and  authority  The  natural  result  of  the 
whole  was,  that  the  JIacGregors  became  a  wild,  a  lawless, 
and  a  broken  sept.*  Up  to  the  very  close  of  the  eighteenth 
century,  the  MacGregors  were  legally  a  nameless  clan,  in 
as  far  as  the  penal  acts  .against  them  still  held  a  place  in 
the  st.atute-book,  though,  practically,  the  law  recognised 
the  n.ame,  and  none  of  the  pen.al  statutes  were  ever  en- 
forced The  British  pai-liament  finally  abolished  all  these 
traces  of  ancient  barbarity.  As  soon  as  this  boon  was  con- 
ferred on  them,  the  MacGregors  showed  remaining  tokens 
of  a  strong  feeling  of  clanship,  by  acknowledging  a  head 
and  chief.  Eight  himdred  and  twenty-six  persons,  of  the 
name  of  MacGregor,  subscribed  a  deed,  admitting  John 
Murray,  Esq.  of  Lanrick.  afterw.ards  Sir  John  MacGregor, 
Bart. ,  as  lawfully  descended  of  the  house  of  Glenstrae,  and 
the  proper  and  true  chieftain  of  Clan  Alpine. 

Patrick  Mac  Gregor  joined  the  great  Duke  of  Montrose

The  family  of  Mackworth  is  of  great  antiquity  In  the 
county  of  Derby.  The  name  is  local,  from  the  parish  of 
Mackworth,  which  comprises  the  township  of  Mai'keaton, 
situated  about  two  miles  north-west  from  the  town  of 
Derby.  The  manor  of  Mackworth,  formerly  the  property 
of  the  Touchets,  Lords  Audley,  has  always  been  held  with 
that  of  Markeaton.  A  considerable  freehold  estate  at 
Mackworth  was  held  under  the  lord  of  the  manor  by  the 
ancient  family  of  De  Mackworth,  who  had  a  castellated 
mansion  there,  the  gatewa}'  of  which  still  remains.  At 
the  battle  of  Poictiers  (1356),  Edward  the  Black  Prince 
was  attended  by  James,  Lord  Audlej^  K.G.,  who  had  four 
esquires,  or  aides-de-camp,  in  immediate  attendance,  a 
member  of  this  family  being  one  of  the  four ;  and  in  the 
late  French  war,  the  representatives  of  these  four  esquires 
all  served  together  as  aides-de-camp  to  General  Lord  Hill. 
John  Touchet,  Lord  Audley,  son-in-law,  and  eventually 
heir,  to  the  said  James,  Lord  Audley,  K.G.,  gr.anted,  in 
consideration  that  John  and  Thomas  Mackworth  were 
valiant  men,  and  for  the  services  rendered  by  them  and 
their  ancestors  to  the  Audley  family,  a  coat-of-arms,  made 
from  the  arms  of  Audley  and  Touchet.  From  Derbyshire 
the  chief  of  the  line  settled  in  Rutlandshire,  by  the  mar- 
riage with  the  heiress  of  Empingham,  in  that  county,  in 
which  parish  Normanton  Hall  was  tiio  ''«sidence  of  the 
Maokworths  for  many  years.  The  manor  of  Ash  (Eisse), 
in  Derbyshire,  appears  to  have  been  held  by  the  Mackworth 
family,  8th  Richard  II.,  a.d.  1385.

II.  Octavia-Helen. 

The  genealogy  contained  in  the  manuscript  discovered  by 
Skene  in  the  collection  of  the  faculty  of  advocates  confirms  the 
ancient  origin  of  this  family,  and  puts  it  beyond  doubt  that  they 
were  one  of  the  three  clans  descended  fiom  the  old  Maonuors 
of  Moray,  sovereigns  of  the  Pictish  race,  which  from  the 
earUest  time  occupied  the  district  of  Moray. 

In  the  12th-century  a  large  grant  of  lands  in  Strath Tay  was 
made  to  the  Macnaghtens,  who  were  styled  Thanes  of  Loch 
Tay.  In  the  13th  century,  in  consequence  of  their  joining 
the  king  as  crown  vassals  in  his  expedition  into  Argyleshire 
against  Somerbad,  Alexander  III.  granted  them  lands  ex- 
tending between  the  south  of  Loch  Awe  and  Loch  Fine,  in- 
cluding the  glens  Aj-a,  Slica,  and  Glen  Fine.  This  king  also 
Issued  a  patent  from  his  court  at  Scone,  on  12th  February,  1267, 
granting  to  Gillichrist  Macnaghtane  and  his  heirs  the  custody 
of  Fraoch  Elan,  on  condition  that  he  woiUd  rebuild  and  keep 
the  castle  in  repair,  and  preserve  it  in  a  fit  state  for  the  recep- 
tion and  entertainment  of  his  majesty,  whenever  it  should 
please  him  to  go  there.  Fraoch  Elan  was  long  one  of  the 
principal  residences  of  the  Macnaghten  family,  who  were 
hereditary  grand  rangers  of  the  forest  of  Benbery,  by  reason 
of  which  the  chief  of  the  clan  is  entitled  to  carry  two  roebucks 
for  supporters.  They  had  possessions  also  in  Upper  Cowal,  and 
one  of  them  is  spoken  of  as  Baron  Cowal.  Other  clans  were 
generally  dependent  on  some  greater  sept.  The  Macnaghtens 
continued  to  exist  without  any  perceptible  increase  or  dimi- 
nution of  strength  from  the  time  of  their  removal  from 
Moray  until  the  beginning  of  the  17th  century,  when  their 
fortunes  declined  with  the  ill-fated  house  of  Stuart.  Gilli- 
christ Macnaghtane,  constable  of  Fraoch  Elan,  was  grand- 
father of  Donald  of  that  ilk,  who  joined  with  his  relative, 
MacDougal  of  Lorn,  against  King  Robert  Bruce  ;  but  struck 
with  the  bravei7  of  that  prince,  went  over  to  his  interests,  and 
continued  faithful  in  allegiance  to  him  for  the  remainder  of 
his  life.  There  is  a  detailed  account  of  this  transaction  in 
Barbour's  curious  poem  entitled  "The  Acts  and  Life  of 
Robert  Bruce."  The  son  of  this  Baron  Macnaghtane  was 
Duncan,  a  loyal  subject  of  King  David  Bruce.  The  sons  and 
daughters  of  the  house  were  connected  by  marriage  with  the 
best  families  in  the  west  of  Scotland.  One  of  the  sons,  Donald 
was  elected  bishop  of  Dunkeld  in  1436 ;  another  accompanied 
Lord  James  Douglas  when  he  went  with  the  intention  of 
depositing  the  heart  of  Robert  Bruce  in  Jerusalem.  The  party 
headed  by  Douglas  was  attacked  on  their  way,  and  many  of 
them  killed.  Lord  James  was  amongst  the  number.  The 
survivors,  one  of  whom  was  Duncan,  brought  back  the  heart 
of  their  late  king  to  Scotland.  In  1510,  Sir  Alexander 
Macnaghtane  followed  James  IV.  to  the  fatal  field  of  Flodden 

732 


He  was  there  slain  with  his  sovereign  and  the  flower  of  the 
Scottish  nobility.  It  was  then  that  each  member  of  the  family 
might  have  exclaimed — 

"Occidit,  occidit, 
Spes  omnis  et  fortuna  nostri 
Nominis." 

The  son  and  heir  of  this  Sir  Alexander  married  Anne,  daughter 
of  Murdoch  Maclean,  Laird  of  Lough  Bay,  in  Midi,  by  his  wife, 
the  sister  of  Randal  MacSorley,  1st  Earl  of  Antrim,  and 
daughter  of  Sorley  Bay,  who  was  in  the  habit  of  making  pre- 
datory incursions  into  the  north  of  Ireland.  By  this  lady" 
he  had  three  sons.  The  eldest  died  without  issue.  From  the 
second,  Malcolm,  called  Gleashian,  proceeded  the  Scottish  line; 
but  this,  from  devoted  attachment  to  the  Stuarts  fell  into  decay, 
and  became  ultimately  lost.  The  third  son,  designated  "Shane 
Dhu,"  or  Black  Isha,  went  to  Ireland  as  secretary  to  his  grand- 
uncle,  Randal  MacSorley  MacDonnell,  1st  Earl  of  Antrim,  and 
settled  in  the  county  of  Antrim  in  1580.  The  last  place  of 
residence  the  Macnaughtens  had  in  Scotland  was  Dundarave, 
a  castle  on  Lough  Fine,  in  Argyleshire.  David  Macnaughton, 
son  and  heir  of  "Shane  Dhu,"  married  Catherine,  niece  of 
the  Primate  George  yowdall,  and  his  son,  John  of  Ben- 
warden,  in  the  count  of  Antrim,  married  Helen,  daughter 
of  Francis  Stafford,  of  Portglanone.  Edmund,  their  son,  was 
born  on  the  10th  of  August,  1679,  and  when  about  ten  years  of 
age  was  taken  by  his  mother,  then  a  widow,  to  the  city  of 
Londonderry,  where  he  remained  with  his  uncle,  the  Right 
Hon.  Edward  Francis  Stafford,  during  the  whole  of  the  me- 
morable siege.  In  the  meantime  the  Scottish  branch  of  the 
family  adhered  zealously  to  the  house  of  Stuart.  On  the  10th 
of  July,  1689,  John  Macnaghtan,  with  a  large  body  of  his  clan, 
joined  Graham  of  Claverhouse,  the  gallant  Dundee,  and  con- 
tributed much  to  the  success  gained  over  William's  army  at 
Killicranlue.  But  victory  was  as  disastrous  as  defeat  to  the 
Macnaghtans  An  entire  forfeiture  of  their  property  in  Scot- 
land was  the  immediate  consequence  of  the  part  tbey  took. 
The  Irish  branch  was  represented  by  the  above-named  Edmund, 
who  resided  at  Beardiville,  in  the  county  of  Antrim.  A  large 
deputation  from  the  Macnaughtons  of  Perthshire  and  Argyle 
shire  came  over  from  Scotland,  soliciting  him  to  assume  the 
chieftainship  of  the  clan.  He  did  not,  however,  see  fit  to 
comply  with  their  request.  He  had  married,  1st,  Leonora 
Vesey,  of  the  De  Vesci  family,  by  whom  he  had  no  issue ;  2ndly, 
Hanah,  daughter  of  John  Johnstone,  Esq.,  by  whom  he  had 
two  sons,  Edmund  Alexander,  for  many  years  M.P.  for  the 
county  of  Antrim,  and  one  of  the  lords  of  the  treasury.  He 
was  born  the  2nd  of  August,  1762.  It  is  believed  the  clan  was 
without  a  recognized  chief  until  1818,  when,  on  the  attestation 
and  at  the  desire  of  upwards  of  400  of  the  Macnaughtans  in 
Scotland,  a  patent  was  issued  by  Thomas,  Earl  of  Kinnoul, 
Lord  Lyon  King  of  Arms,  acknowledging  Edmund  Alexander  to 
be  chief  of  the  ancient  name  and  clan,  and  the  same  was 
registered  accordingly.  Edmund-Alexander  died  s.p.,  in 
March,  1832,  when  the  patrimonial  estate  and  the  chieftainship 
were  inherited  by

with  the  fallen  monarch,  as  Alfgar,  Earl  of  Mercia,  whose

Robert,  Lokd  Mallet,  his  eldest  son,  succeeded,  and 
inherited  vast  possessions,  amounting  to  293  lordships. 
His  baronial  residence  appears  to  have  been  at  Eye,  in 
Suffolk,  where  he  founded  a  monastery.  He  was  Sapifer, 
or  high-steward  to  Henry  I.,  but  on  his  taking  the  part  of 
Robert  Coarthose,  his  estaies  were  conriscated,  and  given  to 
Stephen,  Earl  of  Biois.  He  retired  to  Normandy,  and  from 
him  descend  the  Malets  of  Graville,  and  other  branches 
in  France,  one  of  whom,  taken  prisoner  at  Crecy,  was 
deemed  of  sufficient  rauk  to  sit  at  the  same  t.able  with  his 
captive  sovereign,  when  waited  upon  by  the  Black  Prince. 

The  family  uf  De  Graville  are  repeatedly  mentioned  by 
the  French  liistorians,  from  ancient  dates  down  to  modern 
times,  and  exists  to  this  day  in  its  last  male  representative, 
the  present  Marquess  Malet  de  Graville,  residing  near  Caen. 
There  is  also  an  ancient  branch  in  Jersey  (which  derives  its 
descent  from  Robert  Malet,  seigneur  de  la  Malletifere,  in  the 
parish  of  Grouville,  in  that  island,  which  formed  a  portion 
of  the  duchy  of  Normandy,)  living  in  1180,  whose  ancestors 
were  settled  there  from  the  latter  part  of  the  reign  of  tlie 
Conqueror,  and  is  so  still  represented  by  the  family  of  the 
late  Rev.  John  Mallet,  rector  of  GrouviUe,  which  has 
reverted  to  the  earlier  siu-name  of  Malet. 

Robert  Lord  Malet's  brothers  temporarily  assumed  the 
name  of  Fitchett,  after  his  and  their  attainder,  but  we 
find  the  thii-d  in  order  of  descent  having  resumed  the  name, 
and  as  William  Lord  Malet,  of  Carrii  and  Shipton  Malet, 
signing  Magna  Charta  with  the  other  barons  confederated 
against  John. 

From  this  period  the  names  of  several  notable  members 
of  the  familj'  occur  in  our  old  historians  ;  many  of  them 
were  Crusaders,  two  of  whose  monuments  still  exist  in  the 
church  of  Sheptou  Mallet ;  and  one  was  a  knight  of  the 
Garter  shortly  after  the  institution  of  the  order. 

The  elder  branches,  however,  twice  came  to  an  end  by 
heiresses:  William,  Lord  Malet,  who  signed  Magna  Charta, 
left  by  his  wife,  a  dau.  of  Thomas,  Lord  Basset,  co  heiresses, 
in.  to  Robert  Mucegros,  and  Uugh  de  Vivonia  ;  and  at  a 
later  period,  the  heiress  of  Enmore  (mentioned  by  De 
Grammont  as  "La  triste  h^ritifere,"  but  of  whose  sterling 
character  a  better  notion  is  formed  from  the  pages  of  Bur- 
nett), TO.  the  well-known  Earl  of  Rochester.  From  these 
heiresses  descend  the  families  of  Peyton,  Vivian,  Vaughan, 
Greville.  &c. 

Sir  Thomas  Malet,  Knt.  of  St.  Audries,  co.  Somerset, 
and  Pointington,  Dorset,  was  great-grandson  of  Sir  Baldwin, 
who  had  been  solicitor-general  to  Henry  VIII.  Sir  Thomas 
was  one  of  the  judges  of  the  King's  Ben  li,  in  the  17th  year 
of  Charles  I.,  and  mention  is  made  in  Clari.ndon's  His- 
tory of  the  Ribdiion,  of  his  steadfast  loyalty,  and  the  suffer- 
ings in  which  it  involved  him.  He  was  arrested  and  im- 
prisoned by  the  parliamentarj-  pai-ty,  his  property  seques- 
trated, and  one  of  his  suns  slain  in  the  battle  of  Roundway 
Down.  At  the  restoration  he  resumed  his  office,  and  was 
one  of  the  judges  who  tried  the  regicides.  Like  many  other 
loyalists,  his  services  were  inadequately  rewarded  by  a 
pension  of  £1000  per  annum  and  a  patent  of  Baronetage 
(the  fiat  bears  date  1662);  but  dying  before  the  warrant 
had  passed  the  great  seal,  the  patent  became  void.

Dc  Monte  Acuta,  and  in  EngUsh,  Montacute  ;  but  the  original

III.  William,  b.  at  Scone,  2  March,  1705;  who,  being  called

profession.  In  1733,  he  was  associated  with  the  attorney-

First  Book  of  Horace,  congratulatory  of  the  circumstance.

John  Churchill,  the  most  celebrated  captain  of  the 
period  in  which  he  lived,  was  b.  at  Ashe,  in  Devonsliire,

He  was  also  v.ith  the  duke  in  108'3,  when  the  "Gloucester"

and  Oar  sand,  and  was  one  of  those  persons  for  whose

Churchill,  of  Sandridge,  co.  Hertford.  Notwithstanding,  how- 
ever, these  sterling  marks  of  royal  ftivour.  Lord  Churchill, 
who  had  assisted  in  defeating  the  unfortunate  Duke  of 
Monmouth  at  Sedgemoor,  was  amongst  the  first  to  attach 
himself  to  the  fortunes  of  the  Prince  of  Orange,  in  1685, 
and  to  vote  in  the  Convention  Parliament  for  the  vacancy 
of  the  throne,  and  for  filling  it  with  the  Prince  and  Princess 
of  Orange.  For  these  good  services  he  was  sworn  of  the  privy 
council  to  the  new  sovereign,  and  created,  9  April,  1689,  Earl 
of  Marlborough  ;  in  which  year  he  was  sent  to  command  the 
English  forces  in  the  Netherlands,  under  Prince  Waldeck, 
general  of  the  Dutch  troops.  He  subsequently  fell  under 
the  disple?sure  of  King  William,  and  was  confined  for  a 
short  time  in  the  Tower.  Upon  the  accession  of  Queen 
Anne,  her  mijesty  appointed  the  Earl  of  Marlborough 
captain-general  of  all  her  forces  in  England,  and  of  those 
employed  in  conjunction  with  her  allies;  and  then  began 
that  military  career  which  is  one  of  the  most  briUiaut 
in  EngUsh  history.  His  first  great  campaign  was  in  1702, 
when  he  accomplished  the  reduction  of  Venloo,  Stevens- 
waert,  Ruremonde,  and  Liege,  and,  in  reward,  he  was 
created,  14  Dec.  1702,  Marquess  of  Blandford,  and  Duke  of 
Marlborouoh.  Within  two  years  afterwards,  13  (2nd,  O.S.) 
Aug.  1704,hisgracewonthegreatvictoryof  Bleinheim,  which 
has  immortalized  his  name,  and  for  which  ho  obtained  a  grant 
from  the  crown,  at  the  desire  of  parliament,  to  himself  and 
his  heirs,  of  the  royal  manor  of  Woodstock  and  hundred 
of  Wooton,  in  Oxfordshire.  Here  a  splendid  palace,  bearing 
the  proud  name  of  Blenheim,  was  erected  at  the  national

Howard,  Earl  of  Arundel,  in  a  debate  upon  the  royal  pre-

ing sheep." — '•  When  my  ancestors  were  keeping  sheep," 
replied  Spencer,  "  your  lordship's  ancestors  were  plotting 
treason."  This  excited  such  irritation,  at  the  moment,  that 
Arundel,  as  the  aggressor,  was  committed  to  the  Tower ; 
but  soon  after,  acknowledging  his  fault,  was  discharged.

The  ancient  family  of  Methuen,  or  Methven,  takes  its 
name  from  the  Barony  of  Methven,  in  Perthshire,  which 
was  bestowed  by  Malcolm  Ganmore,  King  of  Scotland, 
on  a  Gorman  of  distinction,  who  accompanied  Queen  JIar- 
garet  from  Hungary,  about  1070.  From  John  Methven, 
secretai-y  of  state  in  Scotland,  a.d.  1440,  descended 

John  Methven,  of  Bishop's  Cannings,  Wilts,  whc  w.as, 
in  the  reigns  of  William  and  Queen  Anne,  successively 
ch.ancellor  of  Ireland,  and  ambassador  to  Portugal ;  and 
was  the  framer  of  tliat  treaty  for  the  mutual  interchange  of 
port  wine  and  woollen  manufactures  which  has  subsisted 
till  within  a  few  years.     His  son. 

Sir  Paul  Methuen,  was  a  much-esteemed  minister  of 
Queen  Anne  and  of  George  I.,  one  of  the  .secretaries  of 
state,  a  knight  of  the  Bath,  envoy  to  various  states, 
ambassador  to  Madrid,  and  comptroller  of  the  household  ; 
and  was  trusted  and  regarded  as  a  man  of  the  highest 
honour  and  uncompromising  integrity.  He  possessed  dis- 
tinguished taste  in  the  fine  arts,  and  formed  a  very  extensive 
collection  of  pictures  during  his  residence  in  Italy  and  other 
courts,  which  he  bequeathed  to  his  cousin,  Paul  Methuen, 
of  Corsham  House.  He  d.  in  1757,  and  was  buried  in 
Westminster  Abbey.     He  was  .1.  by  his  cousin, 

Paul  Methuen,*  Esq.  of  Cor.sham,  M.P.    for  Warwick  ;

The  Earldom  of  Moray  became  vested  in  the  crown  of 
Scotland  by  the  forfeiture  of  Archibald  Douglas,  Earl  of 
Moray,  in  1455,  and  it  remained  dormant  nntil  the  i-eign 
of  James  IV.,  who,  by  letters  patent,  dated  20  June,  1501, 
conferred  it  upon 

James  Stuart,  his  natural  son,  bj'  the  Hon.  Janet 
Kennedy,  the  Lord  Kennedy's  daughter  ;  but  this  nolile- 
nian  dying  without  male  issue,  in  1544  (his  only  child,  JIary,

the  crown,  and  was  presented  by  Queen  Mary,  m  1548,  to

Doune.

The  Earl  of  Moray  eventually  fell  a  victim  to  one  of  his 
foes,  Hamilton  of  Bothwellhaugh,  a  man  distinguished  for 
a  vindictive  disposition.  Having  taken  singularly  active 
measures  for  effecting  his  purpose  and  his  escape,  Hamilton 
lurked  in  an  empty  lodging  in  a  street  in  Linlithgow, 
mortally  wounded  the  Earl  of  Moray  by  a  shot  from  a 
carabine  as  he  rode  through  the  town,  and,  though  closely 
pursued,  got  in  safety  to  France.  Moray  fell,  23  Jan.  1570 
in  the  37th  year  of  his  age.     He  was  «.  by  his  oldest  dau.

high-admii-al  of  Scotland ;  and  in  1572,  i-ogent  of  the  king-

worth,  and  received  the  honour  of  knighthood  from  his 
victorious  chief  on  the  field  of  battle.  He  was  afterwards 
sworn  of  the  privy  council,  and  appointed  comptroller  of 
his  household  by  the  new  monarch.  He  obtained,  likewise, 
grants  of  the  castle,  honour,  &c.,  of  Totness,  and  the  m.anor

The  family  of  Naesmyth  is  one  of  remote  antiquity  in  Tweed- 
dale,  and  has  possessed  lands  there  since  the  13th  century. 

Sir  Michael  Naesmyth,  chamberlain  of  the  archbishopric  of 
St.  Andrews,  (descended  from  Sir  Michael  Naesmyth,  who 
fought  in  the  wars  between  Bruce  and  Baliol),  obtained  the 
estates  of  Posso,  in  the  year  1544,  as  a  dowry  with  Elizabeth, 
dau.  of  John  Baird,  of  Posso.  During  the  intestine  troubles  in 
Scotland,  in  the  reign  of  Queen  Mary,  Sir  Michael  espoused  the 
cause  of  the  unfortunate  princess,  and  fought  under  her  banner 
at  Langside,  in  1568.  He  was  subsequently  banished,  and  his 
property  seized  upon  by  the  regent  Moray.  He  d.  at  an 
advanced  age,  about  the  year  1609.  Sir  Michael's  second  son, 
John,  was  chief  chirurgeon  to  his  Most  Serene  Majesty,  and  to 
the  King  of  France :  he  d.  at  London,  a.d.  1613,  and  in  his 
testament,  he  leaves  "his  hert  to  his  young  maister  the 
Prince's  grace,"  (Prince  Henry  of  Wales.)  Sir  Michael's  eldest 
son  and  successor  was 

James  Naesmyth,  of  Posso,  who  was  appointed  falconer  to 
King  James  VI.  The  royal  eyrie  of  Posso  Crag  is  in  the  family 
estate ;  and  the  lure  worn  by  Queen  Mary  and  James,  presented 
to  him  by  the  latter,  is  preserved  as  an  heirloom. 

James  Naesmyeh,  Esq.,  son  of  the  Falconer,  was  member  of 
the  Scottish  parliament  in  1627,  and  sheriff  of  the  co.  Peebles. 
This  gentleman  m.in  1610,  Agnes,  dau.  of  Wilham  Bumet4, 
Esq.  of  Barns,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son, 

James  Naesmyth,  an  eminent  lawyer,  who  was  known  by 
the  soubriquet  of  "  the  Deilo'Dawyk."  He  d.  in  1706,  and  was 
s.  by  his  son,

Lord  Napier,  an  eminent  military  commander,  is 
the  son  of  the  late  Major  Charles-Frederick  Napier, 
R.A.  (who  d.  March,  1812),  and  Catherine  his  wife 
(whom  he  m.  iu  ISOJ),  dau.  of  Codriugton  Car- 
rington,  Esq.  of  The  Chapel  and  Carringtou,  Bar- 
badoes.  His  lordship,  having  entered  the  Bengal 
engineers  in  1826,  was  highly  distinguished  in  the 
Sutlej  campaigns,  at  the  siege  of  Moultan,  at  Goo- 
jerat,  and  at  the  capture  of  Lucknow,  in  1858. 
He,  the  same  year,  defeated  the  Sepoy  rebels,  at  the 
battle  of  Powree,  and  was  made  a  K.C.B.,  and  re- 
ceived the  thauks  of  parliament.  He  again  received 
the  thanks  of  parliament  in  1861,  for  his  conduct 
in  the  operations  which  led  to  the  capture  of  Pekin. 
He  was  a  member  of  the  Council  of  India  from 
18G1  to  18o.'>,  when  he  was  appointed  commander- 
in-chief  of  the  Bombay  army,  with  the  rank  of 
general.  He  was  appointed  in  May,  1867,  to  com- 
mand the  expedition  to  Abyssinia,  and  his  admirable 
management  of  that  whole  affair,  which  ended  with 
the  storming  of  Magdala  and  the  death  of  King 
Theodore,  resulted  in  complete  success,  and  is  a 
brilliant  matter  of  history.  He  was,  in  reward, 
made  a  G.C.B,,  and  was  raised  to  the  peerage,  a.? 
Lord  Napier  of  Magdala,  17  July,  1868.  An  Act 
of  Parliament,  viz.,  the  31  and  32  Vic,  cap.  91,  was 
passed  31  July,  1868,  granting  an  annuity  of  £2,000 
to  his  lordship  and  his  next  surviving  heir  male'  for 
the  term  of  their  natural  lives.  '

Sir  Joseph  Napier,  a  very  eminent  lawyer,  orator, 
and  judge,  was  first  educated  at  the  Belfast  Aca- 
demical Institution,  where  he  was  a  distinguished 
pupil  of  James  Sheridan  Knowles  and  Dr.  James 
Thompson;  he  entered  Trinity  College,  Dublin, 
Nov.  1820,  and  obtained  premiums  and  honours  in 
classics  and  science ;  he  graduated  B.A.  in  1825, 
and  M.A.  in  1828  ;  he  had  subsequently  the  hono- 
rary degree  of  LL.D.  of  Dublin  Universitj'',  and  the 
honorary  degree  of  D.C.L.  of  Oxford  University, 
conferred  upon  him  ;  he  was  president  of  the  Dublin 
College  Historical  Society  in  1856  ;  he  was  called 
to  the  Irish  bar  in  Easter  term  18-31,  and  having 
obtained  considerable  practice  and  a  high  position 
in  his  profession,  was  made  a  Q.C.  in  Nov.  1811. 
His  subsequent  promotion  was  rapid.*  He  was 
M.P.  for  Dublin  University  in  1848,  Attorney-Gene- 
ral for  Ireland  and  P.C.  in  1852,  and  Lord  Chancellor 
of  Ireland  in  1858.  He  was,  in  1866,  offered  the 
office  of  Ljrd  Justice  of  Appeal,  but  declined  it. 
He  was  created  a  Baronet  9  April,  1867,  and  was 
appointed  Vice-Chancellor  of  the  University  of 
Dublin  (Trinity  College)  in  the  Oct.  of  the  same 
year.

"One  of  the  greatest  names,"  says  Sir  Egerton  Brydges, 
"  which  will  hereafter  occur  in  the  annals  of  British  history, 
or  perhaps  in  the  annals  of  the  world, — at  least  as  far  as 
the  operations  of  war  are  concerned, — will  be  Nelson." 
That  name,  indeed,  stands  alone  beyond  the  power  of  rank 
or  title  to  ornament  it ;  for,  the  fact  is  remarkable,  that 
while  every  other  great  man  in  our  past  records,  who 
belonged  to  or  attained  nobility,  is  usually  designated,  and 
in  some  measure  elevated,  by  his  title,  —  while  even 
WeUington  has  his  appellation  of  "the  gi-eat  Duke," — 
Nelson,  like  Casar,  retains  almost  invariably  his  patro- 
nymic only.  His  knighthood  and  his  admiral's  rank,  his 
Sicilian  dukedom,  his  Eughsh  baronj'  and  viscountcy,  cling 
but  feebly  to  the  mention  of  Nelson.  In  these  pages  too, 
where  these  honoiu's  are  necessarily  registered,  it  is  felt 
right  to  accompany  them  with  a  somewhat  lengthened 
summary  of  those  services,  which,  while  their  brilliancy 
throws  the  lustre  of  nobility  into  the  shade,  form  of  them- 
selves a  roll  of  glory,  to  be  learnt  by  all  and  to  be  forgotten 
by  none. 

The  family  of  Nelson  (filius  Nigelli,  according  to  Cam- 
den's derivation),  appears  to  have  been  of  very  ancient 
existence  in  the  co.  of  Lancaster.  Their  seat  at  Maudesley, 
where  they  held  lands  by  military  service,  is  now  in  pos- 
session of  the  Riddells  of  Northumberland,  to  whom  it  came 
by  female  descent,  some  notice  of  them  wiU  be  found  in 
the  pedigi-ee  of  Earl  Nelson,  in  Sir  Bichard  Hoare's  History 
of  South  Wilts,  under  the  head  of  Parish  of  Downton, 
p.  50.  There  is  little  doubt  that  the  immediate  ancestry  of 
William  Nelson,  living  temp.  Elizabeth  and  Edward  VI., 
came  out  of  Lancashire  in  the  suite  of  Dr.  James  Stanley, 
warden  of  Manchester,  youngest  son  of  Thomas  Stanley, 
1st  Earl  of  Derby,  which  Dr.  James  Stanley  was  elected 
Bishop  of  Ely,  22nd  Henry  VII.,  and  settled  in  Norfolk, 
where  the  See  of  Ely  had  considerable  property.  The  arms 
of  Nelson  of  Maudesley  were  borne  by  the  Norfolk  Nelsons, 
as  may  be  seen  in  old  books  and  papers  formerly  belonging 
to  the  Rev.  Edmund  Nelson,  of  Birmham  Thorpe. 

The  above-mentioned  William  Nelson,  living  temp.  Eliza- 
beth and  Edward  VI.,  was  father  of  Thomas  Nelson  of

The  5th  son  of  the  Rev.  Edmund  Nelson, 

Horatio  Nelson,  was  bom  at  the  Parsonage  house, 
Burnham  Thorpe,  Norfolk,  29  Sept.  1758,  and  received  the 
name  of  Horatio,  after  his  godfather  and  relative,  Horatio, 
2nd  Lord  Walpole,  of  Wolterton,  and  1st  Earl  of  Orford, 
of  the  second  creation.  Nelson  was  educated  at  the  high 
school  of  Norwich,  and  at  a  school  at  North  Walsham. 
He  in  1771,  through  the  interest  of  his  kind  luicle  and 
patron,  Captain  Maurice  Suckling,  joined  that  captain's 
ship,  the  "  Raisonnable,"  64  guns.  Captain  SuokUng 
being  soon  after  appointed  to  the  "  Triumph"  guard- 
ship  in  the  Medway,  Nelson  was  also  received  on  board 
that  vessel,  but,  for  more  active  employment,  went  a 
voyage  to  the  West  Indies  in  a  merchant  ship,  and  in 
1773  he  accompanied  the  expedition  under  Commodore 
Phipps  to  Greenland  and  towards  the  North  Pole.  On 
his  return  from  Greenland,  Nelson  was  rated  a  midship- 
man on  board  the  "  Seahorse."  His  ruicle.  Captain 
Mamice  Suckling,  became,  in  1775,  comptroller  of  the 
navy,  and  Nelson  was  soon  afterwards  nominated  to  act 
as  4th  lieutenant  of  the  '  Worcester,"  comm.anded  by 
Capt.  Mark  Robinson.  On  the  Sth  April,  1777,  he  passed 
his  examination  as  lieutenant,  and  the  next  day  received 
his  commission  as  2nd  lieutenant  of  the  "Lowestoffe" 
frigate,  from  which,  at  the  end  of  a  year's  active  service, 
he  was  appointed  3rd  lieutenant  of  the  "  Bristol,"  the  flag- 
ship of  Admiral  Sir  Peter  Parker.  In  1778,  at  the  close  of 
the  year,  he  was  commander  in  the  "  Badger"  brig  ;  and 
in  Jan.  1779,  post-captain.  Thus  much  for  his  early  pro- 
motions. WTiat  ensued,  requires  volumes  to  fully  relate. 
An  outline  is  given  in  the  following 

Chronological  Summary  : — 1779,  June  11,  Nelson  was 
appointed  to  the  "Hinohinbroke,"  20  gims.  In  1780,  in 
the  expedition  against  the  Spanish  settlements  situate  in 
the  river  St.  John,  in  the  giilf  of  Mexico,  Captain  Nelson 
commanded  the  naval  part  of  the  expedition,  and  materially 
contributed  to  the  captui-e  of  Fort  St.  Juan.  At  the  close 
of  this  year  he  returned  to  England,  on  accoiuit  of  ill  health. 

1781,  Aug.,  he  was  appointed  to  the  "  Albemarle,"  of  28 
guns,  and  went  to  Newfoimdland,  and  was  then  ordered  to 
cruise  off  Brest ;   he    prooeeded   afterwards  to  Quebec  in 

1782,  and  continued  actively  and  efl5ciently  employed 
during  the  remainder  of  the  American  war.  On  the  con- 
clusion of  peace,  he  attended  Prince  William  Henry  (after- 
wards William  IV.)  on  his  visit  to  the  Governor  of  the 
Havannah.  1784,  March,  he  was  appointed  to  the  "Boreas," 
frigate,  28  giuis,  a  cruiser  for  the  Leeward  Islands,  on  the 
peace  estabUshment.  In  this  sei-vice.  Nelson  acted  with 
memorable  spirit  and  energy,  in  foiUng  the  scheme  of  the 
Americans  to  trade  with  our  islands,  under  pretext  that 
their  ships  were  British  registered,  though  such  registra- 
tion merely  appUed  to  them  prior  to  their  separation  from 
the  mother  coimtry.  Nelson's  determined  and  rightful 
conduct  on  this  occasion  subjected  him  to  attempted  legal 
proceedings  and  to  much  vexation,  but  he  eventually, 
aided  by  government,  triumphed  completely  over  his 
opponents.  1787,  March  11,  he  married  Mrs.  Nisbet, 
and  it  was  Prince  Wilham-Henry,  then  captain  of  the 
"Pegasus,"  that  gave  away  the  bride.  From  this  period 
till  the  war  with  France,  Nelson  lived  chiefly  in  retire- 
ment at  his  father's  parsonage  of  Biimham  Thorpe  until 
1793,  when  on  Jan.  30,  just  as  war  was  declared,  he  was 
appointed  to  the  "  Agamemnon,"  of  64  guns,  and  sailed 
for  the  Mediterranean,  and  jomed  the  fleet  under  Lord 
Hood.  Fe  served  at  Toulon,  and  bore  the  despatches 
to    Naples   to   the  British    envoy.   Sir  Wilham  Hamilton, 


N  E  L 


N  E  L 


and  then  first  made  acquaiiitanoe  with  the  beautiful  and 
accomplished  Emma,  Lady  Hamilton,  who  exercised  such 
influence  over  his  subsequent  fortunes,  and  who  may  be  well 
said  to  have  been  the  Agues  Sorel  of  his  glorious  career. 
In  1794,  he  commanded  the  detachment  of  seamen  on  shore 
in  Corsica,  and  maiuly  contributed  to  the  capture  of  Bastia 
and  Calvi:  he  lost  an  eye  at  the   siege  of  Calvi.     In  1795, 
March    13,   a   gallant  encoiuiter  took    place    between  the 
"  Agamemnon, "  commanded  by  Nelson,  and  the  "Ca  Ira,' 
84  guns,   a   French  republican    ship,    in    which   the    "Ca 
Ira"   escaped   for   the  moment   with   difficulty ;    but   the 
following  morning,  in  a  renewed  contest,  had,    as    well  as 
the  "Censeur,"  to  strike  to  Nelson.     In  July,  1795,  Nelson 
sailed   -ndth   a   small  squadron  of  five  ships  of   war,    and 
performed  numerous  exploits,  scouring  the   coast  of  Italy, 
and   destroying  nine  French    ships  of  war   in    the   neigh- 
Dourhood  of  Vado ;  and  in  December  he   hoisted  his  broad 
pendant  on   board   "  La  Minerve,"  32  guns  ;  Dec.    19,    he 
captured  "La  Sabine,"   of   40   guns.      1797,    Feb.    13,    he 
shifted   his   pendant  on  board  the    "  Captain,"  and   the 
next  day  occurred  the  B.\ttle  of  St.  Vincent,  won,  under 
the  command   of  the   illustrious  Sir  John  Jervis.      Nelson 
performed   prodigies  of  valoiu-.      The    "  St.  Nicholas"  and 
"San  Josef"  were  successively  taken,  Nelson  personally 
heading  the  assailants,  and  exclaiming,  as   he  rushed  into 
the   latter  vessel,    "  Westminster  Abbey  or  victory  1"    The 
battle    of   St.   Vincent  may   be    said   to   have  opened  the 
era  of  naval  conquest   that  followed.     Jervis  received  an 
earldom,  and  Nelson  was  rewarded  with  the  order  of  the 
Bath,   and  a  gold  medal  from  the  King  :  he  was  presented 
by  the   City  of  London  with  its  freedom  in  a  gold  box. 
Feb.    20,    1797,    Nelson    was    promoted    to    the    rank    of 
rear-admiral  of   the  Blue  ;    and   was    despatched,   in   the 
April  following,  to  bring  off  the  garrison  of  Porto  Ferrajio; 
and  May  27th,  he   commanded  a  detachment  of  the  fleet 
employed  in  the  blockade  of  Cadiz  ;   July  3rd,  he,   in  his 
barge,  with  ten   men,   engaged  and  captured  Don  Miguel 
Tregoyen,  the  Spanish  commander  at  Cadiz,  in  his  galley, 
with  a  crew  of   twenty-six   men  ;    July  27,    in   company 
with   the    "Theseus,"    "Culloden,"    and    the    "Zealous," 
the    "Leander,"  and    other   vessels,    he    makes  a  daring 
attack    on    the   town   of   Santa    Cruz,    but   in   the    midst 
of  the   conflict  he  loses  his  right  arm  by  a  cannon-shot. 
His  Ufe  is   saved  by  his  son-in-law.    Captain  Josiah  Nisbet, 
after  which  the  English  take  possession  of  the  town,  but  are 
eventually  obliged  to  retire.     Nelson  returns   to    England 
for  the  recovery  of  his  health;  October,  a  pension  of  1,000Z. 
a-year  granted  him,  he  having  by  this  time  been  engaged 
against  the  enemy  one  hmidred  and  twenty  times  ;  Dec. 
19,  hoists  his  flag  on  board   the   "  Vang-uard,"  and  is  de- 
tached with  three   ships  of  the  line,   two   frigates,  and  a 
sloop,  to  watch  the  motions  of  a  formidable  French  arma- 
ment, and  follows  them  to   Egypt.     1798,  June  5,  joined  at 
sea  by  Captain  Troubridge,   with  ten  sail  of  the  line  and 
a  50  gun-ship ;   Aug.   1,    Battle  of   the  Nile,  and  utter 
destruction  of  the  French  armament  in  the  Bay  of  Aboukir. 
The  French  fleet  consisted  of  17  ships;  13  were  taken  or 
burnt,  and  4  only — two  ships  of  the  line  and  two  frigates — • 
escaped.    Nelson  was   severely  wounded  in  the  forehead, 
but  when  his  woimd  was  di-essed,  he  came  back  upon  deck 
to  see  the  battle  concluded,   and  to  save   as  many  as  he 
could  of  the  enemy  from  the   ships  that  were  on  fire.     The 
stupendous    victory    of    the    Nile    timied   the   feeling   of 
Europe  in  favour  of  Britain  and  against  France.    Nelson 
was  created   6  Nov.  1798,   Baron  Nelson,  of  the  Nile,  and 
ofBurnham  Thorpe,  in  the  co.  of  Norfolk.    Parliament  decreed 
Nelson   a   vote  of  thanks,   and  2,000^.  a-year  for  his  own 
life,   and  the   lives  of  his  two  immediate  successors.     He 
received  from   the    parliament   of    Ireland    l.OOOi.    aryear. 
The    East   India    Company    also    voted    him    10,000;.      A 
service   of    plate   from   the   Turkey   merchants ;   a  sword 
from  the  city  of  London  ;  a  magnificent  diamond  aigi-ette, 
with  a  plume  of  triimiph  and  a  robe  of  honour  from  the 
Sultan,   and  other   valuable  presents   from    the   Emperor 
of  Russia,  the  King  of   Naples,  and  the  King  of  Sardmia 
were   bestowed  on  Nelson  ;  Aug.   IS,   1798,   Nelson   sailed 
from  Egypt ;    and  Sept.   22  arrived  at  Naples,  where  he 
was  received  with   every  demonstration  of  joy  and  afiec- 
tion   by  the  king,   queen,   and   people.      In  October,   he 
blockaded  Malta ;    and    Dec.   21,    rescued   the  Neapolitan 
royal   family  from    the  palace  at  Naples,    and   conveyed 
them    safely  to  Palermo  :    he   became  at   this   time   still 
more  attached  to  the  society  of  Lady  Hamilton.     In  1799 
occurred    the   transactions   in   the  Bay  of   Naples  ;    and, 
in   June   28    of   that   year,  the    execution   for   treason   of 
Admu-al  Caraccioli,  in  which  affair  Nelson's  conduct  has 
been  so  severely  commented  on.     The  French  were  driven

from    Naples,   and   the    king  reconducted   to   his   capital.

kir ;  Nov.  6,  landed  at  Yarmouth,  and  proceeded  to  London,

and  Commons  for  the  attack  on   Copenhagen.     Nelson  was 
created   22   May,   1801,    Vincount  Nelsoyi,  of  the  Nile,  and  of

two   unsuccessful   attacks  on  the  gmiboats  oS'  Boulogne. 
Nelson  was  created  IS  Aug.   1801,  Baron  Nelson  of  the  Nile, 
and  of  Hilborough,  co.  Norfolk,  with  remainder,   failing  his 
heirs  male,  to  his  father  and  his  heirs  male,   and   failing

Matcham.     In  Sept.    12,  of  the  same  year,  he  also  received 
the  British  royal  licence    to   accept  for   himself   and   his 
heirs  the  title   of  Duke  of  Brontd,    with  the  fief  of  the 
duchy  annexed.     1802,   peace   of  Amiens,  when  Nelson  re- 
tired for  a  time  into  private   life.     1803,   his  friend,    Sir 
■WiUiam   Hamilton,   died,    "expiring,"  says  Southey,  "in 
his  wife's  arms,  and  holding  Nelson  by  the  hand,  to  whose 
protection  almost  in  his  last  words  he  left  her,  requesting 
him  that  he  would  see  justice  done  her  by  the  government, 
as  he  knew  what  she  had  done  for  the  country."    May  12, 
1S03,  Nelson  hoists  his  flag  on  board  the   "  Victory,"  100 
guns,  and  proceeds  to  Gibraltar.     1804,  August  IS,  arrives  at 
Portsmouth,   after    having    traversed  the  space   of   ocean 
stretched  between  Eui'ope  and  America,   within  a  period 
incredibly  short,   in  search  of  the  allied  fleets  of   France 
and  Spain.     1805,  Sept.  15,  left   England  for  the  last  time, 
and  put  to   sea  at  Portsmouth  on   board  the  "Victory," 
with  the  "Ajax"  and  the    "Thunderer,"  to  join  Admiral 
Collingwood,   who   was  watching  the  combined  fleets  then 
in  Cadiz  harbour  ;  Oct.   21,   discovers  the  combined  fleets 
off  Trafalgar  Bay  ;  Oct.   21,    Battle  or  Trafalqae,   when 
Nelson  gained  the  object  of  his  own  prayer — a  great  and 
glorious  victory — the  greatest  and  most  glorious,  indeed, 
that  Englaiiii  ever  won.     Nelson  himself  gave  the  memor- 
able  signal,    "  England    expects   every   man    will   do   his 
duty,"  and  his  flag-ship  led  the  weather  column.     The  ac- 
tion began  at  twelve  o'clock,  and  by  three  o'clock  the  British 
fleet  had   captured  nineteen  sail  of  the  line  out  of  thirty- 
three  from  the  enemy,  to  whom  it  was  not  defeat  alone,  but 
annihilation.     England  lost  her  hero.     At  fifteen  minutes 
after  one  o'clock.   Nelson,   while  with  Captain  (afterwards 
Vice-Admiral  Sir  Thomas-Masterman)  Hardy  on  the  quarter- 
deck  of  the  "Victory,"  was  mortally  woimded  in  the  left 
shoulder  by  a  musket  ball  fired  from  the  mizen-top  of  the 
French  ship,   the    "  Redoutable."     He  was  carried  to   the 
cockpit  by  Sergeant  Seeker,  and  laid  on  a  mattrass,  and 
was  attended  by  Mr.    (afterwards  Sir  William)  Beatty,  the 
surgeon,  the  Rev.  Mr.  Scott,   and  the   purser,  Mr.  Burke, 
and   he   was    constantly   visited   by  Captain   Hardy,   who 
cheered   him   in   his    agony,    with   the    certainty   of    his 
triumph.      His   last   audible   words  were,    "  Thank  God, 
I  have   done  my  duty."     He  died  at  thirty  minutes  past 
foiu-  o'clock.     The   "Victory"  carried  Nelson's  body,  pre- 
served in  spirits  of  wine,  to  England,  and  after  stopping 
at   Gibraltar    on    the    way,    arrived    at    the   Nore.      The 
remains  were  enclosed  in  the  coffin  that  had  been  made 
from   the  mainmast  of  Admiral  Brueys',  the  French  com- 
mander's ship,  the   "Orient,"  and  presented  to  Nelson  by 
his  friend   Captain  HaUowell,  after  the  battle  of  the  Nile. 
The  body  lay  in  state  for  three  days  in  December,  in  the 
Painted   Hall  of  Greenwich  Hospital  ;   and   again   at   the 
Admiralty  ;  and  on  the  9  Jan.  1806,  it  was  honoured  by  a 
public  fvmeral,  and  deposited  in  the  Cathedral  of  St.  Paul's, 
adjacent    to  where    repose   the   remains   of  Nelson's   two 
gallant  companions  in  arms  at  Trafalgar,  ColUngwood,  and 
Northesk,    and    also    the    remams    of    the   great   Duke 
of   Wellington.      "  The   most    triumphant    death,"  wi-ites

The  family  of  Netterville  is  of  Norman  descent  and  of  con- 
siderable antiquity ;  it  took  from  an  early  period  an  import- 
ant and  historic  position  in  Ireland,  and  made  high  connec- 
tions and  alliances  there.  It  was  settled  at  Douth,  co.  Meath, 
in  the  reign  of  Henry  II.

justices  of  the  court  of  Queen's  Bench  in  Ireland,  15  Oct.  1559.

*  The  family  of  Bandini  was  originally  seated  in  Tuscany, 
and  was  one  of  the  most  ancient  and  noblehousesof  that  duchy. 
Bernard  Bandini,  in  1478,  took  a  prominent  part  in  the  con- 
spiracy against  the  Medicis,  called  the  Conjuration  of  Pazzi, 
and  in  consequence  the  family  quitted  Tuscany,  and  established 
themselves  in  the  Roman  States.  In  1512,  Leonardo  Bandini 
was  master  of  the  horse  to  Pojie  Julius  II.,  and  commanded  the 
Papal  army  at  the  siege  of  Pesaro,  a  fortress  which  had  been 
seized  by  Galeazzo  Sforza,  and  upon  its  reduction  was  appointed 
castillan  or  governor  of  the  castle.  Cornelius  Bandini  highly 
distinguished  himself  at  the  battle  of  Montemarlo,  in  1537.  "  On 
the  29th  of  October,  1721,  the  Castle  of  Varano,  and  the  adjoin- 
ing territory,  were  erected  into  a  lordship,  in  favoiu-  of  the 
Bandini  family;  and  Alexander  Bandini,  Lord  of  Verano,  and 
several  other  lordships,  and  chamberlain  to  the  Emperor,  was, 
on  the  30tli  of  May,  1753,  created  Marquess  Bandini  of  Lanciano 
and  Rustano,  in  the  Roman  States.  Charles,  the  4th  and  late 
JIarquess  Bandini,  was  the  great-grandson  of  Alexander,  and 
the  head  of  the  Camerino  branch  of  the  Bandini  family. 

t  In  the  recent  diploma,  mentioned  in  the  text,  giving 
the  title  of  Prince  to  Lord  Kynnaird,  Pope  Pius  IX.  thus 
records  the  ancestorial  fame  of  the  family: — "The  Race 
of  the  Bandini  were  men  conspicuous  in  war  and  in  peace, 
and  flourishing  from  the  olden  times  For  it  appears  that 
in  the  Fifteenth  Centuiy,  Slelchior  Bandini,  one  of  the 
Knights  of  Jei-usalem,  having  been  appointed  to  the  Highest 
Offices  in  that  Order,  discliarged  them  with  the  greatest 
glory.  Again  in  the  Sixteenth  Century,  Cornelius  Bandini, 
having  been  made  a  General  of  the  French  Troops  in  the  Army 
of  King  Francis  the  First,  gave  illustrious  proofs  of  military 
valour;  nor  have  Piene  and  Itodolph,  most  distinguished  Chiefs 
sprung  from  the  same  stock,  less  excelled  in  the  science  of  war- 
fare or  greatness  of  mind.  Nor  do  we  deem  it  right  to  pass  over 
that  experienced  Councillor  at  the  Court  of  Our'Predecessor  of 
happy  memory  Julius  the  Second,  Leonard  Bandini,  on  whose 
ability  and  trustworthiness  Our  said  Predecessor  is  said  so  nnich 
to  have  relied,  that  he  sent  him  against  Galeatius  Sfortia  and 
the  Aragonese  to  regain  the  Fortress  of  Pesaro,  and  appointed 
him  Commander  of  the  same  Fortress.  Philip  Bandini  also  was 
Gentleman  of  the  Bed  Chandler  of  Our  Predecessor,  Innocent  the

*  The  end  of  the  ill-staiTed  Charles  Radcliffe,  titidar  Earl  of 
Derwentwater,  was  somewhat  summary  and  peculiar.  After 
his  conviction,  in  1716,  he  received  several  reja'ieves  ii'om  time 
to  time,  and  probably  on  account  of  his  youtli,  and  the  govern- 
ment wishing  to  shed  no  more  of  the  blood  of  tis  house,  he 
would  have  been  pardoned,  but  he  and  thirteen  others  made 
their  escape  from  Newgate  11  Dec.  1716,  and  thus  placed  them- 
selves beyond  the  benefit  even  of  the  general  act  of  grace  which 
was  passed  about  that  time.  Radcliffe,  on  reaching  the  con- 
tinent, went  to  Rome,  and  obtained  a  small  pension  from  the 
Chevalier;  he  then  settled  in  Paris,  and  there  man-ied  Lady 
Newburgh:  he  twice,  during  liis  exile,  came  to  London,  and, 
though  his  presence  was  known  to  govennnent,  his  visits  passed 
unmolested.  The  rising  of  1745  brought  him  again  into  action. 
He  sailed  fi-om  Calais  in  the  November  of  that  year  on  board  a 
French  man-of-war,  with  his  son,  and  with  some  other  officers, 
and  a  quantity  of  ammunition  of  war.  The  vessel,  no  doubt 
bound  for  Scotland  in  aid  of  the  insurgents  (though  there  was 
no  legal  proof  given  of  the  fact),  was  seized  in  open  sea  by  the 
Sheeniess  man-of-war,  and  brought  to  Deal.  Radcliffe  and  his 
son  were  committed  to  the  Tower.  The  son  being  deemed  a 
foreigner,  was  exchanged  on  the  first  cartel ;  but  Radcliffe  him- 
self was  confined  till  the  rebellion  was  over,  when  in  Michaelmas 
term  1746,  he  was  brought  to  the  bar  of  the  Court  of  King's 
Bench,  to  have  execution  awarded  against  him  on  his  fonner 
sentence :  he  pleaded  that  he  was  not  the  same  person  as  the 
party  convicted,  and  prayed  time  to  bring  witnesses;  but,  as  he 
would  not  deny,  in  his  affidavit  relative  to  the  absence  of  wit- 
nesses, that  he  was  the  attainted  Charles  Radcliffe,  the  court 
proceeded  and  decided  against  his  plea:  he  then  wished  to 
plead  the  general  pardon  of  1710,  but  the  court  (one  judge,  Sir 
Michael  Foster,  dissenting)  would  hear  no  further  plea,  and  the 
prisoner  was  ordered  for  execution.  Though  then  legally  no 
nobleman,  regard  was  so  far  paid  to  the  rank  and  station  of  his 
familv  that  he  did  not  undergo  the,  in  those  days,  o.dinary  and 
horrible  punishment  for  treason,  but,  like  his  brother,  tlie  Earl 
of  Derwentwater,  he  was  decapitated  on  Tower  Hdl.  He  died 
as  he  ha<l  lived,  one  of  the  most  unbending  and  devoted  ad- 
herents of  the  House  of  Stuart,  and  behaved  at  his  execution 
with  dignified  calmness  and  courage.  Charies  Radcliffe  was 
the  mainspring  of  the  support  bis  house  gave  to  the  Chevalier: 
he  and  his  brother,  beside  their  lives,  lost  in  the  cause,  300,000?  . 
in  real  value.

This  family  is  supposed  by  some  to  derive  its  surname 
of  Clinton  from  a  lordship  iu  a  valley  three  miles  north  of 
Woodstock,  in  the  co.  of  Oxford,  at  present  denominated 
Glimptou,  and  to  deduce  its  descent  from  William  de 
Villa  Taucredi,  chamberlain  of  Normandy,  and  Maud  his 
wife,  dau.  of  William  de  Arches,  descended  from  Wevia, 
sister  to  Gunora,  Duchess  of  Normandy.  By  others,  how- 
ever, It  is  said  to  be  of  Anglo-Saxon  origin. 

John  de  Clinton,  of  Amington,  co.  Warwick,  was  sum- 
moned to  Parliament  as  Baron  Clinton,  of  Maxtock,  in  the 
27th  Edward  I.,  6  Feb.  1299  ;  and  in  a  summons  to  meet 
the  king,  with  horse  and  arms,  in  1300,  he  is  denominated 
of  Maxstock,  co.  Warwick.  He  m.  Ida.  dau.  of  Sir  William-de 
Odingsells,  Lord  of  Maxtock  Castle,  and  other  possessions 
in  Warwickshire,* and  had  two  sons ;  the  younger  of  whom, 

Sir  William  de  Clinton,  m.  Julian,  dau.  and  heiress  of 
Sir  Thomas  de  Leyburne,  Knt.,  and  widow  of  John,  Lord 
Hastings  of  Bergavenny,  by  which  alliance  it  is  presumed 
that  his  subsequent  advancement  in  life  was  considerably 
promoted ;  he  was,  however,  himself  a  very  eminent  person, 
and  fully  entitled  by  his  own  deeds  to  the  high  honours  he 
attained.  In  the  year  ensuing  his  marriage.  Sir  William 
was  made  justice  of  Chester,  and  within  less  than  two 
months  afterwards  constable  of  Dover  Castle,  and  warden 
of  the  Cinque  Ports.  Shortly  after  this,  being  one  of  those 
who  surprised  the  great  Mortimer,  at  Nottingham  Castle, 
lie  had  summons  to  parliament  as  Baron  Clinton,  on  the 
6th  Sept.  1330,  and  from  that  period  to  the  14th  Jan.  1337. 
In  three  years  subsequently,  7th  Edward  III.,  his  lordship 
was  constituted  Lord  Admiral  of  the  seas,  from  the  Thames 
westwai-d,  and  in  that  year  he  was  engaged  in  the  Scottish 
wars,  as  he  was  in  the  yth  and  10th  of  the  same  reign.  In 
the  11th  Edward  III.,  then  enjoying  the  highest  favour  of 
the  king,  his  lordship  was  created,  by  letters-patent  dated 
16th  March,  1337,  Earl  of  Huntingdon,  having,  at  the 
same  time,  not  only  £l:0  per  annum  given  him  out  of  tne 
issues  of  the  county,  to  be  paid  by  the  sheriflf,  but  one 
thousand  marks  per  annum  in  land,  to  hold  to  himself  and 
his  male  heirs  for  ever.  He  subsequently  participated  in 
his  gallant  sovereign's  wars,  both  in  Scotland  and  France, 
and  was  frequently  employed  iu  foreign  embassies  of  the 
first  importance.  He  was  a  second  time  constituted  lord 
admiral,  and  a  second  time  appointed  constable  of  Dover 
Castle,  and  lord  warden  of  the  Cinque  Ports.  His  lord- 
ship d.  in  1354,  leaving,  according  to  Banks,  an  only

Norfolk,  Duke  of  (Henry  Fitzalan-Howard), 
Earl  of  Arundel,  Surrey,  and  Norfolk,  Baron  Fitz- 
alan,  Clun,  Oswaldestrie,  and  Maltravers ;  Earl- 
Marshal  and  Hereditary  Marshal  of  England  ; 
premier  duke,  immediately  after  the  princes  of  the 
blood-royal,  and  premier  earl,  h.  27  Dec.  1847,  s.  his 
fathei  as  15th  duke,  25   Nov.  1860. 

Etitragf. 

This  ducal  house  stands,  next  to  the  blood-royal,  at  the 
head  of  the  peerage  of  England,  and  is  the  chief  of  the 
family  of  Howard,  of  whose  origin  Dugdale  thus  speaks :-  • 
"  There  are  those,  perhaps,  who  will  expect  that  I  should 
ascend  much  higher  in  manifesting  the  greatness  of  this 
honourable  and  large-spreading  fariiily  of  Howard,  in  re- 
gard I  do  not  make  any  mention  thereof  above  the  time  of 
Edward  I.,  some  supposing  that  their  common  ancestor, 
in  the  Saxon  time,  took  his  original  appellation  from  an 
eminent  ofl5ce  or  command  ;  others,  afterwards,  from  the 
name  of  a  place.  And  some  have  not  stuck  to  derive  him 
from  the  famous  Hereward,  the  chief  conductor  of  those 
forces  which  so  stoutly  defended  the  Isle  of  Ely,  for  a  time, 
against  William  the  Conqueror  and  his  army.  B  it  to 
this  last  I  cannot  well  assent,  by  reason  that  Ingulph,  then 
abbot  of  Crouland,  who  was  his  contemporary,  affirms  that 
Hereward  left  no  other  issue  than  an  heir  female,  named 
Turfrida,  wife  to  Hugh  de  Evermue,  Lord  of  Doping,  co. 
Lincoln.  I  shall,  therefore,  after  much  fruitless  search  to 
satisfy  myself,  as  well  as  others,  on  this  point,  begin  with 
William  How.ard,  a  learned  and  reverend  judge  of  the  Court 
of  Common  Pleas,  for  a  great  part  of  the  reign  of  Edward  I. 
and  beginning  of  that  of  Edward  II."  Despite,  however, 
of  Dugdale's  inability  to  discover  the  parentage  of  the  judge, 
it  appears  clearly  proved  from  various  charters,  that  that 
learned  personage  was  son  of  John  Howard  and  grandson 
of  Robert  Howard,  or  Herward,  "filius  Hawardi"  and  that 
the  name  was  originally  Herward  (see  Burke's  Extinct 
Peerage,  Ed.  1866). 

This  William  Howard,  the  judge  of  whom  we  hav& 
Just    spoken,   was  chief  justice    of    the    Common    Pleas,.

Sir  John  Howard,  an  eminent  Yorkist,  not  only  on 
account  of  his  princely  birth  (maternally)  and  magnificent 
fortune,  but  from  the  stations  of  high  trust  which  at  different 
periods  had  devolved  upon  him.  After  distinguishing  him- 
self very  early  in  life  in  the  French  wars  of  Henry  VI.,  Sir 
John  was  constituted  by  Edward  IV.,  in  1401,  constable 
of  the  castle  of  Norwich,  appointed  sheriff  of  the  cos.  of 
Norfolk  and  Sutfulk,  aud  granted  some  of  the  forfeited 
manors  of  James  Butler,  Earl  of  Wiltshire,  in  England,  and 
of  Ormonde,  in  Ireland.  In  14GS,  being  treasurer  of  the 
king's  household.  Sir  John  Howard  obtained  a  grant  of  the 
whole  benefit  that  should  accrue  to  the  king  by  coinage  of 
money  in  the  city  and  Tower  of  Loudon,  or  elsewhere  in 
the  realm  of  England,  so  long  as  he  should  continue  in  that 
office.  In  1470,  when  he  was  summoned  to  parliament 
under  the  title  of  Lord  Ilou-aixl,  he  was  made  captain- 
general  of  all  the  kuig's  forces  at  sea  for  resisting  the  I

I.  Henrv,  K.G.,  Earl  of  Surrey,  b.  in  1517,  one  of  the 
brightest  ornaments  of  the  house  of  Howard,  whose  ini- 
quitous execution  was  the  last  tyrannical  act  of  IIenby  VHI. 
This  distinguished  statesman,  i-ioet,  and  warrior,  Sir  Egerton 
Biydges  thus  characterizes: — "Excellent  in  arts  and  in 
anns;  a  man  of  learning,  a  genius,  and  a  hero;  of  a  gene- 
rous temper  and  a  refined  heart;  he  united  all  the  gallantry 
and  unbroken  spirit  of  a  rude  age  with  all  the  elegance  and 
grace  of  a  polished  era.  With  a  splendour  of  descent,  in 
possession  of  the  highest  honours  and  abundant  wealth,  be 
relaxed  not  his  efforts  to  deserve  distinction  by  his  personal 
worth.  Conspicuous  in  the  rough  exercises  of  tilts  and 
tournaments,  and  commanding  armies  with  skill  and  bravery 
in  expeditions  against  the  Scots  under  his  father,  he  found 
time,  at  a  period  when  our  literature  was  rude  and  barba- 
rous, to  cultivate  his  mind  with  all  the  exquisite  spirit  of  the 
models  of  Greece  and  Rome,  to  catch  the  excellencies  of  the 
revived  muses  of  Italy,  and  to  produce  in  his  own  language, 
compositions,  which,  in  simplicity,  perspicuity,  graceful 
ornament,  and  just  and  natural  thought,  exhibited  a  shining 
contrast  with  the  works  of  his  predecessors,  and  an  example 
which  his  successors  long  attempted  in  vain  to  follow."  The 
Earl  of  Surrey  underwent  the  penalty  of  his  unjust  sentence 
during  the  lifetime  of  bis  father  (whom  the  death  of  the 
kingpreservedfromtbosamefate),  21  Jan.  l.'j47,  leaving  issue

The  Phipps  family  was,  during  the  16th  and  early  part  of 
the  17th  century,  resident  upon  landed  property  in  the  co. 
of  Lincoln,  on  which  Col.  William  Phipps  raised  a  regiment 
of  horse  for  the  service  of  King  Charles  during  the  civil 
wars.     His  grandson.

Edward  North  was  bom  about  the  year  14P6,  and 
brought  up  to  the  profession  of  the  law  ;  in  which  he  made 
so  fair  a  progress,  that  he  was  elected  one  of  the  council  for 
the  city  of  London.  In  the  22nd  Henry  VIII.,  Mr.  North 
was  appointed  joint  clerk  of  the  parliament,  .and  in  six 
years  afterwards  (1536)  he  became  one  of  the  king's  serjeants- 
at-law.  On  the  surrender  of  the  former  post,  h-  was  made 
treasurer  of  the  Court  of  Augmentations,  an  oflBce  newly 
erected  upon  the  dissolution  of  the  monasteries  ;  and  he 
became  afterwards  chancellor  of  the  court.  He  was  soon 
after  knighted,  and  returned  to  parliament  as  representative 
of  the  CO.  Cambridge.  We  next  find  Sir  Edward  a  privy- 
councillor,  and  in  such  favour  with  the  kmg,  as  to  obtain 
various  grants  of  lands  from  the  crown,  and  at  his  High- 
ness's  death,  to  be  appointed  one  of  his  executors,  with  a 
legacy  of  £300.  After  the  accession  of  Edward  VI.,  he 
was  re-sworn  of  the  privy  council,  and  re-elected  for 
Cambridgeshire.  But  upon  the  decease  of  that  monarch, 
Sir  Edward  seems  to  have  espoused  the  cause  of  Lady 
Jane  Grey.  He  made  his  peace,  however,  very  soon  with 
Queen  Mary,  for  on  her  accession  he  was  again  sworn  of 
the  privy  comicil,  and  elevated  to  the  peerage  in  the  first 
year  of  her  reign,  17  Feb.  1553-4,  being  then  summoned  to 
parliament  as  Baron  NoHh,  of  Kirtling,  co.  Cambridge  (a. 
manor  which  he  piu-chased  about  the  time  he  was  appointed 
clerk  of  the  parliament).  In  the  reign  of  Elizabeth,  Lord 
North  was  constituted  lord-lieutenant  of  Cambridgeshire 
and  the  Isle  of  Ely.  His  lordship  in.  1st,  Alice,  dau.  of 
Oliver  Squyer,  Esq.  of  Southby,  co.  Southampton,  and 
widow  of  Edward  MyrfFun,  Esq.,  and  of  John  Brigadine, 
Esq.  of  Southampton.  By  this  lady  he  acquired  a  con- 
siderable fortmie,  and  had  two  sons  and  two  daus.,  viz.,

The  great  antiquity  and  high  respectability  of  this  family 
is  clearly  proved  by  an  ancient  and  coiiious  pedigree,  pre- 
served in  the  College  of  Arms,  accompanied  by  a  great 
number  of  family  deeds,  fines,  wills,  &c.,  to  several  of 
which  are  affixed  their  seals  of  arms  ;  which  pedigree  is 
continued  down  to  the  visitation  of  1020,  in  the  reign  of 
King  James  I.  There  is  no  doubt  whatever  that  the  name 
is  of  local  derivation,  being  originally  written  Al,  or  De 
Northcote,  a  hamlet  or  manor  in  the  parish  of  Inwardlegh, 
in  Devonshire,  which,  as  Sir  William  Pole  says,  "gave  name 
unto  bis  dwellers,  of  whom  John  Northcot,  in  King, 
Henry  the  IVth's  time,  left  Jone,  bis  daughter,  man-ied 
unto  John  Loterell,  and  by  this  means  the  land  became 
Loterel's."  And  in  .another  place  he  observes,  "  Joell  de 
Northcote  held  four  parts  of  a  knight's  fee  of  the  Bishop  of 
Exon,  in  King  Henry  the  Ilnd's  time.  The  name  reinaynes  ; 
the  land  in  others."  The  first  ancestor  we  find  on  record  is 
in  the  year  1103,  being  the  third  year  of  the  reign  of  King 
Henry  L,  when  Galfridus  Miles  bad  his  seat  at  Northcote,  in 
the  parish  of  East  Down,  in  the  co.  of  Devon.  He  was  s. 
by  John,  his  son,  styled  "Johannes,  filius  Johannis  Galfride 
Miles,  habitantis  in  Northcote,  in  i^arochia  de  East  Down, 
in  Devon  ;  mutavit  nomen  cum  loco."  Thus,  says  an 
ancient  record,  late  in  the  possession  of  Thomas  Wescote, 
gent.  This  John  was  s.  by  Galfridus  de  Northcote,  in 
1118,  of  whomitis  observed,  "Galfridusde  Northcote  tenet 
in  Northcote  mium  fcedium  de  Abbate  de  Tavi.stock  in 
manerio  de  Burington  et  hundred  de  North  Tawnton." 
He  held  lands  also  in  Colston,  in  Witheridge  Hundred,  and 
had  two  sons,  viz.,  William  and  Walter.  William  de

The  Duke,  prior  to  his  accession  to  the  peerage,  sat

AVe  cannot  more  appropriately  introduce  the  lineage  of  the 
Percys,  than  by  the  following  extract  from  a  periodical  work  of 
great  ability  and  influence — the  Percys,  whose  nobility  dates 
as  remotely  as  the  sovereignty  of  Normandy,  and  whose  renown, 
coeval  with  its  noliility,  has  flourished  in  every  age,  and  co- 
existed with  every  generation  since:  "Not  more  famous  in 
arms  than  distinguished  for  its  alliances,"  says  the  writer  to 
whom  we  refer,  "  the  house  of  Percy  stands  pre-eminent  for 
the  number  and  rank  of  the  families  which  are  represented  by 
the  present  Duke  of  Northumberland;  whose  banner,  conse- 
(juently,  exhibits  an  assemblage  of  nearly  nine  hundred  armoi'ial 
ensigns ;  among  which  are  those  of  King  Henry  VII.,  of  several 
younger  branches  of  the  Blood  Royal,  of  the  Sovereign  Houses 
of  France,  Castile,  Leon,  and  Scotland,  and  of  the  Ducal  Houses 
of  Normandy  and  Brittany,  forming  a  galaxy  of  heraldic 
honours  altogether  unparalleled." 

The  house  of  Percy  was  founded  in  England  by  one  of  the 
Norman  chieftains  (William  de  Percy),  who  accompanied 
William  the  Conqueror  in  106G,  and  it  derives  its  name  from 
the  village  of  Percy,  near  Villedieu.  The  family  of  Percy,  of 
Noi-mandy,  deduced  its  pedigree  from  Geoffrey  (son  of  Main- 
fix'd,  a  Danish  chieftain,)  who  assisted  RoUo,  in  912,  in  subju- 
gating that  principality,  and  acquired  considerable  possessions 
there. 

William  de  Percy  being  in  high  favour  with  the  victo 
rioixs  duke,  obtained,  according  to  Madox,  in  his  Baroaia 
Aiiglica,  a  barony  of  thirty  knights'  fees  from  that  mo- 
narch in  his  new  dominions,  and  thus  became  a  feudal  lord 
of  the  realm  from  the  Conquest.  This  lord,  William  de 
Percy,  who  was  distuiguished  among  his  contemporaries 
by  the  addition  of  als  Gernons  (William  with  the  Whiskers), 
whence  his  posterity  have  constantly  borae  the  name  of 
Algernon,  restored,  or  rather  refoundod,  the  famous  abbey 
of  St.  Hilda,  in  Yorkshire,  of  which  his  brother,  Serlo  de 
Percy,  became  first  prior.  Accompanying,  however,  Duke 
Robert  in  the  first  cru.sade,  1096,  he  died  at  Moimtjoy,  near 
Jerusalem,  the  celebrated  eminence  whence  the  pilgrims  of 
the  cross  first  viewed  the  holy  city,  leaving  four  sons  and 
two  dans.,  by  his  wife,  Emma  de  Port,  a  lady  of  Saxon 
descent,  whose  lands  were  amongst  those  bestowed  upon 
him  by  the  Conqueror  ;  and,  according  to  an  ancient 
writer,  "  be  wedded  hyr  that  was  very  heire  to  them  in 
discharging  of  his  conscience."  His  lordship  was  s.  in  bis

The  family  of  Smithson  derives  its  surname  from  an 
ancient  town  in  the  North  Biding  of  Yorkshire,  called 
Sinithion  or  Smethton,  in  which  district  the  Sraithsons  have 
possessed  considerable  estates  since  the  Conquest. 

In  Domesday-Book  the  name  is  written  Smethton,  and 
Malorum  de  Smethton  held  a  manor  there. 

RfiBERT  deSmvthton  and  Thomas DE  Smythton,  brothers, 
or  1st  cousins,  were  both  summoned  to  appear  on  a  jury 
in  an  inquisition  taken  on  Thursday,  the  Feast  of  St. 
Catherine,  anno  1333  ;  and  it  appears  that  the  family,  about 
this  period,  removed  from  Smithton  to  Yafford,  which  latter

This  family  paternally  derives  from  the  ancient  Milesian 
sept  of  O'Rtilly,  princes  of  Lower  Brefney  (see  Burke's

to  Camden,  makes  the  following  observations: — "Whence 
Mr.  Camden  received  his  information  that  the  O'Reillys 
derive  from  the  Ridleys  does  not  conceni  us  to  inquire. 
Spencer  falls  into  a  similar  error ;  he  derives  the  Mac 
Mahons  from  the  Veres  of  England,  because  the  one  in 
Latin,  and  the  other  in  Irish,  have  some  affinity  in  sound 
to  the  name  of  boar  jiig  in  those  languages  ;  but  both  are 
equally  the  impositions  of  etymologj-.  Before  the  English 
got  footing  in  Ireland,  the  O'Reillys  of  Cavan,  the  Mac 
Mahons  of  Monaghan,  the  Mac  Guii-es  of  Fermanagh,  the 
O'Donels  of  Donegal,  with  other  chieftains  in  their  own 
septs,  were  tributaries  to  O'Xial  of  Ter  Oen.  Such  of  the 
descendants  of  those  chieftains  as  I  have  conversed  with 
seem  rather  to  glory  in  their  Milesian  extraction.  When 
Hugh  O'Nial  threw  off  his  allegiance  to  Queen  Elizabeth, 
he  also  threw  off  the  title  of  Earl  of  TjTone,  saying,  that 
'he  would  rather  be  O'Xialof  Ulster,  than  King  of  Sp.ain.'"

This  family  of  Oglander,  or  Orglandes  (according  to  the 
modem  French  spelling  of  tlie  name),  is  of  Scandinavian 
origin,  and  has  flmirished  since  a  very  early  period  both  in 
France  and  En^dand.  "  The  family  of  Orglandes  (formerly 
written  Oglandres)  has,"  says  M.  deGerville  in  his  Memoirs 
of  the  Society  of  Antiquaries  of  Normandy,  vol.  i.,  p.  300, 
"the  rare  advantage  of  being  preserved  both  in  France  and 
England  since  the  memorable  and  distant  era  of  the  Con- 
quest, and  to  have  enjoyed  in  either  country  a  consideration 
which  has  never  abated."  The  English  branch,  which 
springs  from  theXonnan  line,*  was  introduced  into  England 
and  established  by 


*  The  Norman  line  was  also  one  of  much  and  frequent  distinc- 
tion. One  of  its  early  celebrities  was  Foulqnes  d'Orglandes,  a 
hero  of  the  Crusades.  The  arms  of  the  family  are  placed  in  the 
Crusaders  Hall  in  the  palace  of  Versailles.  This  Nonnan  line 
is  now  represented  by  Armand-Gustavus-Camille,  Count 
D"ORGLA^^DEs,  and  is  seated  at  the  Chiteau  de  Lonne,  near 
Bellfime,  Department  of  the  Orne,  Normandy.  The  Count's 
father, 

Nicholas-Francis-Camille -Dominique,  Count d'Or';lani>es 
(son  of  M.  d'Oi-glandos,  Coimt  de  Briouze,  by  his  wife  the 
Baroness  de  Cuy),  b.  19  Feb.  1767,  attained  a  very  high  public 
reputation  during  the  stoi'iny  periods  of  the  French  Revolution, 
Empire,  and  Restoration.  He  was  a  stanch  royalist,  and  showed

The  2ud  son  of  Mr.  Benjamin  Outram,  of  Butterley  Hall, 
Derbyshire, 

James  Outram,  whose  active  and  glorious  co-operation  in 
crushing  the  Indian  mutiny  won  him  lasting  fame,  was  b. 
at  Butterley  Hall,  29  Jan.  1803,  and  went  to  India  as  a  cadet 
1819,  and  rose  to  be  a  lieut. -general  there,  through  a  series 
of  deeds,  civil  and  military,  of  infinite  good  to  the  public 
■weal.  He  was,  while  resident  and  commissioner  at  Lucknow, 
sent,  in  Nov.  1856,  to  command  the  British  forces  in  Persia, 
where  he  was  invariably  fortunate.  He  was  present  at 
Bushire,  gained  the  battle  of  Kooshab,  8  Feb.,  and  took 
part  in  the  victory  of  Mohammerah,  28  March,  1857.  From 
Persia  he  returned  to  India,  to  aid  in  the  suppression  of 
the  insurrection,  then  at  the  very  height  of  its  guilt  and 
cruelty.  He  marched  to  relieve  Havelock,  and  formed  an 
effective  junction  with  him,  when  they  together  stormed 
Lucknow,  and  saved  the  garrison  of  the  Residency.  Outram 
shared  also  in  the  heroism  of  the  holding  out  until  Lord 
Clyde  arrived,  and  in  all  that  fierce  and  armed  struggle^ 
never  to  be  forgotten — which  ensued,  and  resulted  in  final 
fluccess.  Sir  James  was  appointed  a  Knight  Grand  Cross 
of  the  MUitary  Division  of  the  Order  of  the  Bath,  29  July, 
1857,  for  his  services  in  Persia,  having  previously  been 
nominated  a  Knight  Commander  (civil),  and  was  created  a 
Baronet  by  patent,  dated  10  Nov.  1858,  for  his  conduct  in 
India.  Sir  James  Outram,  who  was  a  lieut. -gen.  and 
member  of  the  council  of  the  governor-general  of  India, 
m.  18  Dec.  1835,  Margaret -Clementina,  dau.  of  James 
Anderson,  of  Bridgend,  Brechin,  co.  Forfar,  Esq. ,  J.  P.  for 
that  county,  and  d.  at  Pan,  11  March,  1863,  and  was  interred 
in  Westminster  Abbey.  He  h^d  an  only  child,  his  successor, 
Sir  Francis-Botd  Odtram,  the  2nd  and  present  baronet. 
Creation— 10  Nov.  1858.

rebellion  broke  out,  was  member  for  Ailesbury;  and  having

crown  and  the  rights  of  the  subject,  was  entrusted  by  the

prisoner,  committed  to  the  Tower,  and  fined  £5000  :  had

At  the  period  of  the  Crusades,  the  members  of  religious 
houses,  who  had  served  against  the  infidels,  were  commonly 
called  palmers,  from  the  palm-branches  they  can-ied  in  their 
hands  to  mark  their  return  from  Palestine.  But  the 
founder  of  the  ancient  and  noble  family  of  Palmer,  for 
centuries  of  the  first  consideration  iu  the  southern  counties 
of  England,  was  a  Norman  soldier,  who  having  repeatedly 
distinguished  himself  in  single  combat  against  the  Saracens, 
received  knighthood  from  the  king  on  the  field  of  battle  by 
that  sm-namo,  which  has  ever  since  been  retained  by  his 
descendants. 

RoQER  Palmer  (alleged  to  have  been  third  son  of  an 
Edward  Palmer,  Esq.  of  Naytou  and  Casterton,  Norfolk) 
went  to  Ireland,  and  had  a  grant  of  the  Castle  Lackin, 
and  many  other  lands  in  the  co.  Mayo,  by  patent,  dated 
1  Nov.  16S4.  His  signature  appears  to  the  address  from  the 
nobility  and  gentry  of  the  co.  JIayo,  to  Charles  II.,  in 
1682.  He  left,  by  bis  wife,  Anne,  dau.  of  Francis  Bressu, 
Esq.  of  Dromore,  co.  Donegal,  five  sous,

This  family  is  cne  of  considerable  antiquity,  descended 
from  Archbishop  Parker,  and  members  of  it  have  uninter-

I.  Peter  Parker,  Esq.,  admiral  of  the  fleet  (son  of 
Rear-Admiral  Chi-istopher  Parker,*  who  was  a  captain  com- 
manding the  "  Speedwell,"  in  Jan.  1712,  and  who  d.  at  a 
very  advanced  age),  was  created  a  Baronet,  28  Dec.  17S2, 
in  token  of  distinguished  services,  particularly  when  in 
command  of  a  squadron,  in  an  attack  on  Charlestown,  in 
South  Carolina.  The  action  was  one  of  the  most  sanguinary 
fought  during  the  American  war.  The  quarter-deck  of  the 
"Bristol"  (his,  the  commodore's  ship)  was  cleared  of  every 
man  but  himself.  The  expedition  failed,  in  con,sequence  of 
the  troops  under  Earl  Cornwillis  being  unable  to  effect 
a  landing ;  but  Sir  Peter  did  his  part,  by  silencing  the 
batteries.  He  'ni.  Margaret,  dau.  of  Walter  Nugent,  Esq., 
by  whom  (who  d,.  18  Jan.  1802)  he  had  issue, 

I.  Christopher,  who  distinguished  himself  in  the  command 
of  the  "  Lowestoff"  frigate,  at  the  taking  of  Fort  Omsa. 
He  led  the  attack,  which  was  planned  by  Sir  Peter,  the 
commander-in-chief  in  the  West  Indies,  and  was  wounded 
iu  the  thigh.  He  attained  the  rank  of  vice-admiral  of 
the  Blue ;  and  d.  26  May,  1804,  leaving  issue  by  Augusta- 
Barbara-Charlotte,  dau.  of  Admiral  the  Hon  John  Byron, 
gi'anddau.  of  the  4th  Lord  Byron,  and  aunt  of  the  poet,
