PAYNE. 

This  Baronetcy,  created  31  Oct.  1737,  in  favour 
of  Sir  Charles  Payne,  Knt.,  of  St.  Christophers, 
major-general  of  the  Leeward  Islands,  the  1st  bart., 
is  now  in  dispute  between  two  claicaants,  viz., 
Charles-Gillies  Payne,  of  Bluuham  House,  St. 
Neots,  Bedfordshire,  barrister-at-law,  J. P.  and  D.L., 
who  has  publicly  borne  the  title  for  the  last  twenty- 
five  years ;  and  Coventry  Payne,  who  maintains 
that  he  is  the  descendant  of  an  elder  branch,  and  is 
the  6th  baronet.  Both  claimants  have  recently 
published  pamphlets  on  the  subject ;  but  in  conse- 
quence of  their  contradictory  and  unsatisfactory 
statements,  and  in  the  absence  of  any  registration 
on  the  part  of  either  of  them  at  the  Herald's 
College,  it  is  thought  better  to  omit  here  any  further 
account  of  the  baronetcy.

Traditionally,  the  Drummonds  derive  their  descent  from 
an  Hungarian  in  the  suite  of  Edgar  Athelino,  but  the 
importance  of  tlie  family  was  based  on  the  ruj'al  alliance  of 
the  Lady  Annabella  Drummond,  dau.  of  Drummond  of 
Stobhall,  with  King  Robert  IU.  From  that  period  the 
Drummonds  held  a  high  position  in  North  Britain,  and 
were  raised  to  the  peerage  in  1487,  by  the  title  of  Lord 
Drummond,  aud  eventually  obtained  the  Earldom  of  Perth, 
iu  1605.  Their  loyalty  to  the  throne  shone  at  all  times 
conspicuous,  but  the  moment  that  called  forth  their  who'e 
energies  and  devotion  was  the  great  contest  which  preceded 
the  final  overthrow  of  the  ancient  djniast}-  of  Scotland.  So 
long  as  the  conflict  was  waged  on  the  battle-field,  the 
Drummonds  fought  manfully  in  the  cause  they  had  es- 
poused, and  at  length,  when  the  last  ruin  of  the  hapless 
race  of  Stuart  was  consummate  at  Culloden,  they  left  their 
native  land,  to  die  banished  and  broken-hearted  in  a  foreign 
cUme.  They  had  fearlessly  set  their  all  upon  the  cast,  and 
they  chivalrously  submitted  to  the  hazard'  of  the  die.

William  Piers,  Esq.,  son  of  Richard  Piers,  Esq.  of  Piers 
Hall,  CO.  York,  was  sent  over  to  Ireland,  in  1506,  by  Queen 
Elizabeth  (whom  he  is  said  to  have  saved,  at  one  lime, 
from  the  fury  of  her  sister,  by  conveying  her  privately 
away),  in  a  considerable  post  in  the  army,  and  was  re- 
warded by  grants  of  laud  of  great  value,  particularly  of 
the  abbey  of  Tristernagh,  in  the  co.  of  Westmeath.  He 
was  subsequently  constituted  governor  of  Carrickfergus ; 
and  seneschal  of  the  county  of  Antrim,  and  he  obtained,  in 
1569,  a  reward  of  1000  marks  for  bringing  in  the  head  of 
the  rebel  Shane  O'Neill.  He  d.  in  1602,  was  interred  at 
Carrickfergus,  and  s.  by  his  only  son, 

Henry  Piers,  Esq.  of  Tristernagh,  who  m.  Jane,  dau.

chancellor  of  Ireland,  by  whom  he  had  four  sons  and  six 
daus.*  Mr.  Piers,  who  was  an  eminent  traveller,  left  behind 
him  an  account  of  his  travels  in  Germany,  Italy,  &c. ,  a 
copy  of  which  was  placed  among  the  MSS.  of  Sir  James 
Ware,  in  the  Chaudos  library.  This  gentleman  conformed 
to  the  church  of  Rome,  and  prevailed  upon  some  of  his 
children  to  embrace  the  same  faith  ;  of  whom

Catholic  Church.

This  family  was  founded  in  England  by  Pigot,  Baron 
of  Boome,  in  Normandy,  one  of  the  forty  knights  who 
accompanied  William  the  Conqueror.  A  branch  (the  elder)

Fuller  says,  that  the  Pilkingtous  were  originally  of 
Rivington,  co.  Lancaster,  and  a  right  ancient  family ;  that 
they  were  gentlemen  of  repute  in  the  shire  before  the  Con- 
quest, at  which  time,  the  chief  of  the  house  being  sought 
after  by  the  Norman  soldiery,  was  faiu  to  disguise  himself 
as  a  thrasher  in  a  bam;  fi-om  which  circumstancp,  partlj 
alluding  to  the  head  of  the  flail  falling  sometimes  on  the  one, 
and  sometimes  on  the  other  side,  and  occasionally  on  him- 
self, he  took  for  the  motto  of  his  arms  "  Now  thus  !  now 
thus  ! "     The  first  of  the  family  we  find  upon  record  is 

Leonard  Pilkington,  of  Pilkiugton  Tower,  co.  Lancaster, 
living  in  the  re;gn  of  Henry  T.;  f'-om  him  descended 

The  Bight  Rev.  James  Pilkington,*  one  of  the  six 
divines  appointed  to  revise  the  Book  of  Common  Prayer, 
who  was  consecrated  Bishop  of  Durham  in  1560.  In  1569, 
the  northern  rebels  coming  to  Durham,  tore  the  Bible  and 
English  Litm-gy  into  pieces,  and  the  bishop  would  most 
probably  have  shared  a  similar  fate  could  they  have  found 
him.  His  lordship  subsequently  instituted  a  suit-at-law 
against  Queen  Elizabeth,  for  the  lands  and  goods  of  the 
rebels  attainted  in  the  bishopric,  and  would  have  succeeded 
had  not  parliament  interfered,  and  adjudged  these  for- 
feitures, pro  hac  vice,  to  the  crown.

Sir  Frederick  Pollock,  a  very  eminent  advocate, 
lawyer,  and  judge,  was  educated  at  St.  Paul's 
Scliool  and  Trinity  College,  Cambridge,  where  he 
graduated  B.A.  as  senior  wrangler  and  Smith's 
prizeman  in  1806.  He  became  M.A.  in  1809,  having 
been  elected  a  Fellow  of  Trinity  in  1807,  in  which 
year  he  was  called  to  the  Bar  by  the  Hon.  Society 
of  the  Middle  Temple,  and  went  the  Northern 
Circuit.  Having  attained  great  success  and  a  wide 
reputation,  he  was  made  a  K.C.  in  1827,  and  was 
Attorney-General  from  1834  to  1835,  and  again 
from  1841  to  1>;44.  He  was  knighted  in  1834.  °He 
was  nominated  Lord  Chief  Baron  of  the  Court  of 
Exchequer  in  1844  and  sworn  of  the  Privy  Council. 
He  held,  with  the  highest  ability  and  credit,  his 
judicial  office  for  two  and  twenty  years,  when,  on  his 
retirement,  he  was  created  a  Baronet,  2  Aug.  1866.

In  11.30,  Roger  le  Poek,  or  Pauper,  Bishop  of  Salisbury, 
called  Roger  the  Great,  was  Lord  Chancellor  and  Chief 
Justiciar  in  the  reign  of  Hekry  I.,  and  Lord  Treasurer  in 
the  roigii  of  Stephen.  He  erected  at  Devizes  one  of  the 
largest  and  strongest  castles  in  England.  His  cathedral  of 
Salisbury  he  dignified  to  the  utmost  with  matchless  build- 
ings and  ornaments.  His  nephew,  Alexander,  called  The 
Magnificent,  held  the  office  of  Chancellor,  and  was  Bishop 
of  Lincoln.  His  successor  as  Chancellor  was  the  natural 
son  of  his  uncle,  "  Roger  the  Great,"  Bishop  of  Salisbury.

The  high  antiquity  of  this  family  is  proved  by  the  fact,  as 
shown  in  the  Heralds'  OfHce,  that  the  late  Sir  Henry  Pot- 
tinger  was  the  thirty-first  in  lineal  descent  from  Egbert, 
the  first  Saxon  king  of  all  England,  grandfather  of  Alfred 
the  Great.  It  is  descended  from  a  common  ancestor  with 
the  Pottingers  of  Berkshire,  seated  in  that  co.  since  the  Con- 
quest, and  members  of  which  frequently  sat  in  parliament  for 
Heading  in  the  17th  century.  The  elder  branch  settled  ia 
Ireland  at  a  very  early  period. 

Thomas  Pottinger,  of  Mount  Pottinger,  was  the  first  sove- 
reign of  Belfast  elected  on  the  grant  of  a  cori)oration  to  that 
town  in  1613.     Of  his  sons, 

Edward  Pottinger,  capt.  R.N.,  had  the  honour  to  convey 
King  William  1 II.  to  Ireland ;  but  sailing  the  day  after  landing 
His  Majesty,  to  intercept  ships  coming  from  France  with 
supplies  for  James,  he  was  lost,  with  all  his  ship's  crew,  in  the 
"  Dartmouth"  man-of-war,  on  the  night  of  the  8th  Oct.  1690, 
leaving,  by  Margaret  his  wife,  dau.  of  Sir  William  Strickland, 
Bart,  of  Boynton,  co.  York,  three  daus.,  his  co-heirs,  the  eldest 
of  whom  in.  Sir  Walter-Dixon  Borrowes,  Bart. ;  the  2nd,  Vesey 
of  Lucan,  ancestor  of  the  noble  family  of  De  Vesci ;  and  the 
3rd,  Leslie  of  Glaslough,  co.  Monaghan,  ancestor  of  the  M.P. 
for  that  CO.

During  his  long  sojourn  in  India,  Sir  Henry  Pottinger  was 
employed  in  every  branch  of  the  public  service.  He  was  above 
seven  years  judge  and  collector  at  Ahmednuggar,  in  the 
Deccau;  fifteen  years  political  resident  in  Cutoh  and  Sciude,  a 
part  of  which  he  ivas  president  of  the  regency  in  the  former 
kingdom,  and  was  raised  to  the  Baronetage  in  1839,  for  the 
manner  in  which  he  discharged  his  duties  at  those  courts.  He 
returned  to  England  in  1840,  and  early  in  I84I  was  selected  by 
Her  Majesty's  Government  to  proceed  to  China,  as  plenipoten- 
tiary and  envoy-extraordinary  for  the  adjustment  of  the  dif- 
ferences then  existing  between  the  two  empires.  In  1842,  he 
received  the  honour  of  a  civil  grand  cross  of  the  Bath,  for 
effecting  the  object  of  his  mission ;  and  on  his  return  to  Eng- 
land, in  Oct.  1844,  he  was,  by  Her  Majesty's  command,  sworn 
as  a  member  of  the  Privy  Council.  In  June,  1845,  a  pension 
of  £1500  per  annum  was  voted  to  him,  nem.  con.,  by  the  House 
of  Commons,  "  in  consideration  of  his  eminent  services."  Sir 
Henry  was  governor  of  the  presidency  of  Madras.  Ho  d.  March, 
1856,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  surviving  sou, 

II.  Sir  Frederick-William,  who  was  h.  27  April,  1831,  and 
was  an  officer  in  the  grenadier-guards.  He  d.  at  Sydney, 
N.  S.  W.,  9  April,  1865,  and  was  s.  by  his  brother.  Sir  He.nrt 
Pottinger,  the  3rd  and  present  baronet.

The  eldest  son, 

Robert,  was  the  illustrious  Robert  Clive,  to  whose 
boldness  in  counsel  and  daring  in  war,  England,  in  a  great 
measure,  owes  the  establishment  of  her  dominion  in  India. 
He  was  born  at  the  family  seat  of  Styche,  Shropshire, 
24  Feb.  1726,  and  after  making  himself  remarkable  at  the 
various  schools  he  went  to,  more  for  his  fiery  and  un- 
daunted spirit  than  his  application,  he  in  1744  entered  the 
Civil  Service  of  the  East  India  Company ;  but  nature  had 
fitted  him  for  a  soldier,  and  in  1747  he  quitted  the  civil  for 
the  military  service  of  the  Company.  His  first  distinction 
was  at  the  siege  of  Pondicherry,  and  at  the  attack  of  Devi 
Cotah,  where  as  a  lieutenant  he  commanded  the  forlorn 
hope  that  stormed  the  breach.  In  1751  he  tuuk  the  city  of 
Arcot,  and  after  a  long  defence  of  it,  he  signally  defeated, 
before  its  walls,  the  enemy  who  came  to  retake  it.  His 
health  then  required  him  to  return  to  England,  but  his 
repose  there  was  short.  On  his  return  to  India  he  found 
the  whole  nation  aroused  by  the  atrocity  of  the  Black 
Hole  of  Calcutta.  Clive  terribly  avenged  the  deed  on  its 
perpetrator,  the  Surajah  Dowlab,  Subah  of  Bengal.  He 
stormed  Calcutta,  and  once  master  of  it,  brought  the 
Sui-ajah  to  immediate  terms.  He  then  entered  into  a  plot 
to  dethrone  him,  and  with  reckless  energy  carried  out  the 
conspiracy,  the  success  of  which  was  achieved  by  the 
famous  battle  of  Plassey,  fought  the  23rd  June,  1757. 
Clive  there,  with  3,000  men,  utterly  routed  the  Surajah 
Dowlah,  at  the  head  of  troops  aniomiting  to  70,000.  The 
result  was  the  execution  of  the  Surajah,  the  installation  of 
bis  minister  Meer  Jaffier  in  his  place,  and  the  rapid  ascend- 
ancy of  the  British  power.  Clive  became  Governor  of 
Calcutta,  and  then  turning  his  arms  against  the  Dutch 
defeated  them  by  sea  and  land,  and  compelled  them  to  a 
treaty  of  infinite  benefit  to  the  East  India  Company.  In  1761 
Clive  again  came  to  England,  and  was  elevated  to  the 
peerage  of  Ireland,  15  March,  1762,  by  the  title  of  Baron 
Clive  ofFlassei/,  co.  Clare;  his  knighthood  of  the  Bath  dates 
in  1764.  In  1765  some  di.stui-bances  in  India  brought  him 
once  more  there  as  President  of  Bengal ;  these  he  settled  to 
the  Company's  advantage,  and  finally  returned  to  England 
in  1767.     He  was  M.P.  for  Shrewsbury  from  1760  to  the  end

of  bis  life,  but  seldom  spoke,  though  on  one  memorable

timely and  lamented  death  was  the  work  of  his  own  hand,

This  family  was  early  settled  at  Beeston  St.  Lawrence, 
in  the  hundred  of  Tunstead,  co.  Norfolk.  It  came  originally 
from  the  village  of  Preston,  in  the  hundred  of  Babergh, 
Suffuik, — where  its  ancestors  held  rank  as  gentlemen  in  the 
reign  of  Edward  III.  Jacob  Preston,  of  OldBuckenham,  was 
the  4th  son  of  Wm.  Preston,  of  Preston,  and  his  wife.  Rose, 
dau.  of  Mr.  Whipple,  of  Dickleburgk.  Jacob  Preston  d.  in 
1630,  and  is  interred  at  Old  Buckenham.  In  1640,  Sir  Henry 
Hobart  conveyed  the  manor  of  Beeston,  with  the  advowson, 
to  Thomasine,  the  widow  of  Jacob  Preston  ;  and  their  son, 
Jacob  Preston,  came  into  possession  in  1658.  He  was  an 
ardent  loyalist  being  an  attached  aud  favourite  servant  of 
Charles  I  ;  aud  one  of  the  four  gentlemen  appointed  to 
wait  upon  that  unfortunate  monarch  during  his  imprison 
ment.  Charles,  as  a  last  tribute  of  affection,  presented 
him,  when  on  the  scalibld,  with  an  emerald  ring,  which  is 
still  preserved  at  Beeston  Hall.  He  m.  Frances  dau.  of  Sir 
Isaac  Applcton,  of  Waldingfield,  in  Sufi'olk,  and  Bokenham 
House,  iu  Norfolk.  Their  son,  Isaac,  was  knighted  at 
Whitehall,  by  William  III.,  in  1695;  and  his  descendants 
have  ever  since  continued  to  reside  at  Beeston  Hall.  Sir 
Jacob  Preston,  who  now  possesses  the  Beeston  property, 
is  a  descendant  of  a  female  branch  of  the  family.

The  Pringles  of  Stichill  are  the  heirs  male  and  repre- 
sentatives of  the  Pringles  or  Hop-Pringlea  of  Craiglatch  and 
Newhall,  in  the  co.  Selkirk.  They  are  believed  to  have 
been  very  old  cadets  of  the  house  of  Smailholm,  though 
the  exact  period  at  which  they  came  off  has  not  been 
ascertained  ;  but  the  circumstance  may  not  only  be  inferred 
from  the  close  vicinity  of  their  land  to  the  ydklrksbire 
properties  of  that  family,  but  appears  to  have  been  a  matter 
of  local  notoriety,  and  is  stated  as  a  fact  in  several  public 
and  family  documents.  It  is  most  probable  that  theiifirst  of 
the  family  was  either  one  of  the  five  sons  of  Robert  Pringle, 
of  Smailholm,  who  hi.  Elizabeth  Dishington,  or  a  younger 
son  of  David  Pringle,  the  next  laird  of  Smailholm.  In  the 
crown  rentals  of  Ettrick  Forest  for  1485  and  1490,  v.  e  find 
the  lands  of  Craiglatch  in  the  possession  of  William  Hop- 
Pringle,  and  Alexander  his  son,  their  cautioner  being 
James  Pringle,  of  Smailholm.  For  four  generations  we 
can  only  trace  their  names  through  their  titles  of  succession, 
though  nothing  can  be  more  accurate.     The  first  was 

William  Pringle,  of  Craiglatch,  also  designed  of  Whit- 
toun,  in  Roxburghshire,  who  had  a  charter  of  the  lands  of 
Hut,  in  that  county,  in  1492,  and  crown  tacks  of  Craiglatch, 
in  1485  and  1490.     He  was  s.  by  his  son, 

Alexander  Pringle,  of  Craiglatch,    (crown  tack  1490), 
who  was  s.  by  his  son, 
Robert  Pringle,  of  Craiglatch  (seisin  1512),  s.  by  his  son, 
Alexander  Pringle,  of  Craiglatch,  (retour  1539),  s.  bj' 
his  son, 

George  Pringle,  of  Craiglatch,  in  whose  behalf  the 
tenure  of  his  Ettrick  Forest  lands  was  changed  to  a  feudal 
holding  by  charter,  1587.  In  these  times  of  violence  and 
insecurity,  the  names  of  the  Scottish  lairds  of  small  pro- 
perties in  the  border  counties  are  rarely  to  be  met  with 
in  the  public  records  of  national  transactions,  except  when 
they  had  the  good  fortune  to  distinguish  themselves  in 
some  of  the  greater  battles  with  their  English  foes,  in  which 
they  were  so  frequently  required  to  bear  their  part ;  for, 
by  the  tenure  of  their  lands,  they  were  required  to  hold 
themselves  always  ready  to  obey  the  summons  of  their 
sovereign  to  attend  his  host,  with  their  sons  and  retainers. 
But  if  we  turn  to  the  pages  of  the  criminal  records,  we 
shall  find  their  names  constantly  occuring,  sometimes  on 
the  lists  of  assize,  but  more  frequently  as  aggressors  or 
sufferers.  The  arm  of  the  law  was  generally  weak,  so  they 
were  tempted  by  the  chance  of  impunity  to  acts  of  violence; 
or,  when  they  had  themselves  suffered  injury  they  were  too 
apt  to  seek  redress  by  acts  of  retaliation,  which  knew  no 
bounds  except  the  extent  of  their  immediate  power  or 
opportunity.  If,  therefore,  we  look  into  those  interesting 
records  of  Scottish  manners  during  the  reign  of  the  Stewart 
monarchs,  Pitcairn'3  Criminal  Trials,  for  the  names  of  the 
Pringles  of  Craiglatch,  we  shall  not  look  in  vain.  In  1555, 
we  find  Alexander  Hop- Pringle,  of  Craiglatch,  and  George, 
his  son,  convicted  of  a  bloody  assault  upon  David  Hop 
Pringle,  son  of  Alexander  Hop-Pringle,  of  Trynliknows, 
their  nearest  neighbour.  Again,  in  156;i,  Wilham  Cranston, 
of  that  ilk,  and  James,  his  brother,  were  cited  to  appear  at 
Selkirk,  for  invading  the  lands  of  Wilhamhope,  belonging  to 
Alexander  Pmigle,  of  Craiglatch,  with  the  purpose  of 
taking  his  life,  and,  on  not  findmg  liim,  taking  revenge 
by  hamstringing  and  slaying  three  of  his  cattle.  It  is 
probable  that  the  arm  of  the  law  failed  to  reach  them, 
for  afterwards  we  find  Alexander  of  Craiglatch,  with  his 
brother  George,  and  his  son  George,  cited  to  answer  for 
a  deed  of  tenfold  retaliation,  by  entering  the  adjoining 
lands  of  Hawtheme,  belonging  to  Cranston,  and  slajing 
forty  of  his  cows.  The  crime  of  march-treason,  or  holding 
communication  with  English  foemen,  and  countenancing 
them  in  their  depredations,  was,  in  those  days,  not  un- 
frequeiit  on  the  borders  ;  and  George  Pringle,  of  Craig- 
latch, with  his  eldest  son  George,  had  the  misfortune,  on

This  family  is  maternally  descended  from 

Sir  John  Ramsay,  Knt.  of  Balmain  and  Fasque,  co. 
Kincardine,  who  was  created  by  James  III.  a  lord  of  par- 
liament in  1433,  and  sat  under  the  title  of  Lord  Bothwell. 
Adhering,  however,  to  his  unfortunate  sovereign,  against 
whom  the  nobles  of  Scotland  rebelled,  his  lordship  was  out- 
lawed, and  his  estates  subjected  to  confiscation,  in  1488, 
by  the  1st  parliament  of  James  IV. ,  while  that  monarch 
conferred  the  dignity  of  Earl  of  Bothwell  upon  Hepburn, 
Lord  Hailes,  whose  descendant  became  the  third  husband 
of  Mary,  Queen  of  Scots,  and  was  the  last  of  his  family 
that  enjoyed  the  peerage.  In  149S,  the  disgraced  lord 
received,  however,  a  royal  pardon,  but  under  the  simple 
designation  of  John  Ramsay;  and  he  obtained,  at  the  same 
time,  some  lands  in  the  cos.  of  Forfar  and  Wigtouu ;  which 
favours  were  followed  by  a  charter,  in  1510,  of  the  Barony 
of  Balmain.     The  grandson  of  this  personage,

The  surname  of  Reade,  which  is  derived  from  the  Saxon  word 
Med,  or  Ra;d,  denotes  the  Saxon  origin  of  the  family.  This 
ancient  name  is  mentioned  in  Froissart's  Chronicles,  but  chiefly 
in  the  Harleian  MSS.  of  the  British  Museum,  where  in  fol.  104, 
1545,  the  Baronet's  house  is  traced  as  the  17th  in  direct  descent 
from  King  Edward  III.  Of  its  distingiushed  members  we  may 
mention  Sir  Reginald  Reade,  Knt.  distinguished  in  the  border 
warfare ;  Sir  Robert  Reade,  Knt.,  Icrd-chief-justice  of  the  Com- 
mon Pleas,  temp.  Henry  Vlll.  (the  founder  and  endower  of  the 
Cambridge  Institute  of  "The  Rede  Lecture,"  on  subjects  of 
science  and  philosophy) ;  and  finally,  another  of  the  same  name, 
who  held  out  Barton  Court,  near  Abingdon,  against  a  troop  of 
parliamentarians,  until  it  was  burnt  over  his  head.

Reay,  Lord  (Sir  Eric  Mackay),  of  Reay,  co.  Caith- 
ness, ill  the  peerage  of  Scotland  ;  aucl  a  Baronet  of 
Nova  Scotia ;  b.  1813;  s.  his  father  as  9th  baron, 
18  Feb.  1863. 

This  very  ancient  family,  according  to  the  best  authorities 
held  possessions  in  the  north  of  Scotland  seven  centuries  ago; 
which  possessions  were  originally  denominated  Strathnaver,  but 
more  recently  Lord  Reay's  Coimtry. 

Odo  Macky,   descended  from  Angus  Dow  Macky,  (who  is 
styled  leader  of  4000  Mackys  of  Strathnaver),  obtained  exten- 
sive territorial  grants  in  the  counties  of  Caithness  and  Suther- 
land in  1499  and  1507.    He  fell  at  Flodden,  and  was  s.  by  his  son, 
John  Macky,  who  was  s.  by  his  brother, 
Donald  Macky,   characterized  by  historians  as   "  a  great 
general,  and  a  wise  and  political  gentleman."     This  personage 
was  at  the  battle  of  Sohvay  Moss,  and  returned  to  Edinburgh 
with  the  king  three  days  after  the  conflict,  when  his  majesty 
bestowed  upon  him  the  fortified  lands  of  several  individuals,  by 
charter,  dated  28  Nov.  1542.    He  c?.  in  1565,  and  was  «.  by  his  son, 
Y  Macky,  who  obtained  his  father's  lands  from  the  Earl  of 
Huntly,  to  whom  they  had  been  granted  by  the  crown.   He  had 
several  conflicts  with  the  Earl  of  Sutherland,  to  whom  sur- 
rendering himself  in  1556,  he  was  sent  prisoner  to  the  castle  of 
Edinburgh.    Being  released,  he  returned  to  Strathnaver,  where 
he  conducted  himself  turbulently  until  his  death,  in  1571.    He

His  grace  assumed  the  additional  surname  of  Gordon,  after  the 
decease  of  his  maternal  uncle,  George,  5th  Duke  of  Gordon,  in 
1836.  The  dulte  was  a  lieut.-col.  in  the  army,  and  was  engaged 
in  active  service  during  the  latter  years  of  the  late  war.  He 
was  at  Waterloo.  He  was  also  a  knight  of  the  garter,  lord- 
lieutenant  and  custos-rotulorum  of  the  co.  Sussex,  col.  of  the 
Sussex  militia,  high-steward  of  Chichester,  aide-de-camp  to 
the  Queen,  and  hereditary  constable  of  Inverness  Castle.  He  d. 
21  Oct.  1860,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son.

RiDDELL,  Sir  Walter-Buchanan,  of  Riddell,  co. 
lloxburgh,  Recorder  of  Maid.stoue,  and  Judge  of  the 
Whitecbapel  Coimty  Court;  h.  8  Aug.  1810;  s.  his 
father,  as  10th  baronet,  April,  1819  ;  m.  18  Aug. 
1859,  Alicia,  youngest  dau.  of  the  late  William 
Ripley,  Esq.,  H.M.  52nd  infantry. 

Ittucacjr. 

The  family  of  Riddell  is  of  Norman  extraction.  The  roll 
of  Battle  Abbey  includes,  as  the  Conqueror's  followers, 
"  Avenell,  Ros,  et  Ridell. "  Avenels  and  Rosses  thereafter 
figure  in  Scottish  records  ;  the  former,  like  the  Riddells,  in 
Roxburghshire,  and  with  the  corre.sponding  name  of  Ger- 
vase  ;  while  Thierry,  in  his  Histoire  de  la  Conquete  de  I'An- 
glettrre  par  les  Normands  (vol.  ii.,  pp.  414-417),  fiu-ther 
specifies  "Ridel"  and  "Revel"  among  the  Norman  con- 
querors. 

The  first  of  this  family  explicitly  proved  settled  in  Scot- 
land is  Gi'RVASius  DE  Ridel,  the  earliest  high-shoriff  of 
Roxburghshire.  He  Is  witness  to  one  of  the  oldest  Scotch 
documents,  the  well-known  Inquisitio  Principis  Davidis,  in 
1116,  by  the  great  Norman  colonizer  of  Scotland,  and  to 
other  legal  deeds.     From  Gervasius  descended, 

Walter  de  Rtddale,  or  Ridel,  who  had  a  charter  from 
David  I.  of  the  lands  of  LiUsclive  and  Whitunes,  co.  Rox-

*  The  ancient  family  of  Ridley  has  been  long  resident  in

the  estate,  during  the  troubles  in  Chakles  the  First's  reign 
were  lost,  and  passed  to  the  possession  of  Sir  Edward  Blacket 
Bart.  These  Ridleys  are  supposed  to  be  descended  from  the 
Ridleys  of  Ridley,  in  Cheshire;  the  arms,  anciently  used  by 
both  families,  are  alike.  Of  the  Ridleys  of  Willymondswyke 
was  Sir  Thomas  Ridley,  Knt.,  doctor  of  the  civil  law,  who  d. 
23  Jan.  1628,  and  was  buried  in  St.  Bennet's  Church,  London.

His  lordship,  an  eminent  lawyer,  was  called  to  the 
Bar  in  1827;  was  made  Solicitor-General  in  1848, 
and  was  then  knighted ;  he  became  Attorney- 
General  in  1850,  and  Master  of  the  Rolls  in  1851 ; 
he  was  created  Baron  Romilly,  3  Jan.  1866. 

Sir  Samuel  Romillt,  a  great  jurisconsult,  advocate,  states- 
man, and  philanthropist,  was  member  of  a  French  Pro- 
testant family  which  had  taken  refuge  in  England  after  the 
revocation  of  the  edict  of  Nantes;  he  was  born  in  1757,  and 
was  in  1783  called  to  the  bar.  After  attaining  a  large  practice 
as  a  chancery  lawyer,  he,  in  1800,  became  King's  Counsel;  in 
1806  he  was  knighted,  appointed  solicitor-general,  and  elected 
a  member  of  parliament.  In  the  House  of  Commons  he  dis- 
tinguished himself  by  his  impressive  eloquence.  He  strenuously 
advocated  the  reform  of  parliament,  the  abolition  of  the  slave- 
trade,  the  mitigation  of  the  criminal  code,  and  the  emancipa- 
tion of  the  Roman  Catholics.  He  published  one  of  his  speeches, 
in  a  pamphlet  entitled  ''Observations  on  the  Criminal  Law,  as 
it  relates  to  capital  punishment,  and  on  the  mode  in  which  it 
it  administered."  His  perseverance  through  life  in  his  efforts 
to  effect  an  amelioration  of  the  then  terribly  severe  laws  rela- 
tive to  the  administration  of  criminal  justice  did  him  the 
highest  honour.  In  1818  he  was  elected  for  Westminster.  Sir 
Samuel  in.  in  Jan.  1798,  Anne,  dau.  of  Francis  Garbett,  Esq. 
of  Knill  Court,  co.  Hereford,  and  d.  in  1818,  having  had  issue, 

William,  6.  1  798  ;  d.  1855. 

John,  created  Lord  Romilly. 

Edward,  b.  in  1804;  m.  Miss  Sophia  Marcet. 

Henry,  b.  in  1805;   )/(.  Miss  Rosa  Morris. 

Charles,  barrister-at-law,  clerk  to  the  crown  in  chancery,  h. 
in  1808;  "/.  13  Jan.  1842,  Georgiana-Elizabcth,  eldest  dau. 
of  John,  6th  Duke  of  Bedford,  and  by  her  (v/hod.  22  March,

RossE,  Earl  of  (Sir  Lawrence  Parsons),  Baron 
Oxmautovvu,  in  the  peerage  of  Ireland ;  and  a  Baronet 
of  the  same  part  of  the  United  Kingdom  ;  b.  17  Nov. 
1840  ;  s.  his  father  as  4th  earl,  31  Oct.  1867. 

This  family,  of  English  origin,  was  brought  into  Ireland 
towards  the  close  of  Queen  Elizabeth's  reign,  by  William 
Parsons,  who  rose  to  great  wealth  ard  power,   and  was 
eventually  one  of  the  loi-ds- justices  of  that  kingdom, — his 
immediate  line  being,  however,  extinct,   we  shall  briefly 
detail  it,  and  then  proceed  with  that  of  the  existing  family. 
WiLUAM    Parsons    settled  in   Ireland   about  the  close  of 
Queen    Elizabeth's  reign,  and  being  a  commissioner  of 
plantations,   obtained   very   considerable  territorial  grants 
from  the  crown.     In  1602,  lie  succeeded  Sir  Geoffi-ey  Fenton 
as  surveyor-general  of  Ireland;  in  1610,  he  obtained  a  pen- 
sion of  £30  a-year,  English,  for  life ;  in  161 1.  he  was  joined 
with  his  brother,  Laurence,  in  the  supervisorsliip  of  the  crown 
lands,  with  a  fee  of  £60  a-year  for  hfe  ;  in  1620,  presenting 
to  the  king,  in  person,  surveys  of  escheated  estates,  in  his 
capacity   of  surveyor-general,   he  received   the  honour  of 
knighthood,  and  was  created  a  Baronet,  10  Nov.  in  the  same 
year.     Sir  WilUam  Parsons  represented  the  co.  of  Wicklow 
in  parliament  in  1639,  and  was  constituted  lord-deputy,  witl) 
Lord  Dillon,  in  1640;  but  that  nobleman  being  soon  removed, 
he  was  resworn  with  Sir  John  Borlace,  master  of  the  ord- 
nance.    He  continued  in  the  government  until  1643,  when 
he  was  removed,  charged  with  treason,  and  committed  to 
prison,  with  Sir  Adam  Loftus  and  others.     He  rn.  Elizabeth, 
eldest  dau.  of  Mr.  Alderman  John  Lany,  of  Dubhn,    and

I.  Mary-Agatha. 

This  distinguished  statesman,  orator,  and  writer  was 
educated  at  Westminster  and  at  the  University  of 
Edinburgh ;  he  entered  Parliament  as  M.P.  for  Ta- 
vistock, in  1813;  ha.?  represented  various  other 
places,  viz.,  Hunts,  Bandon,  Devon,  Stroud,  and  the 
city  of  London  ;  and  has  sat  in  the  Lower  House  for 
forty-seven  years,  during  which  period  his  name  has 
been  eminently  connected  with  most  of  the  political 
events  of  his  country.  He  has  filled  many  of  the 
highest  oiSces ;  he  has  been  Secretary  of  State  for 
the  Home,  Foreign,  and  Colonial  Departments,  Lord 
President  of  the  Council,  Comaiissioner  to  the  Con- 
gress at  Vienna,  &c.,  and  was  First  Lord  of  the 
Treasury  from  1846  to  1852.  He  was  appointed 
Foreign  Secretary,  IS  June,  1859,  and  held  that 
office  till  he  again  became  First  Lord  of  the  Treasury, 
in  1865,  and  retired  in  1866.  He  was  raised  to  the 
peerage,  as  Earl  Russell  and  Viscount  Amberley, 
by  patent,  dated  30  July,  1861,  and  made  a  K.G.  21 
May,  1862.  His  lordship  is  the  author  of  a  tragedy 
entitled  Don  Carlos,  and  of  various  historical  and 
biographical  works  of  note.

This  distinguished  nobleman,  who,  prior  to  his  acces- 
sion to  the  peerage,  represented  in  Parliament  Lis- 
keard  (from  1824  to  1832)  and  East  Cornwall  (from 
1837  to  1845)  has  filled,  with  eminent  ability,  several 
very  high  and  important  offices.  In  1835,  being  then 
Lord  Eliot  he  went  as  Envoy  to  Spain  and  concluded 
the  famous  "  Eliot  Cimvention."  In  1841  he  was 
made  Chief  Secretary  for  Ireland,  and  continued  as 
such  until  19  Jan.  1845,  when  he  s.  his  father  as  3rd 
Earl  of  St.  Germans.  In  the  Nov.  following  he  was 
appointed  Postmaater-General,  and  in  Dec.  1852,  was 
constituted  Lord-Lieutenant  of  Ireland,  which 
dignified  office  his  lordship  resigned  in  March,  1855. 
Subsequently  he  became  Lord  Steward  of  the  House- 
hold 23  Nov.  1857,  resigned  in  1858,  was  re-ai^pointed 
to  the  same  office  18  June,  1859,  and  again  resigned 
it  in  1866.  In  1857,  he  was  given  the  Grand  Cross 
of  the  Order  of  the  Bath.

Scarvagh),  clerk  of  the  Writs  and  Records,  Ireland 
and  has  issue. 

His  lordship,  an  eminent  lawyer,  and  author  of 
several  standard  legal  works,  became  a  member  of 
Lincoln's  Inn,  aud  was  called  to  the  bar  in  1807  ; 
was  made  King's  counsel  in  1822 ;  solicitor-general 
and  knighted  in  1829,  which  office  he  resigned  in 
1830  ;  Lord  Chancellor  of  Ireland  for  the  first  time 
in  1834,  which  he  resigned  in  1835.  His  lordship 
became  Lord  Chancellor  of  Ireland  for  the  2nd 
time  in  1841,  and  again  resigned  in  1846.  He  was 
appointed  Lord  High  Chancellor  of  Great  Britain, 
27  Feb.  1852,  and  raised  to  the  peerage  1st

t  This  motto  is  a  graceful  and  seamanlike  allusion  implying 
perfect  rectitude.  "  Thns  "  is  the  word  of  direction  given  to  the 
steersman  by  the  quartermaster  when  the  ship  is  going  in  a 
perfectly  correct  course.  For  instance,  if  he  wish  the  vessel  to 
proceed  to  the  right,  he  says  "Starboard;"  if  to  the  left: 
"Port;  "  but  if  the  ship  be  going  quite  as  it  ought  to  do,  he 
says  "Keep  thus,"  or  "Thus"  simply,  corrupted  in  nautical 
pronunciation  into  "Theis."

The  founder  of  the  ancient  and  far-spreading  family  of 
Scott,  in  North  Britain, 

Uchtredus  filtus  Scoti,  was  witness  to  the  foundation 
charters  of  the  abbeys  of  Holyrood  House  and  Selkirk,  by 
David  II.,  in  the  years  1128  and  1130.  It  does  not  appear, 
however,  that  this  person  had  assumed  the  name  of  Scot  as 
a  surnanre,  but  that  ho  was  designated  "  filius  Scoti,"  as  a 
son  of  a  Scotsman,  to  distinguish  him  from  other  persons 
called  Uchtred,  which  was  then  a  common  Christian  name 
beyond  the  Tweed.     This  Uchtred  was  father  of 

Richard,  who  did  assume  the  surname  vf  Scot,  and  was 
living  in  the  reigns  of  Malcolm  IV.  and  William  the  Lion. 
This  Richard  Scot  founded  the  priory  of  St.  Andrews,  and 
('.  in  1158,  leaving  two  sons, 
Richard,  ancestor  of  the  Dukes  of  Buecleuch ;  and 
Sir  Michael  Scott,  a  piorson  of  great  power  in  the  co.  of 
Fife  about  the  middle  of  the  twelfth  ceutiu-y.  This  gentle- 
man m.  Margaret,  dau.  of  Duncan  Syras,  of  that  ilk,  by 
whom  he  had  one  son,  Duncan,  with  whose  consent,  and 
that  of  his  lady.  Sir  Michael  made  a  donation  to  the  monas-

the  lands  of  Gascumenfers,  in  Fifeshire.  The  great-grandson 
of  this  Sir  Michael, 

Sir  Michael  Scott,  2nd  Earon  of  Balwoary,  traditionally 
named  the  Wizard,  was  a  person  of  very  extraordinary  abili- 
ties, and  made  a  remarkable  figure  at  the  time  in  which  he 
lived.  After  pursuing,  with  unusual  success,  the  study  of 
languages,  belles-lettres,  and  mathematics,  at  home.  Sir 
Michael  travelled  into  France,  where  he  remained  several 
years,  and  thence  passed  into  Germany,  where  he  .S23ent 
some  time  at  the  court  of  Frederick  II.  The  extraordinary 
discoveries  of  Sir  Michael  in  the  science  of  chemistry  obtained 
him  the  character  of  a  magician ;  and  to  this  day  there  are 
marvellous  tales  told  in  Scotland  of  his  communings  with 
the  Evil  One.  In  the  year  1290,  Sir  Michael  Scott  and  Sir 
Michael  de  Wemyss  were,  by  the  states  of  the  nation,  deputed 
p.mliassadors- extraordinary  to  the  court  of  Norway,  to  bring 
home  Queen  Margaret,  then  the,  undoulited  heir  to  the 
Crown  of  Scotland,  and  who  was  to  have  espoused  Prince 
Edward  of  England ;  but,  unfortunately,  her  majesty  died 
at  Orkney,  in  her  way  to  Scotland,  in  1 291.  Sir  Michael, 
who  is  honourably  mentioned  by  Dante,  in  his  Inferno,  d. 
about  the  year  1294,  and  from  him  lineally  descended 
Sir  W^illiam  Scott,  taken  prisoner  at  Flodden,  and 
Sir  W^illiam  Scott,  ofB.alweary,  who,  in  the  lifetime  of 
his  father,  was  put  in  possession  of  the  lands  and  barony  of 
Innertiel,  and  was  long  designated  by  that  title.  This 
gentleman  had  two  sons.

The  ancient  family  of  Scott  has  been  seated  at  Great  Barr,

the  ancestor  of  the  present  haronet,  who  was  in  the  siute  of

woods)  would  allow  them.

Shaw,  Sir  Robert,  of  Bushy 
Park,  CO.  Dublin ;  deputy-lieut. 
of  Dublin;  b.  28  Sept.  1796;  s. 
his  father,  as  2nd  baronet,  10

Etncasr. 

This  family  was  originally  Scotch,  and  formed  a  part  of 
the  Clan  C'hattan.  This  branch,  at  an  early  period,  settled 
in  Hampshire,  in  England. 

William  Shaw,  the  immediate  ancestor  of  the  present 
Bart,  went  to  Ireland  about  the  year  1089,  in  the  army 
of  William  III.  He  was  captain  in  the  regiment  of 
Gen.  Ponsonby,  ancestor  of  the  Earl  of  Bessborough.  Their 
families  were  connected  by  marriage;  and  when  Gen. 
Ponsonby,  was  wounded  at  the  battle  of  the  Boyne,  Capt. 
Shaw  carried  him  from  the  field  ;  they  lived  afterwards  on 
terms  of  intimate  friendship  ;  both  received  grants  of  for- 
feited linds  from  the  Crown,  in  the  counties  of  Kilkenny 
and  Tipperary  ;  and  Gen.  Ponsonby  also  made  a  lease  of 
a  portion  of  the  demesne  lands  of  Bessborough  to  Capt. 
Shaw,  upon  which  he  built  a  residence,  Grilled  The  Saud- 
Pits,  where  the  family  resided  for  three  generations.  The 
eldest  sou  of  William  Shaw  left  an  only  dau.  who  to.  into 
the  family  of  the  Helys  of  Johnst02on,  and  by  that  means 
a  large  portion  of  the  family  property  passed  from  it. 
Robert,  the  second  son,  m.  Mary,  dau.  of  Bernard  Mark- 
ham,  Esq.  ;  by  her  he  had  six  sons  and  two  daus.  Robert 
Shaw  (father  of  the  1st  Bart.)  was  the  fifth  son  ;  early  in 
life  he  left  the  co.  Kilkenny,  and  became  subsequently  an 
eminent  merchant  in  Dublin,  where  he  realised  a  large  for- 
tune ;  he  was  the  most  considerable  holder  of  the  Govern- 
ment Loan  Contracts  of  that  day  ;  he  was  also  Accountant 
General  of  the  Post  Office.  He  m.  1st,  Mary,  dau.  of  Hig- 
gins  of  Higginsbrook,  co.  Meath,  and  by  her  had  issue,

Sir  John  Talbot,  K.G.,  6th  baron;  who  having m.  Maud, 
eldest  dau.  and  co-heir  of  Thomas  Nevil,  Lord  Fumival, 
had  been  summoned  to  parliament  in  1409,  as  "  Johannes 
Talbot  de  Fumyvall."  He  was  appointed,  in  1412,  lord-jus- 
tice of  Ireland,  and  in  two  years  afterwards,  lord-lieutenant 
of  the  same  kingdom  :  he  governed  there  for  seven  years. 
This  Lord  Talbot,  whom  Shakespeare  terms  "  the  great 
Alcides  of  the  field,"  was  one  of  the  most  renowned  captains 
of  the  warlike  age  he  lived  in,  His  earlier  feats  of  arms 
were  under  Henry  V.,  in  Franco,  at  the  siege  and  capture 
of  Meaux.  He  was  with  the  king  when  he  died,  in  1422, 
and  he  seems  to  have  inherited  the  heroic  spirit  of  his  royal 
master.  He  gloriously  sustained  the  cause  of  Henry  VI., 
throughout  his  French  realm,  in  battle  after  battle,  until 
the  very  name  of  Talbot  became  a  terror  to  Frenchmen. 
He  was,  for  a  moment,  checked  in  his  career  by  the  Maid 
of  Orleans,  at  Patay,  in  1429,  when  his  army  being  routed,  he 
■was  taken  prisoner.  He  was  exchanged  for  Ambrose  deLore, 
a  celebrated  Fi-ench  partisan ;  and  was  soon  in  activityagain, 
the  master-mind  and  master-director  of  the  fierce  contest 
in  France,  doing  good  and  effective  service  every  day.  In 
reward,  he  was  created,  20  May,  1442,  Earl  of  Shrews- 
bury. He  was  subsequently  re-constituted  lord-lieutenant 
of  Ireland,  and  elevated  to  the  peerage  of  that  kingdom, 
17  July,  1446,  as  Earl  of  Waterford,  having  been  appointed 
at  the  same  time  lord-high-steward  of  Ireland.*  After  tliis, 
he  went  once  more  to  fight  in  France.  He  commanded  a 
fleet,  lauded  and  took  Falaise,  and,  as  Lieutenant  of  the 
duchy  of  Acquitaine,  marched  to  the  south  and  made  Bor- 
deaux surrender,  and  the  surrounding  minor  towns  send  in 
instant  submission.  He  thence  advanced  to  the  relief  of 
Chastillon,  and  met  the  besieging  French  army  commanded 
by  their  then  greatest  leader,  Duuois,  Bastard  of  Orleans. 
In  the  battle  which  ensued,  20  July,  1453,  Talbot,  in  the 
eightieth  year  of  his  age,  received  a  wound  in  the  thigh, 
■which  proved  immediately  mortal.  Talbot  had  been  vic- 
torious in  forty  different  battles  and  dangerous  skirmishes  ; 
his  death  proved  fatal  to  the  English  dominion  in  France, 
which  never  flourished  afterwards.  The  earl  had  two  sur- 
viving sons  by  his  1st  wife, 

I.  John,  his  successor.  ii.  Christopher  (Sir). 

And  by  his  2nd,   Margaret,   eldest  dau.  and  co-heiress  of

Lisle  in  Berkshire;  and  in  1452,  Viscount  Lisle.'  His  lord- 
ship fell  endeavouring  to  rescue  his  father's  body  at  the 
battle  of  Chastillon.  He  m.  Joan,  dau.  and  co-heiress  of 
Sir  Thomas  Chedder,  of  Chedder,  in  Somersetshire,  and

The  eldest  son, 

Charles  Talbot,  6.  1684,  was  called  to  the  bar  by  the 
Inner  Temple,  in  1710,  and  attained  the  summit  of  hia 
profession,  and  established  the  highest  legal  reputation. 
He  was  also  an  active  politician,  and  was  M.P.  for  Tregony, 
and  for  Durham.  On  the  23  April,  1726,  Mr.  Talbot  was 
appointed  solicitor-general,  which  office  he  continued  to  fill 
until  29  Nov.  1733,  when  he  was  constituted  Lord  High- 
Chancellor  OP  England,  sworn  of  the  privy  council,  and 
elevated  to  the  peerage,  5  Deo.  following,  by  the  title 
of  Baron  Talbot,  of  Hensol,  co.  Glamorgan.  Lord  Talbot  is 
thus  eulogised  by  Dr.  Birch:  ''This  noble  lord  obtained 
the  honour  and  reverence  of  his  country  at  a  season  when 
no  foreign  or  domestic  occurrence  occasioned  any  remark- 
able event.  In  apprehension,  he  so  far  exceeded  the 
common  rank  of  men,  that  he  saw  by  a  kind  of  intuition 
the  strength  or  imperfection  of  any  arguments ;  and  so 
penetrating  was  his  sagacity,  that  the  most  intricate  and 
perplexing  mazes  of  the  law  could  never  so  involve  and 
darken  the  truth  as  to  conceal  it  from  his  discernment. 
As  a  member  of  each  House  of  Parliament,  no  man  ever 
had  a  higher  deference  paid  to  his  abilities,  or  more  confi- 
dence placed  in  his  public  spirit ;  and  so  excellent  was  his 
temper  and  so  candid  his  disposition  in  debate,  that  he 
never  offended  those  whose  arguments  he  opposed.  Though 
removed  at  a  time  of  life  when  others  begin  to  shine,  he 
might  justly  be  said  "satis  et  ad  vitamet  ad  gLoriam  vixisse."

The  family  of  Sinclair  of  Ulbster  is  a  branch  of  the  noble 
house  of  Sinclair,  Earls  of  Caithness,  and  has  possessed  the 
estate  of  Ulbster  for  between  two  and  three  hundred  years. 
It  has  risen  to  first-rate  position  in  the  north,  by  the  im- 
portance of  its  alliances,  and  the  extent  of  its  possessions.

eminence.  He  was  31. P.  for  York  :  he  was  first  chosen  one 
of  the  king's  Serjeants,  and  in  the  33rd  of  Edward  III., 
made  a  judge  of  the  Common  Pleas.  In  thi-ee  years  after- 
wards, he  was  sworn  in  lord-chief-barqn  of  the  Exchequer, 
from  which  oflBce  he  was  removed  in  1365;  he- was  re- 
instated a  judge  and  made  chief  justice  of  Ireland,  25  April, 
1371  :  he  retired  in  1373,  and  was  again  a  judge  of  the 
Common  Pleas  in  England,  from  8  Oct.  1377  tni  1388  :  he 
d.  1391.  As  a  judge,  he  deported  himself  so  uprightly,  that 
his  name  is  handed  down  liy  our  liistorians  with  the 
highest  honour.  "The  Collar  of  Esses,"  (says  an  old 
writer),  "  now  worn  by  the  judges,  first  introduced 
from  the  initial  letters  of  Sanctus  Simon  Simplicius,  an 
uucorrupted  justicier  in  the  primitive  times,  well  suited 
this  Sir  William  Skipworth,  who  died  fidl  of  honour."

knightly  degree,  was  founded  in  Ireland  by  a

In  the  reign  of  David  II. ,  in  13.J8,  a  grant  of  the  lands  and 
barony  of  Carnegie,  in  Forfarshire,  was  made  by  Walterus 
de  Maule  to  John  de  Balinhafd,  who  afterwards  took  the 
name  of  Carnegie.  The  charter  runs  thus  : — "  Quam 
quondam  W.  de  Maule  fecit  et  concessit  Joanni  filio  et 
heredi  quondam  Joannis  filii  Christini,  filii  Joannis  de  Ba- 
linhard,"  <fec.  This  last-named  Jolm  was  he  who  died  c.  1275. 
Of  the  origin  of  the  De  Balinhards  we  have  no  record,  all 
the  early  family  charters  havuig  perished  when  the  house 
of  Kinnaird  was  burnt,  in  1452. 

GocELVNUS  de  Balinhahd  witnesses  several  charters,  Ac. 
(undated,  but,  by  collateral  evidence,  drawn  out  between 
1204  and  1235),  in  the  Arbroath  and  St.  Andrew's 
cbartularies  ;  of  his  relationship,  however,  there  is  no  proof. 

John  de  Balinhard,  to  whom  the  grant  of  the  lands  of 
Carnegie  was  made,  and  who  afterwards  took  the  name  of 
Carnegie,  was  great-grandson  of  John  de  Balinhard,  who 
died  c.  1275.     He  d.  in  1370,  and  was  ,t.  by  his  son, 

Duthacus  de  Carnegie,  who  acquired  from  Robert,  Duke 
of  Albany,  governor  of  Scotland,  a  charter,  dated  21  Feb. 
1409,  confirming  "  Duthaco  de  Carnegy,  omnes  et  sin- 
gulas  terras  villa;  de  Kynnard,  ac  superioritatem  brasinee 
ejusdem,  on  the  signation  of  Mariota  de  Kynnard."  Dutha- 
cus de  Carnegie  fell  at  the  battle  of  Harlaw,  in  1411,  leaving 
an  infant  son, 

Walter  de  Carnegie,  of  Kinnaird,  who  took  part 
against  the  Earl  of  Crawford,  at  the  battle  of  Brechin, 
18  May,  1452,  when  his  adherents  were  defeated  by  the 
royal  troops  under  the  command  of  the  Earl  of  Huntly  ; 
and  Walter  de  Carnegie's  house  of  Kinnaird  was  burnt  by 
Crawford  in  retaliation.  Walter  Carnegie,  of  Carnegie, 
and  Jolin,  his  son,  are  mentioned  in  a  perambulation  of 
the  muir  of  Balnamoon,  27  July,  1456.  He  d.  in  1479, 
leaving  a  son, 

John  de  Carnegie,  of  Kinnaird,  who,  4  Nov.  1480,  had  a 
grant  from  his  cousin,  David,  Earl  of  Crawford,  of  a  life- 
rent out  of  the  lands  of  Glenesk  ;  and  dying  in  1 508,  left  a 
son,  by  his  wife,  a  lady  of  the  name  of  Vaus, 

John  de  Carnegie,  of  Kinnaird,  who  fell  at  the  battie  of 
Flodden,  9  Sept.  1513,  leaving  by  his  wife,  Euphame 
Strachan,  a  dau.  Janet,  m.  to  William  Maule,  of  Boath,

This  family  was  of  great  antiquity  in  the  county  of  Not-

and  branches  spread  into  Sussex,  Sun'ey,  Essex,  &c.

that  foUoweth,  taken  out  of  the  pedigree  of  the  Jerning- 
hams  by  a  judicious  gentleman  ;  Anno  mxxx.  ,  Canute,  king 
of  Denmarke  and  of  England,  after  his  return  from  Rome, 
brought  divers  captains  and  souldiers  from  Denmarke, 
whereof  the  greatest  part  were  christened  here  in  England, 
and  began  to  settle  themselves  here  ;  of  whom  Jernegan, 
or  Jerneghara,  and  Jernihingho,  now  Jennings,  were  of 
the  most  esteeme  with  Canute,  who  gave  unto  the  said 
Jerningham,  certaine  manors  in  Norfolke  ;  and  to  Jennings 
certain  manors  lying  upon  the  sea-side,  near  Harwich;  in 
regard  of  their  former  services  done  to  his  father,  Swends, 
King  of  Denmarke."

Note—Sir  William  Howard,  K.B.  (younger  son  of  Tliomas, 
23rd  Earl  of  Arundel,  by  creation  Earl  ot  Noi-folk  and  Earl  Mar- 
shal, K.G.),  m.  the  Hon.  Mary  Stafford,  sister  and  heiress  of 
Henry  Statford,  12th  Baron  Stafford,  and  was  created  Baron 
Stafford,  while  her  ladyship  was  created  Baroness  Stafford,  with 
remainder  to  their  heirs  male  and  general,  male  or  female, 
12  Sept.  1640.  Lord  Stafford  was  subsequently  advanced  to  the 
viscounty  of  Stafford,  11  Nov.  1640,  but  being  beheaded  and 
attainted  in  1678,  his  descendants  were  debarred  inheriting  the 
baronies  of  either  himself  or  the  baroness  until  the  reversal  of 
the  attainder  in  1824.  The  viscounty  expired  at  his  lordship's 
decease.

STAMFORD    AND    WARRINGTON. 


Stamford,  Earl  of  (George-Harry  Grey),  Earl  of 
Warrington  ;  Baron  Grey,  of  Groby  ;  and  Baron 
Delamere,  of  Dunham-Massey,  co.  Chester  ;  b.  7  Jan. 
1827  ;  s.  his  grandfather  26  April,  1845  ;  m.  1st,  23 
Dec.  1848,  Elizabeth  (who  d.  22  Oct.  1854),  da\i.  of 
Mr.  Billige,  of  Wincanton  ;  and  2nd]y,  29  Aug.  1855, 
Katherine,  2nd  dau.  of  the  late  Henry  Cocks,  Esq. 

Henry  de  Grey  obtained  from  King  Richard  I.  the  manor  of 
Turroc  in  Essex,  and  had  the  same  confirmed  by  King  John, 
with  the  privilege  of  hunting  the  fox  and  hare  in  any  lands 
belonging  to  the  crown  except  the  king's  own  demesnes.  In 
the  reign  of  Henry  III.,  he  had  a  grant  of  the  manor  of 
Grimston,  co.  Nottingham,  from  Robert  Bardolph,  whose  niece 
and  co-heiress,  Isolda,  he  married,  and  eventuaUy  shared  in  the 
inheritance  of  all  the  said  Robert's  lands.  From  his  2nd  son 
by  this  lady, 

John  de  Grey,  descended  the  lords  Grey  de  Ruthin,  (see 
Burke's  Extinct  Peerage)  the  extinct  Earls  and  Dul<es  of  Kent, 
the  extinct  Dulves  of  Suffolk,  the  Earls  of  Wilton,  and  the  house 
of  which  we  are  now  treating.  The  2nd  son  of  Reginald,  3rd 
Lord  Grey  de  Ruthyn, 

Sir  Edward  de  Grey,  m.  Elizabeth,  dau.  and  heiress  of 
Henry,  son  and  heir  apparent  of  William,  5th  Lord  Ferrers,  of 
Groby,  and  in  consequence  assumed  that  title.  His  lordship  d. 
in  the  36th  year  of  Henky  VI.,  and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son. 

Sir  John  de  Grey,  as  7th  Lord  Ferrers  of  Groby,  who  m. 
EUzabeth,  eldest  dau.  of  Richard  Widvile,  Earl  of  Rivers,  by  whom 
he  liad  two  sons.  Sir  John  fell  at  the  battle  of  St.  Albans,  fight- 
ing under  the  banner  of  Henry  VI.,  in  the  39th  year  of  that 
prince's  reign,  and  his  widow  became  subsequently  queen- 
consort  of  Edward  IV.    Sir  John  Grey's  eldest  son  and  heir, 

Sir  Thomas  Grey,  through  the  influence  of  his  mother,  was 
created,  in  the  11th  year  of  Edward  IV.,  Earl  of  Huntingdon, 
and  in  four  years  afterwards  advanced  to  the  Mccrquisate  of 
Dorset.  After  King  Edward's  death,  however,  his  lordship  was

bank.

This  noble  family,  which  derives  its  surname  from  the  town 
of  Stourton,  co.  WUts  was  of  considerable  rank  antecedently  to 
the  Conquest ;  for  we  find  at  that  period  one  of  its  members, 
Botolph  Stourton,  the  most  active  in  gallantly  disputing  every 
inch  of  gTound  with  the  foreigner,  and  finally  obtaining  from 
the  duke  his  own  tenns.  Having  broken  down  the  sea-walls  of 
the  Severn,  and  guarded  the  passes  by  land,  Botolph  entered 
Glastonbury  when  that  victorious  Norman  had  made  his 
appearance  in  the  west ;  and,  thus  protected,  compelled  William 
to  grant  w^hatsoever  he  demanded.  From  this  patriotic  and 
gallant  soldier  lineally  descended.

JCuuage  of  CampIjcII. 


This  family,  originally  from  Argyllshire,  has  been  settled 
nearly  two  centuries  in  the  co.  of  Fife. 

George  Campbell,  a  steady  adherent  of  his  clan,  and  of 
its  chief,  the  1st  Marquess  of  Argyll,  by  which  his  fortune 
became  considerably  impaired,  if  not  entirely  ruined, 
settled,  in  1662,  at  St.  Andrews,  and  became  proprietor  of 
the  estate  of  BaltuUa,  in  the  parish  of  Cores.  His  eldest 
son,  John,  took  the  degree  of  Master  of  Arts  at  St.  An- 
drews, in  the  year  1687,  and  gained  the  highest  honours  of 
the  miiversity,  then  of  high  reputation  for  all  branches  of 
learning.     His  grandson.

The  2nd  son, 

John  Campbell,  b.  15  Sept.  1779  ;  was  a  distinguished 
lawyer,  advocate,  judge,  and  biographical  writer ;  he  was 
educated  at  the  University  of  St.  Andrews,  where  he  took 
the  degree  of  A.jM.  ;  he  studied  law  at  Lincoln's  Inn,  and 
was  called  to  the  bar,  by  the  Hon.  Society  of  that  Inn,  in 
Michaelmas  Term,  1806  ;  he  went  the  Oxford  Circuit,  and 
having  attained  a  very  high  position  in  the  profession,  he 
was  made  king's  counsel  in  1827  ;  in  1S30,  he  was  returned 
to  parliament  for  the  borough  of  Stafford,  and,  in  1832,  for 
the  liorougb  of  Dudley  ;  in  November  of  the  same  year,  he 
was   appointed    solicitor-general  to    the   King,   and  was

Strathnairn,  Baron  (Sir  Hugh-Henry  Rose, 
G.C.B.,  K.S.I.,  P.C.),  of  Strathuahn,  in  the  co.  of 
Nairn,  and  of  Jhansi,  in  the  East  Indies,  in  the  peerage 
of  the  United  Kingdom  ;  a  general  in  the  army,  now 
commanding  the  forces  in  Ireland  ;  col.  of  the 
92nd  highlanders ;  b.  1803.  This  distinguished 
diplomatist  and  military  commander  entered  the 
British  army  in  1820.  His  earlier  services  were 
iu  Syria,  where  he  attained  the  rank  of  lieut.-col. 
He  was  constd-general  in  Syria,  and  was  made  a 
C.B.  iu  1842.  His  able  conduct  as  charge  d'affaires 
at  (Constantinople,  and  as  commissioner  at  head- 
quarters of  the  French  army  during  the  Eussian  war, 
was  acknowledged  by  his  being  made  a  K.C.B.,  a 
knight  commander  of  the  Legion  of  Honour,  and  a 
knight  of  the  Medjidie.  He  subsequently  com- 
manded the  Central  India  force  during  the  Sepoy 
mutiny,  and  for  his  brilliant  services,  including  the 
capture  of  Jhansi,  received  the  thanks  of  Parlia- 
ment, and  was  made  a  G.C.B.  He  became  a  lieut.- 
general  in  1860,  and  a  K.S.I,  iu  liGl  ;  he  was 
appointed  iu  1860.  commander-in-chief  in  India,  and 
held  that  post  till  1865,  when  he  was  given  the 
command  of  the  forces  in  Ireland,  and  was  made  a 
general  and  a  P.O.  He  was  rai.sed  to  the  peerage  as 
Lord  Strathnairn,  31  July,  1866. 

This  family  of  Eose  derives  its  descent  from  Hugh  Rose, 
of  Kilravoch  and  Ea.ster  Geddes,  who  d.  about  the  year 
1306  :  he  m.  Mary,  dau.  of  Sir  Andrew  do  Bosco,  Knt.,  by 
his  wife,  Elizabeth  (Lady  of  Kihavoch),  3rd  dau.  of  Sir 
John  Bisset,  Knt.  Upon  this  Elizalieth,  Lady  of  Kilravoch, 
the  lands  of  Kilravoch  were  settled  iu  doTver,  and  by  her 
dispo.sed  to  her  son-in  law,  Hugh  Rose,  whose  descendant, 

William  Rose,  11th  laird  of  Kilravoch,  ra.  Lilias,  sister 
of  William  Hay,  of  Dalgetie,  and  d.  in  1011,  leaving  (with

The  Right  Hon.  George  Rose,  b.  at  Brechin,  in  Scotland, 
17  Jan.  1744,  M.P.  for  Christchurch,  who  was  a  distinguished 
statesman  and  writer  of  the  last  century.  In  the  ad- 
ministration of  Mr.  Pitt,  whose  friendship  and  confidence 
he  enjoyed  in  an  especial  degree,  Mr.  Rose  was  president 
of  the  Board  of  Trade  and  treasurer  of  the  navy.  He  also  held 
the  lucrative  office  of  clerk  of  the  Parliaments.  He  d.  at

The  family  of  Strang  or  Stronge,  of  Balcaskie,  co.  Fife, 
was  one  of  considerable  antiquity,  and  was  seated  at  Balcaskie, 
A.D.  1363. 

Matthew  Stronge,  Esq.  of  Strabane,  in  1670,  and  Clonleigh, 
in  1686,  a  scion  of  Strang  of  Balcaskie,  was  warden  of  Lifford, 
CO.  Donegal,  in  1713.  This  gentleman  acquired  a  considerable 
tract  of  land  in  the  co.  Derry,  by  lease  from  the  corporation  of 
goldsmiths  of  London,  and  in  consideration  of  services  done 
and  losses  sustained  at  the  memorable  defence  of  Derry ,  and  in 
1689  obtained  a  renewal  thereof.  He  purchased  lands  in  the 
counties  of  Tyrone  and  Donegal,  and  in  1688  he  was  attainted 
by  James  II.'s  parliament.  He  d.  in  1716,  leaving,  by  Anne 
his  ^vife,  a  son,

Sib  William  Tracy,  of  Toddington,  was  sheriff  of  Glou- 
cestershire, in  the  5th  Henry  VIII.  anno  1513.  He  was  a 
gentleman  of  excellent  parts  and  soimd  learning,  and  is 
memorable  for  being  one  of  the  first  who  embr.aced  the 
reformed  religion  in  England,  as  appears  by  his  last  will, 
d.ated  22  Henry  VIII. ,  which  was  condemned  in  the 
Bishop  of  London's  Court,  after  his  decetse,  and  an  order 
sent  to  Parker,  chancellor  of  Worcester,  to  raise  his  body  ; 
but  he  too  officiously  burning  the  corpse,  the  recorder  only 
warranting  him  to  raise  the  body  according  to  the  law  of 
the  church,  he  was  afterwards  fined  £J00,  and  turned  out 
of  the  chancellorship.  Sir  William's  fimous  will  is  a 
curious  document — most  characteristic  of  the  times.  Sir

Lord  Thomas  IIowakd,  the  heir  of  his  mother's  estates,

The  name  of  Sykes,  is  derived  from  the  Anglo-SaXuu 
."kh,  intei-preted  by  Somner  as  sulcus  aquarius,  a  watcr- 
c  nirse,  or  water-fuiTOw.  Northern  topography  abounds 
with  the  word  syke,  which  is  usually  applied  to  a  small 
running  stream,  or  rivulet.  The  arms  in  use  from  a  remote 
period,  are  derived  from  the  same  source,  being : — "  Argent, 
a  chov.  sa.,  between  three  heraldic  foimtains,  or  sykes." 

Thoresby  says,  the  Sykoses  of  Leeds  "spning  from  those 
of  the  name  at  Sykes'  Dyke,  near  Carlisle  (whose  servants 
Wore  the  Branded  Bull*  as  their  badge)." 

Extant  documents,  in  Latin  and  in  English,  prove  that 
some  of  them  were  located  at  Flockton,  in  the  parish  of 
Thornhill,  near  Leeds,  about  the  year  1200,  when  Agnes  del 
Sicke  acquired  lands  at  "Floketon,"  adjoining  those  prc- 
vlouxlyhet'lhy  William  del  Sicke  :  that  in  1346,  (IS  Edw.  TIL) 
John  del  Syk,  of  "Fflokton,"  conveyed  ancestral  lands, 
there,  to  his  son,  Michael ;  that  in  1550,  (4  Edw.  VI.)  John 
Sykys  conveyed  tenements  and  land  in  Flockton  ;  with 
remainder  to  his  eldest  son,  Charles,  and  second  son, 
William  ;  that  in  1577,  (19  Eliz.)  Charles  Sykys,  whose  wife's 
name  was  Christian,  sold  certain  pastures  in  Nether 
Flockton  :  and  that  some  of  the  descendants  of  William 
Sykys,  who  settled  at  Leeds  as  a  clothier,  held  for  a  con- 
siderable period,  lands  at  Flockton.

The  castle  and  lordship  of  Malahide,  on  the  sea-coast, 
near  Dublin,  have  been  possessed  by  the  family  of  Talbot 
from  a  period  contemporary  with  the  first  introduction  of 
English  goverament  into  Ireland,  and  at  this  moment  they 
furnish  an  instance  unusually  rare,  of  a  baronial  estate 
having  continued  for  upwards  of  650  years  in  the  male 
heirs  and  name  of  him  on  whom  it  had  been  originally 
conferred  by  Henry  II.  It  is  remarkable,  too,  that  of  the 
ancient  seigniorial  estates  in  Ireland,  whose  lords  were 
vested  with  the  dignity  of  parliamentary  barons,  not  one 
can  be  traced  to  have  been  held  directly  and  vamedi- 
ateUj  under  the  crown  but  the  Lordship  of  Malahide. 
HowTH,  the  peninsula  so  called,  which  so  lately  as  the 
14th  century  is  admeasured  at  merely  twenty-seven  acres, 
was  held  certainly  xn  capite  by  grant  from  the  King  of 
England;  but  the  adjoining  manors,  which  formed  the 
strength  and  substance  of  the  baronial  estate,  were  held 
of  subjects,  by  rent,  suit,  and  service;  viz.,  Ratheny,  Kil- 
loster,  &c.  manors  were  held  of  the  monks  of  Christ- 
church  at  a  chiefry  of  Ss.  id.  yearlj-.  KilbaiTock,  at  a 
service  paid  for  or  under  the  family  of  De  Tuyte  of  a  pair 
of  furred  gloves.  Delvin,  which  has  been  time  imme- 
morial inherited  by  the  Nugent  family  exclusively,  whether 
styling  themselves  De  Nogent,  De  Capella,  or  Fitz-John, 
was  but  a  subinfeudation  made  to  his  kinsman  by  Hugh 
de  Lacy,  as  an  ancient  copy  of  his  charter  for  that  pur- 
pose still  extant  fully  evinces.  Lixnaw  was  held  as  a  sub- 
infeudation under  the  lords  of  the  liberty  of  Desmond, 
Athenry'  was  feudatory  to  the  lords  (and  lady-doieagers 
occasionally)  of  the  Lordship  of  Conuaught  for  the  time 
being  as  a  manor.*  Slane,  another  of  the  .ancient  ba- 
ronies, was  held  of  the  heirs  of  De  Verdon  as  of  their 
manor  ofDulak,  to  whom  the  Lords  Le  Fleming  yearly 
rendei'cd  rent  and  service.  Of  the  other  remaining  digni- 
ties,— viz.,  De  Courcy,  or  Kingsale,  Offaley,  (the  first  title 
obtained  by  the  ancestors  of  the  Duke  of  Leinster  in  the 
country,)  Gormanstown,  Killeen,  .and  Dunsany, — though 
they  may  have  existed  in  Ireland,  long  before  the  practice 
of  creating  peers  by  patent  commenced,  and  in  that  sup- 
position only  .are  here  named,  yet  they  are  of  such  recent 
or  modern  acquirement  in  the  families  which  now  possess 
them,  that  they  are  excluded  from  any  consideration  in  the 
discussion  of  a  fact  solely  relating  to  seignioral  territories 
.acquired  in  the  reign  of  Henry  II.  and  now  possessed  by 
the  descendants  of  the  blood  and  name  of  the  original 
founders.  In  this  respect  Malahide  seems  to  have  been 
unique  in  Ireland,  and  its  lords,  pursuant  to  the  nature  of 
their  original  tenure  and  the  terms  of  their  royal  char- 
tei-s,  never  rendered  homage,  suit,  or  service,  to  any  but 
the  crown,  nor  acknowledged  any  superior  but  the  King  of 
England  alone.  Richard  de  Talbott,  who  is  mentioned  in 
Domesday-Book,  was  the  common  ancestor  of  the  Lords 
of  Mal.ahide  and  of  the  Earls  of  Shrewsbury ;  and  in  con- 
sequence of  the  well-known  affinity  of  those  two  branches, 
the  family  in  IroL-md,  by  aucient  entails  and  settlements, 
made  the  members  of  the  house  of  Shrewsbury  next  heirs 
in  rem.ainder  to  their  Irish  estates.

V/hile  King  James  was  arming  (for  the  battle  of  the  Botne) 
in  Slane  Castle,  another  scene  equally  striking  was  acted  in  the 
hall  of  Malahide.  Before  the  dawn  of  day,  the  Talbots,  with 
their  kinsmen,  to  the  number  of  fourteen,  assembled,  amied  to 
the  teeth,  round  the  breakfast  table,  at  which  the  niece  of  tlm 
king's  lieut.-gen.  (Tirconnel),  the  Lady  Frances,  widow  of  the 
head  of  this  ioyal  party  (Richard  Talbot,  of  Malahide,  who  d.  in 
1703),  presided.  They  set  forth  with  a  light  to  join  their  Idns- 
man  the  duke,  the  king's  camp  lying  on  the  neai-  shore  of  the 
Boyne,  and  found  Tirconnel,  with  the  Duke  of  Bei-wick,  recon- 
noitering  the  position  of  King  William  on  the  opposite  side  of 
the  river.  While  William  was  mounting  his  horse,  it  happened 
that  a  man  and  two  horses  standing  near  him  were  killed  by  a 
cannon  ball.  A  second  bullet  rebounding,  glanced  over  the 
right  shoulder  of  the  gallant  William,  and  inflicted  a  flesh 
wound ;  his  officers  crowded  round  him,  and  it  was  thought  by 
the  enemy  that  he  was  killed.  A  shout  of  joy  rose  fiom  the 
.'rish  camp ;  and  Tirconnel,  prompt  to  avail  himself  of  the  great 
event,  sent  forth  a  squadron  of  cavalry  to  profit  by  the  conster- 
nation. In  this  petulant  attack  perished  the  party  of  the 
Talbots,  one  only  returning  to  the  castle  to  tell  the  story  of  tlie 
eventftil  day.  this  one  was  a  stripling  youth,  Richard,  son, 
heir,  and  successor  of  the  then  Talbot  of  Malahide.— iady

TEMPLE. 

Temple,  Sir  Grenville-Louis-

5  Jan.  18.58;  s.  bis  father,  as  12th

Ctncagc. 

This  ancient  family  (whatever  doubt  there  may  be  as  to  this 
baronetcy  still  existing)  derives  its  surname  from  the  manor 
of  Temple,  oo.  Leicester,  and  it  deduces  its  descent  from 
Leofric,  Earl  ofChester  (erroneously  styled  Earl  of  Leicester), 
who  lived  in  the  reign  of  Edward  the  Confessor.  This 
Leofric  i/(.  the  celebrated  Godiva,  the  heroine  of  Coventry, 
who  is  said  to  have  appeased  the  wrath  of  her  offended 
lord,  and  to  have  obtained  a  restitution  of  privileges  for  the 
good  citizens  of  Coventry,  by  riding  unclothed  through 
that  city  on  horseback.  This  she  did  in  submission  to 
what  her  husband  had  hastily  sworn,  viz.,  that  until  she 
so  rode,  he  would  not  relieve  the  citizens.  Thus  goes  the 
narrative,  but  certain  it  is  that  pictures  of  the  earl  and  his 
countess  were  set  up  in  the  south  window  of  Trinity 
church,  in  that  ancient  city,  about  the  reign  of  Richard  II., 
more  than  three  centuries  after  the  occuiTence  of  the  sup- 
posed event ;  his  lordship  holding  a  charter  in  his  right 
blind,  with  the  words, 

I  Lurick,  for  love  of  thee. 
Do  set  Coventry  toll-free. 
And  there   is  stUl  a  triennial  procession  of  a  naked  figure 
observed  by  the  grateful  citizens   on   Friday  after  Trinity 
Sunday.     Prom  this  Earl  of  Chester  lineally  descended,

Sir  James,  whose  patronymic  is  Emerson,  has 
assumed,  by  royal  licence,  the  additional  surname 
and  arms  of  Tennent.  He  was  M.P.  for  Belfast 
and  Lisburn.  He  held,  under  the  Gdvenimeut  of 
Sir  Robert  Peel,  the  office  of  secretary  to  the  India 
Board,  and  was  appointed  by  him  colonial  secretary 
and  lieut. -governor  of  Ceylon,  on  which  occasion  he 
received  from  Her  Majesty  the  honour  of  knight- 
hood. Under  the  Government  of  the  Earl  of  Derby 
he  was  secretary  to  the  Poor  Law  Department, 
which  he  resigned  to  become  jiermaneut  secretary 
to  the  Board  of  Trade,  from  which  he  retired  in 
1S67.  He  was  created  a  Baronet  14  Feb.  1867.  He 
is  a  J. P.  for  the  cos.  Down,  Antriu^  and  Fermanagh, 
and  knight  commander  of  the  Greek  Order  of  the 
Saviour,  and  was  a  D.L.  of  Fermanagh  and  Sligo. 
Sir  James  Emerson-Tennent  is  author  (amongst 
others)  of  the  following  works  : — Travels  in  Greed 
in  1825,  Letters  from  the  jEyean ;  Etsay  on  the 
Copyright  of  Designs  ;  Belgium  ml840;  History  of 
Blodern  Greece;  History  of  Christianity  in  Ceylon; 
Wine,  its  Use  and  Taxation ;  and  Ceylon,  An 
Account  of  the  Island.

I.  Patrick  Threipland,  Esq.  of  Fingask  Castle,  co. 
Perth,  was  made  a  knight-bachelor  by  King  Charles  II., 
in  the  year  1674,  and  aftei-wards  a  5a rorati  of  Nova  Scotia, 
by  King  .James  II.,  10  Nov.  1687,  with  remamder  to  his 
heirs  male.  Sir  Patrick  was  a  stanch  supporter  of  the 
family  then  on  the  throne.  He  took  an  active  lead  in  the 
politics  of  his  country  during  the  usurpation  of  Cromwell, 
and  for  many  years  successively  discharged,  with  infinite 
credit,  several  important  public  duties,  which  were  com- 
mitted to  bis  care.  He  m.  13  March,  166.5,  Eupbemia,  dau. 
of  John  Conqueror,  Esq.  of  Frierton,  by  whom  he  had  one 
son  and  six  daus.,  and  dying  in  1689,  was  .«.  by  his  son, 

II.  Sir  David,  who  m.  1st,  in  1688,  Elizabeth,  dau.  of 
Sir  James  Ramsay,  Bart,  of  Banff,  by  whom  he  had  seven 
sons  and  three  daus.  ;  and  2udly,  in  1707,  Dame  Catherine 
Smythe,  of  Barnhill,  by  whom  he  had  two  sons  and  four 
daus.  Sir  David  Threipland  having  imbibed  all  the  Tory 
principles  of  his  father,  held  a  secret  correspondence  with 
the  son  of  James  II.  and  his  adherents,  and,  in  1715,  he 
was  among  the  first,  with  his  sons  and  a  party  of  followers, 
to  aid  the  Earl  of  Mar  in  setting  up  the  standard  of  the 
Chevalier  de  St.  George,  and  in  proclaiming  that  prince 
king  luider  the  title  of  James  VIII.  of  Scotland  and  III. 
of  England ;  in  consequence  of  which.  Sir  David's  title 
was  attainted  by  act  of  iiarliament,  in  the  1st  year  of  King 
George  I.,  and  his  estates  and  effects  were  annexed  to  the 
crown.  He  d.  in  1 746,  and  was  s.  by  his  youngest  and  only 
surviving  son, 

HI.  (Sir)  Stuart,  who  being  also  strongly  attached  to  the 
cause  of  the  house  of  Stuart,  linked  his  fate  with  that  of  the 
unfortimate  Charles-Edw-ard  in  1745,  and  participated  in  ad 
the  difficulties  and  misery  which  that  prince  and  his  followers 
were  doomed  to  undergo.  After  the  result  of  the  battle  of 
CuUoden,  so  fatal  to  the  hopes  of  the  Jacobites,  Sir  Stuart 
Threipland's  maternal  property,  as  had  been  the  case  with  his 
paternal  in  1716,  was  forfeited:  and  a  reward  having  been 
offered  for  his  apprehension,  he  contrived  to  escape  into  France, 
where  he  remained  at  the  court  of  the  Stuarts,  until  the  act  of 
indemnity  permitted  his  return  to  Scotland  in  security  ;  when, 
at  a  sale  of  forfeited  lands,  in  1782,  he  repurchased  the  family 
estates,  which  are  now  in  the  possession  of  his  descendants.  He 
m.  1st,  in  1753,  Jannet,  eldest  dau.  of  David  Sinclair,  Esq.  of

less; and  2ndly,  in  1761,  Bliss  Jannet-Budge  MuiTay,  of  Penny- 
and,  by  wdiom  he  had  four  sons  and  a  dau.  viz., 

Patrick-Murray,  late  baronet. 

Richard,  who  d.  in  India.

Hincasc. 

Sir  John  Throckmorton,  Knt.,  descended  from  Joliti  de 
Throckmorton  (who,  according  to  Sir  William  Dugdale,  was  lord

quest), was  a  very  eminent  personage  in  the  reigns  of  Henry  V. 
and  Henry  VI.,  and  in  the  latter  bore  the  title  of  under-treasurer 
of  England.  Sir  John  m.  Eleanor,  dau.  and  co-heiress  of  Sir  Guy 
de  Spineto,  Lord  of  Coughton,  co.  Warwick,  and  dying  in  1445, 
was  s.  by  liis  eldest  son,* 

Thomas  Throckmorton,  Esq.,  high-sheriff  of  Warwick  and 
Leicester  in  the  5th  of  King  Henry  IV.  This  gentleman  m. 
Margaret,  dau.  and  co-heiress  of  Sir  Robert  Olney,  Knt.  of  Weston, 
CO.  Buckingham,  and  was  *:.  by  his  eldest  son. 

The  Right  Hon.  Robert  Throckmorton,  one  of  the  privy 
council  of  King  Henry  VII.  This  gentleman,  who  was  remark-

This  family — one,  it  is  stated,  of  importance  in  the  co.  of

time  has  reduced  to  the  present  appellation  of  Tichborne.

of  Gordon  of  Gicht,  being  the  aunt  of  George,  Marquess  of 
Huntly,  the  leader  of  the  king's  party  in  the  north 
of  Scotland)  as  well  as  from  community  of  faith,  warmly 
espoused  the  cause  of  Charles  I.,  I'aised  and  maintained 
at  his  own  expense  a  body  of  horse,  under  the  banner 
of  his  relative,  the  Marquess  of  Huntly  ;  in  acknow- 
ledgment for  which  services  he  was  created  a  Baronet  of 
Nova  Scotia  in  the  year  1638.  After  the  decease  of  Sir  John 
Turing,  the  devoted  adherent  of  Charles  II.,  the  title  lay 
dormant  until  the  year  1792,  when  Sir  Robert  Turing,  his 
lineal  descendant,  assumed  the  title  and  family  honours

The  antiquity  of  the  noble  and  illustrious  name  of  Hait 
is  sufficiently  attested  both  by  ancient  and  modern  his- 
torians ;  and  though  there  has  been  no  positive  di.sproof  of 
the  traditional  account  of  their  origin,  from  the  battle  of 
Loncarty,  about  the  year  980,  which  is  so  fully  narrated  in 
many  Scotch  histories,  yet  some  other  conjectures  have 
been  mooted  which  rest  on  much  presumptive  evidence, 
a  singular  concurrence  of  circumstances.     For  instance, — 

The  surname  of  Hay  came  originally  from  France  :  that 
there  were  lands  and  a  lordship  of  that  denomination  in 
Normandy,  from  which  it  is  presumable  the  surname  was 
first  assumed,  long  before  the  time  of  William  the  Con- 
queror.    This  is  attested  by  undoubted  authority. 

Humphry,  sm-named  De  Vetulis,  Lord  of  Pont  Audemar, 
in  Normandy,  and  one  of  the  most  consideraljle  families  in 
that  country,  ra.  Albreda  de  la  Haie,  or  Haya,  by  whom 
he  had  a  son,  Roger  de  Bellamont,  or  Beaumont,  Lord  of 
Pont  Audentar,  who  gave  the  name  of  Beaumont  Roger  to 
a  town  in  Normandy,  and  was  one  of  the  council  who 
persuaded  William,  Duke  of  Normandy,  to  invade  England, 
before  the  year  1066. 

In  the  list  of  the  great  captains  that  came  over  from 
Normandy  to  England  with  that  famous  prince,  Le  Sieur 
de  la  Haya  is  expressly  mentioned,  with  several  others  of 
the  same  name  ;  which  plainly  shows  that  they  were  a 
numerous  and  flourishing  family  before  the  Conquest. 

There  were  several  religious  houses  founded  by  them, 
which  appears  from  the  same  history,  particularly  Lo 
Abbay  de  Blancheland,  in  the  diocese  of  Contasines,  was 
fomided  and  endowed  by  Richard  de  la  Haya,  in  Noi'tnandy, 
anno  1155. 

The  Hays  in  Normandy  had  the  same  aitnorial  bearings 
with  those  in  Scotland.  For  some  generations  after  they  were 
settled  in  Scotland  many  of  them  were  designed  by  the 
appellation  of  De  la  Haya  ;  all  which  are  strong  presump- 
tive proofs  that  they  came  originally  from  France  ;  and  it 
is  certain  that  there  are  families  of  that  snmame  subsisting 
in  Normandy  to  this  day,  who  deduce  their  pedigree  above 
a  himdred  years  before  the  Conquest. 

As,  then,  there  is  clear  proof  that  several  of  that  name 
came  to  Britain  in  the  year  1066  ;  and  as  it  appears  from 
many  records  that  they  were  settled  and  making  a  figure 
in  Scotland  within  less  than  a  hundred  years  thereafter, 
it  is  extremely  probable  that  some  of  that  race  came  to 
Scotland  with  King  David  I.  ;  for  it  is  shown  by  all 
Scottish  histories,  that  several  of  Norman  extraction,  who 
had  contracted  a  friendship  vsdth  that  amiable  prince 
when  in  England,  went  with  him  on  his  retmn,  and 
settled  in  Scotland,  from  whom  some  of  the  most  consider- 
able famiUes  in  Scotland  descend,  such  as  Bruce,  Maules, 
Somei-villes,  Colviles,  Normanviles,  Montgomeries,  Baliols, 
and  many  others.  Yet  whatever  may  be  the  strength  of 
these  conjectui'es,  it  is  certain  that 

William  de  Haya  settled  in  Lothian  neai-ly  seven  cen- 
turies ago,  and  filled  the  office  of  royal  Butler  during  the 
reigns  of  Malcolm  IV.  and  William  the  Lion.  He  d.  about

J. -A.  -jBernard  Law,  Marquis  of  Lauriston,  Marshal  of  France, 
d.  1828.  The  Marshal's  grand-son,  ^Uexander-Louis-Josepb 
Law,  3rd  Marc^uis  of  Lauriston,  is  the  present  represen- 
tative of  the  family.  Of  this  family  of  Law  was  the  cele- 
brated financier,  John  Law  (maternally  of  the  blood  of 
tlie  ducal  house  of  Argyle),  comptroller-general  of  the  ex- 
chequer iu  France,  b.  at  Edinburgh,  April,  1671;  who,  under 
the  patronage  of  the  Regent,  Duke  of  Orleans,  established, 
to  remedy  the  deficiency  of  the  circulating  medium,  a  Royal 
Bank  at  Paris,  with  paper  is.sues.  His  system,  which  has 
been  subjected  to  much  acrimonious  ct.niment,  did,  without 
doubt,  at  the  time  greatly  relieve  the  distressed  condition  of 
the  public  funds,  and  revive  the  mercantile  and  manufac- 
turmg  energies  of  France.  For  the  excesses  to  which  the 
■system  gave  rise,  and  especially  for  the  Mississippi  scheme, 
that  ruined  so  many,  the  French  people  themselves,  rather 
than  Law,  were  answerable.  Law,  whose  personal  honesty 
and  honour  have  not  been  disinited,  took  with  him  from 
the  enormous  wealth  he  had  realized  in  France  only  sufl5- 
eient  to  live  on,  when  he  left  that  comitry,  14  Dec.  1720  ; 
and  he  d.  at  Venice,  in  1729.

Sir  Walter  Tvrell,  a  Norman  knight,  came  into

same  person  who  shot  William  Rufus  in  the  New  Forest,

jVnselm,  through  the  persuasion  of  a  fanatic  monk,  as  it  is 
asserted  by  Alan  de  Insulis,  we  are  not  able  to  determine," 
It  is  far  indeed  from  being  an  ascertained  point  that  this 
family  is  descended  from  the  Walter  Tyrell  who  slew  Rdfus, 
and  as  far  is  it  from  being  certain  that  the  deed  was  done 
designedly.  Ordericus  Vitalis,  in  his  History  of  Normandy, 
relates,  that  Sir  Walter  Tyi'ell,  on  hi«  death-bed,  decl.ared 
that  ho  was  not  .so  much  as  in  the  field  when  William 
Rufus  was  killed.     From  Sir  Walter  Tyrell  descended

has  it),  derived  their  name  from  their  office,  being  formerly 
King's  valvasor,  a  degree  then  little  inferior  to  the  baronial. 
"There  are,"  says  Bracton,  "for  the  civil  government  of  man- 
kind, emperors,  kings,  and  princes,  magnates,  or  valvasors, 
and  knights." 

Sir  Mauger  le  Vavasor  is  mentioned  in  Domesday  Book,  as 
holding  in  chief  of  the  Percys,  Earls  of  Northumberland,  con- 
siderable manors  and  estates  in  Stutton,  Eselwood,  Saxall 
(Saxon),  &c.    He  was  father  ot  another

Percy,  Countess  of  Warwick.  To  this  abbey  he  himself  also 
made  a  considerable  donation  of  land.    He  was  s.  by  his  son.

years  afterwards,  by  cutting  out  one  of  the  window-bars  with  a 
tile,  and  letting  himself  down  by  a  rope  conveyed  to  him  by  his 
servant,  with  whom  he  changed  clothes.  Sir  Edward  lived  to 
the  of  advanced  age  ninety-eight,  and  was  s.  at  his  decease  by

The  family  of  Vivian  is  of  great  antiquity  in  tbo  co.  of 
Cornwall.  Mr.  Whitaker,  in  his  Treatise  on  the  Ancient 
Cathedrals  of  Cornwall,  claims  for  them  a  Roman  descent, 
and  in  support  of  bis  opinion  cites  a  passage  from  Tacitus, 
in  which  mention  is  made  of  Vivianus  Annius,  a  com- 
mander in  the  Roman  legion,  and  son-in-law  of  C'cn-bulo, 
who  had  been  a  leader  in  the  imperial  armies  in  Gaul  and 
Germany.  Dr.  Borlase  and  others  consider  the  name  Celtic 
.'ind  that  the  family  is  of  Celtic  origin.  Be  this  as  it  may, 
whether  descended  from  the  Romans  or  the  Celts,  the 
Vivians  of  Cornwall  are  indisputably  to  bo  considered 
amongst  the  oldest  inhabitants  of  the  coiuity.  The  family 
before  ns  is  descended  from  the  branch  that  resided  at 
Trenowotb,  in  the  parish  of  St.  Columb,  in  the  reign  of 
IIe.vry  VII.,  and  after  that  at  Trewau,  in  the  same  parish 
These  estates,  with  Witbiel  and  other  property  in  the  co.' 
of  Cornwall,  passed  to  the  Trelowarren  family  in  the  reign 
of  William  III.,  by  the  m.arriage  of  the  heiress,  Mary 
Vivian,  with  Sir  Richard  Vyvyan,  Bart,  of  Trelowarren.
