The  Wakes  are  mentioned  by  Brompton  as  in  the  imme- 
diate'train  of  The  Conqueror  ;  but  it  is  the  opinion  of  anti- 
quaries that  the  individual  of  the  name  of  Wake  recorded 
in  the  roll  of  Battle  Abbey,  was  one  of  those  who  being 
weary  of  Harold's  rule,  fled  into  Normandy,  and  invited 
Duke  William  ;  hence  the  family  is  supposed  to  have  been 
of  importance  prior  to  the  Conquest.  The  celebrated  Arch- 
bishop Wake,  mentioned  below,  wrote  a  history  of  the  Wake 
family,  in  which  he  ascribes  to  Hereward  le  Wake,  the  feat 
of  having  successiuUy  opposed  and  finally  made  terms  with 
William  the  Conqueror.  As  Augustin  also  mentions  Wakes 
in  Normandy,  it  is  probable  that  there  were  two  parties  in 
the  family  at  that  time.  An  historical  novel  has  been 
wi-itten  upon  the  feats  of  Hereward,  in  harassing  the 
Normans,  and  defending  the  Abbey  of  Brun  after  the  Con- 
quest. His  tomb  is  still,  or  was  to  be  seen,  not  many  years 
ago  in  Lmcolnshh-e.     From

Eturaflc. 

This  Anglo-Saxon  family  was  amongst  those  who  fled  into 
Scotland  at  the  period  of  the  Conquest,  and  being  hospitably 
received  by  King  Malcolm  Canmore,  settled  in  that  kingdom. 
Of  the  Wardlaws,  Cardinal  Wardlaw  compiled  a  genealogical 
account  from  their  first  coming  from  Saxony  into  England, 
about  the  beginning  of  the  6th  century,  up  to  his  own  time,  a 
copy  of  which  was  in  the  royal  library  of  France  until  the 
Revolution;  and,  according  to  family  tradition,  the  elder

Sir  Fulke  Greville,  Knt.,  m.  Elizabeth  Willoughby,  the 
ward  of  his  father,  and  the  greatest  heiress  then  in  England 
(see  Bdrke's  Extinct  Pierage).  The  account  of  this  marriage 
is  in  a  manuscript,  entitled  The  Geiualogie,  Life,  and  Death 
of  Robirt,  Lord  Brooke,  written  in  164-t,  and  in  the  possession 
of  Earl  Brooke.  "  In  the  days  of  Henry  VIII.  (says  the  author 
of  the  manuscript),  I  read  of  Sir  Edward  Grevil,  of  Milcote, 
who  had  the  wardership  of  Elizabeth,  one  of  the  daus.  of  the 
Lord  Brooke's  son.  The  knight  made  a  motion  to  his  ward, 
to  be  married  to  John,  his  eldest  son ;  but  she  refused,  saying, 
that  she  did  like  better  of  Fulke,  his  2nd  son.  He  told  her 
that  he  had  no  estate  of  land  to  maintain  her ;  and  that  he 
was  in  the  king's  service  of  warre  beyond  the  seas,  and  there- 
fore his  return  was  very  doubtful.  Shee  replied  and  said,  that 
shee  had  an  estate  sufficient  both  for  him  and  for  herself,  and 
that  she  would  pray  for  his  safeties  and  wait  for  his  coming. 
Upon  his  returne  home,  for  the  worthy  services  he  had  per- 
formed, he  was,  by  King  Henry,  honoured  with  knighthood  ; 
and  then  manied  Elizabeth,  the  dau.  of  the  Lord  Brooke's 
son."  By  this  marriage,  the  manor  of  Alcester,  and  many 
other  fair  lordships  and  lands,  came  in  right  of  his  wife  to  Sir 
Fulke,  who,  seating  himself  at  Beauchamp's  Court,  and  aug- 
menting his  large  estate  by  the  purchase  of  sundry  lands  in  the 
neighbourhood,  raised  his  family  to  high  distinction  in  the  co. 
Warwick.    Of  this  marriage  there  were,  with  other  issue,

Sir  Roger  Le  Poer,  Knt.,  who  accompanied  Strongbow 
into  Ireland,  obtained  for  his  services  there  considerable 
territorial  grants.  Of  Sir  Roger,  Giraldus  Cambrensis 
writes:  "  It  might  be  said  withaut  offence,  there  was  not 
a  man  wh  i  did  more  valiant  acts  than  Roger  le  Poer ;  who, 
although  he  were  young  and  beardless,  yet  he  showed  him- 
self a  lust3',  valiant,  and  courageous  gentleman,  and  who 
grew  into  such  good  credit,  that  he  had  the  government  of 
the  country  about  Leighlin,  as  also  in  Ossory,  where  he  was 
traitorously  killed ;  on  whose  slaughter  a  conspiracy  was 
formed  among  the  Irish  to  destroy  the  English,  and  many 
castles  were  destroyed."    Sir  Roger  m.  a  niece  of  Sir  Amory

The  family  of  Weldon  of  Swanscomb,  in  Kent,  of  which 
that  of  Rahenderry  is  a  branch,  derived  descent  from 
Bertram  de  Weltden,  who  was  of  the  retinue  of  Walther, 
Earl  of  North umbei-land,  and  Bishop  of  Durham  at  the 
Conquest.  His  descendant  was  Lord  of  Weltden,  in  North- 
umberland, temp.  Richard  I.  From  him  sprang  Hugh 
Weltden,  Sewer  to  King  Henry  VII.,  who  left  four  sous: 
Hugh,  ancestor  of  the  Weltdens  of  Shottesbrooke,  in  Berk- 
shire ;  Edward,  progenitor  of  the  Weldons  of  Swanscomb, 
Kent  ;  Thomas,  coflerer  to  King  Edward  VI.  and  Queen 
Elizabeth,  whose  descendants  were  of  Cookham,  Berks; 
and  William,  whose  issue  settled  at  Thornby,  in  North- 
amptonshire. The  second  son,  Edward  Weldon,  Master  of 
the  Household  to  King  Henry  VIII.,  was  father  of 
Anthony  Weldon,  Esq.,  Clerk  of  the  Spicery,  afterwards 
promoted  to  the  board  of  Green  Cloth,  to  whom  Queen 
Elizabeth  granted  the  manor  of  Swanscombe  in  fee.  This 
Antony  Weldon,  having  performed  some  extraordinary 
public  service.  Queen  Elizabeth  said  to  him  that  she  wished 
to  show  her  estimation  of  his  conduct,  and  would  grant 
him  anything  in  her  power  that  he  wished  to  ask  for,  on 
which,  he  replied,  that  if  she  would  allow  him  to  use  her 
bust  as  his  orest,  to  hand  down  to  posterity,  it  would  more 
than  fully  compensate  him  for  any  good  he  might  have 
done.  This  the  Queen  granted,  with  the  motto,  "  Bene 
factum,"  saying  that  he  had  "  well  done,  and  so  made  good 
his  name,"  which  expression  of  royal  satisfaction  is  partly 
quoted  on  the  family  tombs,  at  Swanscombe,  Kent.  Mr. 
Antony  Weldon,  d.  1(51.3.  His  son  and  successor.  Sir  Ralph 
Weldon,  of  Swanscombe,  clerk  of  the  kitchen  to  Queen 
Elizabeth,  and  afterwards  clerk-comptroller  to  Jame.s  1., 
d.  in  1609,  being  then  Clerk  of  the  Board  of  Green  Cloth. 
By  Elizabeth  his  wife,  he  left  four  sons,  Anthony  (Sir),  Knt. 
of  Swanscombe  ;  Henry  ;  Lewen  ;  and  Ralph.

lesley,  K.G.,  P.O.),  Marquess  of  Douro,  Marquess  and

pointed, 21  Jan.  1853,  Master  of  the  Horse,  which

The  very  eminent  family  of  Wesley,  or  Wellesley,  or, 
as  it  was  formerly  written,  De  Welesley,  alias  Welseley, 
was  founded  in  Ireland  by  a  warrior  of  that  name,  of 
an  ancient  Anglo-Saxon  family,  who  held  the  honourable 
post  of  standard-bearer  to  King  Henry  II.  ;  and  having 
accompanied  that  monarch  into  Ireland  in  1172,  obtained 
for  his  military  services  large  grants  of  laud  in  the  counties 
of  Meath  and  Kildare,  From  this  successful  soldier  de- 
scended. 

William  de  Wellesley,  who  appears  to  have  been  sum- 
moned to  parliament  as  a  baron  of  the  realm,  by  the  title 
of  Baron  of  Noragk,  in  1330,  and  had  a  grant  by  patent  from 
Edward  II.  of  the  custody  of  the  castle  of  Kildare  for  life  ; 
but  that  monarch,  conferring  subsequently  the  office  upon 
John-Fitz  Thomas,  Earl  of  Kildare,  together  with  the  county 
of  Kildare,  to  hold  to  his  heirs  male,  for  ever,  William  de 
Wellesley  was  removed,  and  lost  the  fee  of  ^'20  a  year 
annexed  thereunto ;  to  compensate  which,  however.  King 
Edward  III.  granted  him  a  commission  dated  at  Molyngar 
Maroh,  1342,  to  have  the  custody  of  the  manor  of  Demor, 
then  in  the  crown,  from  1  Aug.  1341,  with  the  annual  fee 
of  20  marks.     This  William  was  father  of 

Sir  Richard  de  Wellesley,  who  served  the  ofiice  ot 
sheriff  of  Kildare  in  the  year  1418.  He  to.  Johau,  eldest 
dau.  and  eventually  heir  of  Sir  Nicholas  de  Castlemartin, 
l_iy  whom  he  obtained  the  lordships  of  Dangau,  Morning- 
ton, Clonebreny,  and  several  other  manors,  and  was  s.  by 
his  son, 

Gerald  de  Wellesley,  of  Dangan,  from  whom  lineally 
descended 

William  Wesley,  Esq.  of  Dangan  Castle,  who  to.  Eliza- 
beth, dau.  of  James  Cusack,  Esq.  of  Portraine,  co.  Dublin, 
and  was  s.  by  his  eldest  son. 

Valerian  Wesley,  Esq.  of  Dangan  Castle.  This  gentle-

The  Hon.  Arthur  Wellesley  (The  Great  Duke  of 
Wellington),  was  the  3rd  son  of  Garrett,  1st  Earl  of  Morn- 
ington, by  Anne,  his  wife,  dau.  of  Arthui  Hill,  1st  Viscount 
Duugannon,  and  was  6.  at  Mornington  Hovise,  Upper 
Merriou  Street,  Dublin,*  1  May,  1769.  The  Earl  of  Mor- 
nington had  also  a  residence  at  Kensington,  where  his 
lordship  d.  in  1781,  and  where  the  young  Arthur  spent 
part  of  his  boyhood.  At  an  early  age  Arthur  Wellesley 
was  sent  to  Eton  ;  and,  at  the  close  of  the  American  war,  he 
went  to  the  military  college  of  Angers,  in  Anjou,  France. 
He  received  his  fii'st  commission  in  the  British  army  as  an 
ensign  in  the  73rd  regiment,  7  March,  1787.  His  service  in 
that  regiment  was  extremely  brief,  for  before  the  close  of 
17S7  he  was  gazetted  to  a  lieutenantcy  in  the  76th.  The 
following  year  he  exchanged  into  the  41st,  and  from  that 
passed  into  other  regiments  of  cavalry  and  foot.  He  was 
made  a  captain  of  the  58th  in  1791  ;  and  in  1793,  he  was 
appointed  to  the  majority  of  the  33rd.  On  the  30  Sept. 
following,  he  became,  by  purchase,  lieut. -colonel  in  the 
same  regiment.  By  this  time  the  new  lieut. -colonel  had 
commenced  his  public,  though  not  his  active  military, 
career.  He  sat  in  the  Irish  parliament  as  member  for 
Trim  in  1790,  and  occasionally  took  an  energetic  part  in 
the  proceedings  of  the  House.  He  supported  the  con- 
cessions to  the  Roman  Catholics,  and  opposed  Parliamen- 
tary Reform.  The  outbreak  of  the  war  with  revolutionary 
France  called  him  from  the  senate.  He  joined  the  cam- 
paign, then  conducted  by  the  Duke  of  York,  in  1794,  and 
he  proceeded  to  Ostend  with  his  regiment,  the  33rd,  which 
was  placed  with  the  gallant  Lord  Moira's  division.  Lieut.- 
Colonel  Wellesley  was  present  at  all  the  skirmishes  in 
repulsing  the  French  at  Antwerp  and  Brussels  ;  and  in  the 
subsequent  retreat,  he,  with  his  regiment,  more  than  once 
successfully  checked   the  advance  of  the  enemy.     On  the

The  ancient  family  of  the  Earls  of  Wemyss,  trace  their 
origin  from  the  celebrated  Macduff,  Thane  and  1st  Earl  of 
Fife,  the  vanquisher  of  the  tyrant  Macbeth. 

The  surname  of  Wemyss,  like  many  others  in  Scotland, 
is  local,  and  was  first  assumed  by  the  proprietors  of  the 
lauds  anciently  called  Wemyss-shire,  which  contained  all 
that  tract  of  ground  lying  betwixt  the  lower  part  of  the 
water  of  Ore  and  the  sea.  These  lands  got  their  name  from 
the  great  number  of  caves  that  ire  on  them,  all  along  the 
sea  coast.  A  cave  in  the  old  Gaelic  or  Celtic  language,  was 
called  Vumhs ;  from  that,  these  lands  got  the  name  of 
Vams-shire.  In  process  of  time  they  came  to  be  called 
Wemyss-shire,  which  name  they  still  retain,  as  will  appear 
from  several  charters  under  the  great  seal. 

GiLLiMiCHAEL,  4th  Earl  isf  Fife,  great-grandson  of  Mac- 
duff, the  1st  Earl,  was  witness  to  the  foundation  charter  of 
the  abbey  of  Holyrood  Hous#,  in  1128,  and  is  mentioned  in 
several  other  charters  of  King  David  I.  He  d.  1139,  leaving 
issue,  Duncan,  5th  Earl  of  Fife,  in  whom  the  line  of  those 
Earls  was  continued,  and  a  2nd  son  Hugo,  direct  ancestor 
of  the  family  of  Wemyss,  who  got  from  his  father,  the 
lands  of  Wemyss-shire,  some  lands  in  Lochoreshire,  and  in 
the  path  Kennoway,  all  holding  of  himself  and  his  succes- 
sors, Earls  of  Fife.  He  obtained  also  from  his  bi other 
Duncan,  the  5th  Earl  of  Fife,  some  lands  in  the  parish  of 
Markinch,  with  the  church  patromge  thereof.  He  d.  in 
1167,  and  was  s.  by  his  son  Hdgo,  or  Ego,  whose  son.  Sir 
John,  succeeded  him  in  all  his  lands.  This  Sir  John 
appears  to  have  been  a  man  of  distinguished  rank  and 
figure,  and  in  his  younger  days  took  the  appellation  of  John 
OF  Methkil,  or  Methill,  from  a  seaport  of  that  name, 
situate  near  the  east  end  of  Wemyss-shire.  As  surnames 
began  about  this  time  to  be  frequently  used  in  Scotland,

II.,  from  his  lands  of  Wemyss-shire,  assumed  that  ol 
Wemyss  for  his  surname,  which  his  whole  posterity  have 
enjoyed  ever  since.  Sir  John  de  Wemyss  had  three  sons,

Lord  We.stbury,  a  very  distinguished  lawyer  and 
statesman,  eldest  son  of  the  late  Richard  Bethell,  M.D., 
was  educated  at  Wadham  College,  Oxford,  where  he 
obtained  a  first-class  in  classics,  and  a  second-class  in 
mathematics,  and  became  a  Fellow  of  the  College, 
and  in  1860,  D.C.L.  He  was  called  to  the  bar  by  the 
Hon.  Society  of  the  Middle  Temple,  in  Nov.  1823, 
and  attained  the  very  highest  eminence  during  a  long 
practice  in  the  Courts  of  Eqviity ;  he  was  made  a 
Q.C.  in  1840,  and  solicitor-general  in  1852.  He 
was  knighted  in  1853.  He  was  M.P.  for  Aylesbury, 
and  afterwards  for  Wolverhampton.  He  was  for 
some  time  vice-chancellor  of  the  co.  Palatine  of 
Lancaster,  and  counsel  to  the  Uuiver.sity  of  Oxford  ;

RiCHi,ED,  12th  Baron  Deivin,  had  summonses  to  parlia- 
ment  in  the  years  1486,  1490,  and  1493,  and  was  constituted 
by  the  lords-justices  and  council,  in  1496,  commander  and 
leader  in  chief  of  all  the  forces  destined  for  the  defence  of 
the  counties  of  Dublin,  Meath,  Kildare,  and  Louth.  His 
lordship  was  subsequently  summoned  to  parliament  in 
1498,  but  failing  to  appear,  he  was  fined  forty  shillings  for 
non-attendance.  In  1504,  Lord  Deivin  accompanied  the 
Earl  of  Kildare  to  the  famous  battle  of  Knocktough,  iu 
Connaught,  and  was  the  first  to  throw  a  spear  into  the 
ranks  of  the  Irish,  by  which  he  chanced  to  kill  one  of  the 
Burkes.  In  1527,  he  vcas  nominated  lord-deputy  of  Ireland, 
and  conducted  the  public  affixirs  with  integrity  and  honour, 
until  treacherously  taken  prisoner  by  O'Connor.  That 
native  chieftain  having  made  inroads  upon  the  confines  of 
the  Pale,  in  1528,  Lord  Deivin  ordered  the  detention  of  a 
yearly  rent  due  to  him  out  of  certain  carucatos  of  lands  in 
the  county  of  Meath  ;  which  procedure  led  to  a  conference 
at  the  castle  of  Rathin,  belonging  to  Sir  William  d'Arcie, 
when  by  stratagem  the  lord-deputy  was  seized  and  de- 
tained prisoner,  many  of  his  attendants  being  slain, 
wounded,  and  taken.  Walter  Wellcsley,  of  Dangan  Castle, 
and   Sir  Walter  Delahide,  of  Moyclare,  were  subsequently

This  noble  family  traces  its  descent  in  the  male  line  to 
an  illustrious  house  which  flourished  in  Normandy  for  a 
century  and  a  half  before  the  conquest  of  England,  and 
obtained  its  surname  from  having  held  the  high  and  power- 
ful office,  in  that  principality,  of  Le  Grovbnour.  The 
founder  of  the  English  Gi-osvenors,  Gilbert  le  Grosvenor, 
came  over  in  the  train  of  the  Conqueror,  and  was  nephew 
of  Hugh  Lupus,  Count  of  Avranches,  aftei-wards  Earl  of 
Chester,  uncle  of  the  victorious  monarch.  The  immediata 
ancestor  of  the  ennobled  family  before  us,

*  One  of  the  marquess's  ance.stors,  Sir  Robert  le  Grosvenor, 
had  a  protracted  litigation  with  Sir  Richard  le  Scrope  about 
a  coat  of  arms,  in  which  that  gentleman  was  plaintiff,  and 
Sir  Robert  defendant.  The  suit  was  tried  before  the  high- 
constable  and  high-marshal  of  England,  and  others  com- 
missioned for  that  purpose,  and  lasted  three  years,  not  being 
decided  until  1389. 

Sir  Richard  le  Scrope  complained  of  Sir  Robert  le  Grosve- 
nor's  using  a  particular  coat,  viz.:  Az.,  a  bend,  or,  which 
belonged  to  him  ;  and  the  decision  of  the  court  coufirn  ed  Sir 
Richard's  right,  but  permitted  Sir  Robert  le  Grosvenor  to  use 
instead  :  Az.,  a  garb,  or;  which  has  ever  since  continued  the 
arms  of  the  family.

Sir  William  Williams  was  created  a  Baroiiet  4  Aug. 
1866. 

The  statistics  of  Cornwall,  and  many  topograjihical  and 
historical  publications,  mention  tliis  family,  and  give  tliem 
credit  for  having,  by  their  skill  and  enterprize,  during  a  long 
connection  with  mining  and  other  undertakings  —  some  of 
great  venture  and  magnitude  —  developed  and  increased  the 
resources  of  Cornwall. 

The  possessions  of  this  family  have  much  increased  during 
the  present  century,  and  comprise  large  estates  in  Cornwall 
and  Devonshire,  and  considerable  property  in  Ireland  and 
South  Wales.

WiLLOUGHBT  DE  Eresby,  Baron  (Sir  Alberic

This  is  one  of  the  vei-y  ancient  baronies  created  by  writ 
of  summons,  which  pass,  being  heritable  by  heirs  male  o» 
female,  at  different  periods  into  different  families,  and  some- 
times remain  for  centuries  dormant ;  for  in  the  instance  of 
there  being  no  male  heir,  but  several  female,  the  barony 
does  not  devolve  upon  the  eldest  dau.,  but  upon  all  con- 
jointly, and  cannot,  consequently,  be  inherited  until  there 
be  a  single  heir  to  the  whole,  without  the  especial  inter- 
ference of  the  crown.

this  barony,  was  settled  by  Wjlliaji  the  Conquerob,  with

It  is  the  opinion  of  Sir  William  Dugdale,  that  this  family  is 
descended  from  a  common  ancestor  with  the  Herberts,  Earls  of 
Pembroke ;  namely,  Henry  Fitz-Herbert,  chamberlain  to  King

that  their  proper  name  is  Herbert,  and  that  with  marriage  of 
the  Finche's  heir,  they  took  Finche's  name.  One  Vincent 
Finch,  in  Henry  IV.'s  days,  recovered  by  a  suit  the  manor  of 
~— ,  by  Winchelsea."  And  in  an  old  inscription  in  Braborae 
ehurch,  the  name  is  written  Herbert,  alias  Finch.

Ht'iirngr. 

The  family  of  Worsley,  or  De  Workesley,  as  it  was 
anciently  written,  is  of  high  antiquity,  being  descendsd 
from  Sir  Elias  de  Workesley,  lord  of  the  manor  of  Workes- 
ley (now  Worsley,  about  seven  miles  from  Manchester),  at 
the  time  of  William  the  Conqueror;  a  circumstance  thus 
alluded  to  in  a  very  old  family  record:- — "This  EJias  was 
lord  of  Workesley  in  the  tymo  of  the  Norman  conqueste,  and 
was  a  giante  (as  some  aft'yrme),  He  hath  ben  commonlie 
written  gycias  in  old  bookes  and  cronocles,  which  makethe 
mention  that  ho  oftentymes  (for  the  loue  of  Christ  Jhesu) 
foughte  manie  battells,  obteyninge  victorie,  and  diede  at 
the  Roades,  where  he  lietlie  buried."  In  confirmation  of 
which  fighting  pi-opensity  he  is  also  mentioned  in  an  old 
chronicle  as  attending  Robert,  Duke  of  Normandy,  in  his 
expedition  for  the  recovery  of  the  Holy  Land.  This  family 
contiaued  to  hold  large  possessions  in  Lancashire  (given,  as 
it  is  supposed,  for  military  services  at  the  time  of  the  con- 
quest), till  the  reign  of  James  I.  Prior  to  this  it  was 
thought  that  Elizabeth,  dau.  and  heiress  of  jSir  Geoffrey

Wrottesley,  Baron  (Sir  Arthur  Wrottesley), 
of  Wrottesley,  CO.  Stafford;  and  a  Baronet;  b.  17 
June,  1824;  s.  his  father  as  3rd  baron,  27  Oct.  1867; 
.%.  18  July,  1861,  Augusta-Elizabeth,  4th  dau.  of 
Albert,  1st  Lord  Londesborough,  and  has  issue, 

I.  William,  I>.  17  May,  1863. 

II.  Bertram-Franois,  b.  20  July,  1864. 
I.  Evelyn-Henrietta,  b.  10  Oct.  1866. 

The  manor  of  Wrottesley  formed  one  of  the  numerous  lord- 
ships bestowed  by  the  Conqueror  upon  Robert  de  Stafford,  his 
kinsman.  In  1088,  Ro'oert  gave  Wrottesley  and  Eivington  in 
free  alms  to  Walter  the  alibott,  and  monastery  of  Evesham. 
Between  1160  and  1167,  the  Abbot  Adam  enfeoffed  Simon,  the 
younger  son  of  William  de  Coctune,  with  the  same  manors  of 
Wrottesley  and  Livintune,  for  which  Simon  released  to  the 
Abbot  all  claim  to  Morton  and  other  lands,  in  Worcestershire. 
This  Simon  was  a  younger  brother  of  Ralph  de  Coctune  or 
Coughton,  in  Warwickshire,  a  military  tenant  of  the  abbots  of 
Evesham,  and  third  in  descent  from  Ralph,  the  brother  of 
Walter,  the  first  Norman  abbot  of  that  house.  .  On  the  pipe-roll 
of  the  Exchequer  of  1167,  Simon  is  returned  .as  having  paid  a 
fine  of  half  a  mark,  set  upon  Wrottesley,  by  the  justiciaries  of 
the  forest.  He  was  hving  in  1172,  and  was  s.,  before  1200,  by 
his  son, 

William  de  Wrottesley,  sometimes  styled  William  Fitz 
Simon,  who  d.  about  1242,  and  was  s.  by  a  son, 

Sir  Hugh  de  Wrottesley,  Knt.,  living  between  1242  and. 
1275.  Sir  Hugh  having  joined  the  insurgent  barons  under 
Simon  de  Montfort,  was  one  of  those  whose  estates  were  con- 
fiscated alter  the  battle  of  Evesham,  and  subsequently  redeemed 
under  the  dictum  of  Kenilworth.  He  m.  a  dau.  of  Ralph  de 
Perton,  and  was  .9.  by  his  son. 

Sir  William  de  Wrottesley,  Knt.,  who  was  employed  ia

leaving,  by  his  wife,  Petronilla,  a  son,

under  age.     He  was  .s.  by  his  elder  son. 

Sir  Hugh  de  Wrottesley,  K.G.,  who  came  of  age  in  Jan.

I.  William  Williams,  Esq.,  an  eminent  laivj-er,  recorder  of 
Chester,  and  speaker  of  the  House  of  Commons  in  the  reign  of 
Ch.arles  II.,  knighted  by  King  James  II.  upon  his  appointment 
to  the  solicitor-generalship,  and  created  a  Baronet,  6  July,  1088. 
Sir  William,  while  speaker,  was  tried  upon  an  information 
brought  against  him  in  the  court  of  King's  Bench,  for  a  libel, 
in  causing  to  be  printed  (as  speaker  of  the  House  of  Commons) 
the  information  of  Thomas  Dangerfield,  Gent. ;  and  although  he 
pleaded  the  privilege  of  parliament,  and  that  he  had  acted  in 
obedience  to  the  orders  of  the  house,  he  was  nevertheless  fined 
ten  thousand  pounds,  the  greater  part  of  which  he  was  even- 
tually compelled  to  pay.  Sir  William  was  constituted  one  of 
the  king's  council  after  the  Revolution,  and  terminated  his 
political  life  by  the  introduction  of  the  Treating  Act,  which 
passed  into  a  law,  and  still  continues  one  of  the  safeguards  to 
the  purity  of  parliament.  He  ni.  Margaret,  dau.  and  co-heiress

To  the  House  of  Gwydir,  now  represented  raatemally  in  one 
of  its  branches  by  the  Williams-Wynns  of  Wynnstay,  must  be 
conceded  the  first  rank  in  Cambrian  genealogy.  This  eminent 
family  deduces  male  descent  through  their  immediate  ancestor, 
Rhodri,  Lord  of  Anglesey,  younger  son  of  Owen  Gwynedd,  Prince 
of  North  Wales,  from  Anarawd,  King  of  North  Wales,  eldest  son 
of  Rhodri  Mawr,  King  of  Wales.  This  last  monarch,  the  descen- 
dant of  a  long  line  of  regal  ancestors  succeeded  to  the  crown  of 
Powys  on  the  demise,  in  843,  of  his  father,  Mervyn  Viych, 
King  of  Powys,  and  by  inheritance  and  marriage  acquired  the 
kingdoms  of  North  Wales  and  South  Wales.  He  was  slain 
A.D.  876,  and  left,  by  Angharad  his  wife,  sister  and  heiress  of 
Gwgan  ap  Meuric,  Lord  of  Caerdigan,  three  sons, 

I.  Anarawd  ap  Rhodri  Mawr.  of  whose  line  we  have  to  treat.

Some  of  the  descendants  of  tlie  Scottish  family  of  Young,  of

The  Rev.  John  Young,  a  clergyman  of  the  established 
church.  His  motlier,  Isabella,  was  a  sister  of  Sir  Peter  Young, 
of  Easter  Seaton,  who  m.  a  kinsman  and  namesake.  In  the 
reign  of  King  James  I.  of  England,  this  Rev.  John  Y"oung  m. 
in  Scotland,  a  dau,  of  the  House  of  Douglas,  and  went  to  the 
north  of  Ireland,  where  they  settled ;  after  some  time  he  ob- 
tained church  preferment,  and  also  considerable  landed  pro- 
perty, through  the  lady's  father,  by  an  exchange  of  lands  in 
the  counties  of  Donegal  and  Derry,  with  Lord  Abercorn,  for  an 
equivalent  in  Scotland,  as  a  settlement  on  his  dau.  and  her 
family.  Part  of  these  lands  are  now  in  the  possession  of 
Richard  Young,  Esq.  of  Coolkeiragh,  their  lineal  descendant. 
The  Rev.  John  Young  had  a  numerous  family.    His  eldest  son, 

James  Young,  resided  in  the  co.  of  Donegal,  where  he 
!/(..,  and  had  several  children,  of  whom  nine  were  sons.  Being 
a  man  of  good  fortune,  much  attached  to  the  Protestant  cause, 
he  was  not  only  an  active  partisan  at  the  siege  of  Derry,  but 
was  enabled  frequently  to  send  aid  to  the  besieged  during  their 
arduous  struggle.  He  was,  in  consequence,  one  of  the  citizens 
of  Derry  attainted  by  James  II.

*^*  Archbishops  and  Bishops  hear  the  arms  of  their  Sees  impaled  with  their  own  family  arms,  without  crest  or  motto,  and  with  a 
mitre  over  the  shield.  The  mitre  of  both  Archbishops  and  Bishops  is  (with  the  exception  of  the  mitre  of  the  Bishop  of 
Durham)  exactly  the  same.  It  is  a  high  golden  cap,  enriched  with  jewels,  pointed  and  divided  at  the  top,  wilh  fringed 
pendants  hanging  from  the  lower  part :  each  top  is  sunnounted  by  a  cross,  of  which  cross  the  more  ancient  and  probably  more 
correct  form  is  as  in  the  above  engi-aving;  the  present  usual  fonn  of  the  cross,  however,  is  that  of  a  eross-pattce.  The 
mitre  of  the  Bishop  of  Durham  differs  from  that  of  the  other  Prelates  in  being  encircled  with  a  ducal  coronet 
As  to  the  designation  and  rank  of  Archbishops  and  Bishops,  see  ante,  Inikoduction.

The  title  of  Baron  and  Magnat  was  conferred  on  this 
family  by  letters  patent  bearing  the  sign-manual  of  hi.s 
Majesty  Leopold,  Emperor  of  Germany,  under  the  great 
seal  of  the  kingdom  of  Hungary,  given  at  Vienna,  the  8th 
April,  1704,  on  Daniel-John  de  Hochepied,  and  was  con- 
firmed to  the  late  Baron  and  to  his  family,  by  royal  licence, 
dated  at  Carlton  House,  London,  27  Sept,  1819. 

This  family,  according  to  the  aforesaid  royal  diploma,  in 
which  are  cited  certain  documents  dated  in  the  year  1210, 
had  been  at  that  period  long  established  in  Belgium,  and  is 
supposed,  by  Jean  le  Carpenter,  in  his  History,  to  have 
been  a  branch  of  the  family  of  Boistrencom-t,  in  the  Cam- 
bresis,  where,  in  the  year  1100,  it  had  been  much  distin- 
guished, and  had  attained  to  the  highest  and  most  conspi- 
cuous stations  of  dignity,  civil  as  well  as  ecclesiastical. 

Nicholas  de  Hochepied,  in  the  year  1575,  was  appointed 
minister  and  ambassador  from  the  states-general  of  Holland, 
to  several  electors  and  potentates  in  Germany. 

Daniel-John  de  Hochepied,  being  minister  from  the 
states  general  of  Holland  at  the  Ottoman  Porte  in  1698,  dis- 
tinguished himself  in  the  negotiations  which  terminated  in 
the  peace  of  Carlowitz,  in  Jan.  1G99  ;  and  having  likewise 
by  his  virtues  and  influence  obtained  the  liberation  of  many 
Christian  slaves  from  Turkish  servitude,  the  Emperor  Leo- 
pold conferred  upon  him  and  his  descendants,  male  and 
female,  the  title  of  Baron  and  Magnat.  He  m.  Clarissa- 
Catherine,  Countess  Collyer,  and  was  father  of

general  of  Holland  at  the  Ottoman  Porte,  6.  6  Jan.  1700, 
who  d.  at  Pera,  11-Feb.  1763,  leaving,  by  Anna-Margaretta 
Boelema,  his  wife,  a  dau  ,  Claua-Catherine,  who  m.  Sir

Jean-Baptiste  Metaxa,  a  Count  of  the  powerful  Venetian 
Republic.  This  title  (with  many  privileges)  was  conferred 
upon  Captain  Auzolo  MetaxU  and  all  his  male  descendants 
in  perpetuum  (by  Franciscus  Mauriceno),  on  12  July,  1691, 
for  bis  eminent  and  valorous  military  achievements  and 
political  services,  rendered  to  the  Venetian  Empire,  in  the 
Ionian  Islands,  Rumelia  and  Livadia,  having  raised  several 
thousand  men,  at  his  personal  expense,  to  support  the 
Venetian  Empire.  The  family  of  Metaxii's  also  distinguished 
themselves  in  favour  of  the  freedom  of  Greece  in  1821,  and, 
up  to  the  present  period,  hold  important  appointments 
under  the  government.  The  title  of  "  Counts,"  according 
to  the  original  grant  of  the  Venetian  Empire,  was  recognized 
by  the  BritLsh  Government,  in  the  United  States  of  the 
Ionian  Islands,  on  3  June,  1840. 

This  title  of  Count  descends  by  inheritance  ;  even  the 
daughters  of  a  count  have  the  right  to  assume  the  title  of 
Countess,  liut  it  is  not  inherited  by  their  descendants. 

The  Count  Jean-Baptiste  MetaxiX,  became  naturalized  on 
30  Nov.  1846.

I.  Eloise-Fanny,  present  countess. 
Sir  Charles  Napier  distinguished  himself  by  a  long  and 
gallant  career.  In  the  French  war,  he  did  many  acts  of 
seamanlike  daring  and  success.  During  an  interval  of  in- 
activity, he  accepted  the  command  of  the  fleet  of  Donna 
Maria,  Queen  of  Portugal,  and  by  his  victories,  was  the 
means  of  placing  her  on  the  Portuguese  throne.  In  reward 
he  was  created  Ccdnt  Cape  St.  Vincent  by  the  Queen  of 
Portugal.  His  chief  exploit  in  the  British  service  was  at 
Acre  in  1841  ;  and  his  chief  command,  that  of  the  Baltic 
fleet,  in  1854.  On  his  return  from  the  Baltic,  Sir  Charles 
was  offered  the  Grand  Cro.ss  of  the  Bath,  which  he  declmed. 
He  was  for  some  time  M.P.  for  the  borough  of  Marylebone, 
and  for  Southwark.     He  d.  5  Nov.  1860.

CRANWORTH,  BARON. 

(Extinct  26  July,  1868.) 

CRAmvoRTH,  Baron  (Sir  Robert-Monsey  llolfe,  P.C,  M.A.) 
of  Cranworth,  co.  Norfolk,  b.  18  Dec.  1790;  w.  9  Oct.  1845 
Laura,  youngest  dau.  of  the  late  T.-\V.  Carr,  Esq.  of  Fiognal 
and  Eshot  Heugh,  Northumberland,  solicitor  to  the  Excise, 
which  lady  d.  s.  p.  15  Feb.  18G8.  This  able,  and  in  every  way 
excellent,  lawyer,  judge,  and  statesman,  was  called  to  the  bar 
in  1816,  made  king's  counsel  in  1832,  solicitor-general  in  1834 
and  in  1835,  and  a  baron  of  the  Exchequer  in  1839.  He  had 
been,  from  1832  to  1839,  M.P.  for  Penryn.  He  was  knighted 
in  1835.  In  1850  he  became  vice-chancellor,  and  on  the  20 
Dec.  of  the  same  year  was  created  Baron  Cranworth.  He 
was  subsequently  a  judge  of  the  Court  of  Appeal  in  Chancery, 
and  was  constituted  lord  high  chancellor  in  Dec.  1852, 
which  high  office  he  resigned  in  1858  ;  was  re-appointed  to  it 
in  1865,  and  again  resigned  in  1866.  He  d.  26  July,  1868, 
when  the  Barony  of  Cranworth  became  extinct.

BALTINGLASS,  VISCOUNTY  OF,  and  PORT- 
LESTER,  BARONY  OF,  in  the  Peerage  of 
Ireland. 

C/ai//iawi— Charles  Stannard  Eustace,  Esq.  of  Robertstown, 
CO.  Kildare. 

Who  considers  himself  de  jure  Viscount  Baltinglass,  and 
whose  descent  from  the  Hon.  William  Eustace,  brother  and 
heir  of  James,  3rd  Viscount  Baltinglass,  has  been  acknow- 
ledged and  confinned  by  the  report  of  H.M.  Attorney-Gen.  for 
Ireland;  his  right  to  the  title  by  inheritance  has  been  admitted 
by  the  same  official  authority,  provided  a  certain  act  of  attain- 
der be  removed. 

This  act  passed  in  the  time  of  Queen  Elizabeth,  and  was 
presumed  to  have  attainted  the  title;  but  recent  researches 
seem  to  show  that  the  legality  of  the  attainder  cannot  be  sus- 


PEERAGES  CLAIMED. 


tained,  anJ  that  consequently  the  dignity  is  at  this  moment 
unobscured  by  any  penal  enactment.  The  claimant  rests  his 
case  on  the  following  grounds : 

I.  The  previous  sanction  of  the  English  privy  council  had 
not  been  obtained  before  the  introduction  of  the  act 
into  the  Irish  parliament.  This  initiatory  proceeding, 
under  Poyning's  Law,  then  in  full  force,  was  indis- 
pensable. 

II.  James,  3rd  Viscount  Baltinglass,  against  whom  the 
act  was  specially  directed,  had  died  three  years  pre- 
viously. 

III.  There  is  no  record  of  the  attainder  to  be  found  in  the 
archives  of  the  privy  council,  London. 

IV.  The  pardon  and  promise  of  indemnity  granted  by  the 
parliament  of  James  I.,  to  all  who  had  opposed  the 
government  of  Elizabeth,  destroyed  the  attainder,  even 
if  such  attainder  were  effectual. 

V.  The  title  was  borne  and  recognised  by  two  viscounts  long 
subsequent  to  the  passing  of  the  statute. 

In  1839,  the  late  Rev.  Charles  Eustace  petitioned  the  crown 
that  his  right  to  the  Viscountcy  of  Baltinglass  might  be  ac- 
knowledged ;  his  petition  was  referred  by  the  Queen  to  her 
majesty's  Attorney-General  for  Ireland,  who,  having  investi- 
gated the  case,  made  an  elaborate  report  thereon  to  the  Govern- 
ment, concluding  thus : 

Sxtractfrom  the  Attwuey-General's  Re}wrt. 

"  I  am  of  opinion  that  the  petitioner  has  shown  sufficient 
evidence  of  his  right  to  the  dignity  of  Viscount  of  Baltinglass, 
in  case  the  attainder  of  James,  the  3rd  viscount,  created  by  the 
Act  of  Queen  Elizabeth,  were  reversed. 

Maziere  Brady." 

Subsequent  reference  was  made  by  the  crown  to  the  Attorney- 
General  for  England,  who  gave  in  a  report  fully  confirming  that 
of  the  Attorney-General  of  Ireland.

BEITISn  OEDEES  OF  KNIGHTHOOD. 


THE    MOST    NOBLE    ORDER    OF    THE    GARTER. 

Instituted  by  King  Edward  III.  about  August,  1348. 


(K.G.) 


HABIT   AND   INSIGNIA. 


The  Garter  of  dark-blue  velvet,  edged  with  gold,  bearing 
the  motto  in  golden  letters,  with  buckle  and  pendant  of  gold 
richly  chased.  The  garter  is  worn  on  the  left  leg  below  the 
knee. 

The  Mantle  of  blue  velvet,  lined  with  white  taflfeta;  on 
the  left  breast  the  star  embroidered. 
The  Hood  of  crimson  velvet. 

The  Surcoat  likewise  of  ci-imson  velvet,  lined  with  white 
taffeta. 

The  Hat  of  black  velvet,  lined  with  white  taffeta ;  a  plume 
of  white  ostrich  feathers,  in  the  centre  of  which  a  tuft  of 
black  heron's  feathers,  all  fastened  to  the  hat  by  a  band  of 
diamonds. 

The  Collar,  gold,  consisting  of  twenty-six  pieces,  each  in 
form  of  a  garter,  enamelled,  azure,  and  appended  thei-eto, 

The  George,  or  figure  of  St.  George  on  horseback,  en- 
countering tiie  dragon.  The  George  is  worn  to  the  collar ; 
and  the  lesser  George,  pendant  to  a  broad,  dark-blue  ribbon 
over  the  left  shoulder. 

The  Star  of  eight  points,  silver,  upon  the  centre  of  which 
the  Cross  of  St.  George,  gules,  encircled  with  the  garter. 
By  a  statute  passed  on  the  17th  Jan.  1805,  the  Order  is  to  consist  of  the  Sovei-eign  and  twenty-five 
Knights-Companions,  together  with  such  lineal  descendants  of  King  George  II.  as  may  be  elected,  always 
excepting  the  Prince  of  Wales,  who  is  a  constituent  part  of  the  original  institution.  Special  statutes  have 
since,  at  different  times,  been  proclaimed  for  the  admission  of  Sovereigns  and  Extra  Knights,  the  latter  of 
whom  have,  however,  always,  become  part  of  the  twenty-five  Companions  on  the  occurrence  of  vacancies.

of  a  glory;  the  ci'oss  and  feet  resting  upon  the  gi'ound,  of  enamelled 
green. 

The  Collar  is  of  Thistles,  intermingled  with  sprigs  of  rue.

THE  MOST  HONOURABLE  ORDER  OF  THE  BATIL 

[netUuted  in  1Z99.     Revived  in  1725.     Enlarged  in  1&15  and  lSi7- 

On  the  2nd  of  Jan.  1815,  it  was  declared  that,  "for  the 
purpose  of  commemorating  the  auspicious  termination  of 
the  long  and  arduous  contest  in  which  this  empire  has  been 
engaged,"  the  Order  should  be  composed  of  three  classes,  and 
on  the  14th  April,  1847,  it  was  farther  extended  by  the 
addition  of  civil  knights  commandei's  and  companions, 
on  which  occasion  new  Statutes  were  promulgated  for  the 
government  of  the  Order,  and  the  number  of  meuibera 
declared  as  follow,  viz., 

1st  Class — to  consist  of  knights  grand  cross;  number  not 
to  exceed,  for  the  miUtary  service,  fifty,  exclusive  of  the 
Sovereign  and  princes  of  the  blood  royal,  and  such  disttn- 
giushed  foreigners  as  may  be  nominated  honorary  knighta 
gi-and  cross  ;   and  twenty-five  for  the  civil  seiwice. 

2nd  Class — Knights  commanders,  numbers  not  to  exceed, 
for  the  military  service,  one  hundred  and  twer-ty-three,  and 
for  the  civil  service  sixty,  exclusive  of  foreign  officers,  who 
may  be  admitted  as  honorary  knights  commanders.  In  the 
event  of  actions  of  signal  distinction,  or  of  future  wars,  the 
numbers  may  be  increased  of  this  as  well  as  of  the  third  class. 
The  members  of  the  second  class  are  entitled  to  the  distinc- 
tive appellation  of  knighthood,  after  having  been  invested 
with  the  Insignia;  to  take  precedence  of  Knights  Bachelors; 
to  wear  the  badge,  &c.,  pendent  by  a  red  ribbon  round  the 
neck,  the  star  embroidered  on  the  left  side. 

3rd  Class— Companions  of  the  Order,  to  consist,  for  military  service,  of  six  hundred  and  ninety, 
And  for  the  civil  service  of  two  hundred ;  they  are  to  take  precedence  of  esquires,  but  are  not  entitled  to 
the  appellation,  style,  &c.,  of  knights  bachelors.  To  wear  the  badge  assigned  to  the  third  class,  pendent 
by  a  narrow  red  ribbon  from  the  button-hole.  No  officer  can  be  nominated  to  the  military  division  of  the 
third  c)ar-8  of  the  Order,  unless  his  services  have  been  marked  by  special  mention  of  his  name  as  having 
distinguished  himself  in  action  against  the  enemy.  This  class  has  never  been  conferred  upon  any  ofiicer 
below  the  rank  of  major  in  the  army  and  commander  in  the  navy. 

The  Badge  for  the  Military  Classes  of  the  Order  is  a  gold  Maltese  cross,  of  eight  points,  enamelled, 
urgent ;  in  tlie  four  angles,  a  lion  passant-guardant,  or ;  in  the  centre,  the  rose,  thistle,  and  shamrock, 
issuant  from  a  scepti-e  between  three  imperial  crowTis,  or,  within  a  circle,  gules ;  thereon  the  motto  of  the 
Order,  surrounded  by  two  branches  of  laurel,  proper,  issuing  fi'om  an  escrol,  azure,  inscribed  IcH  Dien 
^l  serve),  m  letters  of  gold.  It  is  worn  by  the  grand  crosses  pendent  from  a  red  ribbon  across  the  right 
choulder,  by  the  knights  commanders  from  the  neck,  and  by  the  companions  from  the  button-hole. 

The  Collar  is  of  gold  (weight,  thirty  ounces  Troy  weight),  and  is  composed  of  nine  imperial  crowna, 
and  tAght  roses,  thistle,  and  shamrock,  issuing  from  a  sceptre,  enamelled  in  their  proper  colours,  tied  or 
linked  together  with  seventeen  gold  knots,  enamelled  white,  having  the  badge  of  the  Order  pendent 
therefrtjm. 

The  Star  of  the  Military  Grand  Crosses  is  formed  of  rays  or  flames  of  silver,  thereon  a  gold 
Maltese  cross,  and  in  the  centi-e,  within  the  motto,  branches  of  laurel,  issuant  as  in  the  badge.

BRITISH  ORDERS  OF  KNIGHTHOOD. 


THE  MOST  EXALTED  ORDER  OF  THE  STAR  OF  INDIA. 


Instituted  by  Her  Majesty  Queen  Victoria,  Fehmary  2Zrd,  1861,  and  enlarged,  March  2%tli,  1866. 

The  Order  consists  of  the  Sovereign,  a  Grand  Master,  and  175  Ordinary  Companions  or  Members, 
together  with  such  Extra  and  Honorary  Members  as  Her  Majesty,  her  heirs  and  successors,  shall 
from  time  to  time  appoint.  The  175  Ordinary  Members  are  divided  into  three  Classes  : — the  first 
Class  are  etyled  Knights  Grand  Commanders,  and  to  consist  of  twenty-five  Members ;  the  second 
Class  to  consist  of  50  Members,  to  be  styled  Knights  Commanders ;  the  third  Class  to  consist  of 
100  Members,  to  be  styled  Companions.  Her  Majesty's  Viceroy  and  Governor-General  of  India  for 
the  time  being  is  Grand  Master. 


The  statutes  enable  the  Sovereign  to  confer  the  dignity  of  Knight  Grand  Commander  of  the  Order  upon 
Princes  and  Chiefs  of  India  as  shall  have  entitled  themselves  to  her  Majesty's  favour,  and  upon  such  of 
her  Majesty's  British  subjects  as  have,  by  important  and  loyal  services  rendered  by  them  to  the  Indian 
Empire,  merited  the  Eoyal  favour ;  and  the  second  and  third  Classes  upon  persons  who,  by  their  conduct 
or  services  in  the  Indian  Empire,  have  mei'ited  the  Royal  favour. 


The  Star. — Rays  of  gold  issuing  from 
a  centre,  having  thereon  a  star  in  dia- 
monds, resting  uiDon  a  light  blue  ena- 
melled circular  riband,  tied  at  the 
ends,  inscribed  with  the  motto  of  the 
Order,  viz. :  —  "  Heaven's  light  our 
GUIDE,"  also  in  diamonds. 

The  Collar. — Composed  of  the  lotus 
of  India,  of  palm  branches,  tied  toge- 
ther, in  saltier,  and  of  the  united  Red 
and  White  Rose.  In  the  centre  is  an 
imperial  crown ;  all  richly  enamelled  on 
gold,  in  their  proper  colours. 


The  Badge. — An  onyx  cameo  of  Her 
Majesty's  effigy,  set  in  a  perforated  and 
ornamented  oval,  containing  the  motto 
of  the  Order,  "  Heaven's  light  ouk 
GUIDE,"  surmounted  by  a  star  all  in 
diamonds.  The  Ribbon  of  the  Order 
is  sky-blue,  having  a  narrow  white 
stripe  towards  either  edge,  and  is  worn 
from  the  right  shoulder  to  the  left  side. 

The  Mantle. — Light  blue  satin,  lined 
with  white,  and  fastened  with  a  cordon 
of  white  silk,  with  blue  and  silver  tas- 
sels, on  the  left  side  a  representation  of 
the  star  cf  the  Order.

BRITISH  ORDERS  OF  KNIGTITHGOD, 


THE  MOST  DISTINGUISHED  ORDER  OF  ST.  MICHAEL 
AND  ST.  GEORGE. 

Instituted  17th  April,  1818,  hy  Letters  Patent,  under  the  Great  Seal  of  Great  Britain,  for  Natives  of  the  United. 
States  of  the  Ionian  Islands,  and  of  the  Island  of  Malta  and  its  Dependencies,  and  for  swh  other  subjects 
of  His  Majcstij  as  may  hold  hif/h  and  confidential  situations  in  the  Mediterranean. 

By  Statutes,  dated  16  Aug.  1832,  the  Order  is  to  consist  of  fifteen  Knights  Grand  Cross,  exclusive  of 
the  Grand  Master,  twenty  Knights  Commauders,  and  twenty-five  Cavalieri  or  Companions. 

The  members  of  the  Order  enjoy  rank  and  precedency  immediately 
after  the  corresponding  classes  of  the  Order  of  the  Bath  ;  that  is  to  say, 
the  Knights  Grand  Cross  after  Knights  Grand  Cross  of  the  Bath ;  the 
Knights  Commanders  after  the  Knights  Commanders  of  the  Bath ;  and 
the  Cavalieri  and  Companions  after  the  Companions  of  the  Bath,  with 
the  exception  of  the  present  Senior  Cavaliere,  who  retains  the  appella- 
tion of  the  British  Knighthood  ("  Sir"),  and  the  precedency  assigned  to 
him  by  the  original  statutes  of  Api'il,  1818.  All  natives  of  the  Ionian 
Islands  and  of  Malta,  who  receive  the  third  class  of  the  Order,  ara 
styled  "  Cavaliere,"  and  all  natives  of  Great  Britain  and  Ireland  "  Com- 
])anion3."  The  Grand  Master  is  the  Fii-st  and  Principal  Knight  Grand 
Cross,  and  the  Lord  High  Commissioner  to  the  Ionian  States  has  pre- 
cedency of  all  other  Knights  Grand  Cross.  The  Knights  Grand  Cross 
are  entitled  to  bear  supporters,  and  to  encircle  their  arms  with  the 
collar,  ribbon,  and  motto  of  the  Order.  The  Knights  Commanders  and 
Cavalieri  also  encircle  their  arms  with  the  ribbon  and  motto ;  and  the 
Companions  suspend  the  badge  of  the  Order  to  their  arms. 

HABIT  AND  INSIGNIA. 

The  Star  of  a  Knight  Grand  Cross  is  composed  of  seven  rays  of 
silver,  having  a  small  ray  of  gold  between  each  of  them,  and  over  all 
the  cross  of  St.  George,  gules.  In  the  centre  is  a  representation  of  the 
Archangel  St.  Michael  encountering  Satan,  within  a  blue  circle,  in- 
scribed with  the  motto  Auspicium  Melioris  ^vi. 

The  Collar  is  fonned  alternately  of  lions  of  England,  of  Maltese  crosses,  and  of  the  ciphers  SM  and 
S  G,  having  in  the  centre  the  imperial  crown,  over  two  v,-inged  lions,  passant-guardant,  each  holding  a 
book,  and  seven  arrows.  At  the  opposite  end  of  the  collar  are  two  similar  lions.  Tlie  whole  is  of  gold, 
except  the  crosses,  which  are  of  white  enamel,  and  it  is  linked  together  by  small  gold  chains. 

The  Badge  is  a  gold  cross  of  fourteen  points  of  white  enamel,  edged  with  gold,  having  in  tlie  centre,  on 
one  side,  the  Archangel  St.  Michael  encountering  Satan,  and  on  the  other,  St.  George  on  horseback, 
eucoimtering  a  dragon,  within  a  blue  circle,  on  which  the  motto  of  the  Order  is  inscribed.  The  Cross  is 
surmounted  by  the  imperial  crown,  and  is  worn  by  the  Knights  Grand  Cross  to  the  Colla,r,  or  to  a  wide 
Saxon-blue  ribbon,  with  a  scarlet  stripe  from  the  right  shoulder  to  the  left  side. 

The  Mantle  is  of  Saxon-blue  satin,  lined  with  Ecarlet  silk,  tied  with  cordons  of  blue  and  scarlet  silk  and 
gold,  and  has  on  the  left  side  the  star  of  a  Knight  Grand  Cross. 

The  Chapeau  is  of  blue  satin,  lined  with  scarlet,  and  surmounted  with  white  and  black  ostrich  feathers. 

The  Knights  Comjianders  wear  the  badge  suspended  to  a  narrower  ribbon  from  the  neck,  and  have  on 
their  left  side  a  star  composed  of  four  rays,  mth  a  small  cross  of  eight  points  in  saltier,  of  silver,  sur- 
mounted by  the  cross  of  St.  George,  gal';s,  and  having  the  same  centre  as  the  star  of  the  Grand   Crosses. 

The  Cavalieri  and  Companions  wear  the  small  cross  of  the  Order  from  a  still  narrovrer  ribbon  at  the 
button-hole  of  their  coa's.

III  Canopo  ut  ad  Canopum.  Louis,  Bt.  The  sense  of  this 
legend  is  the  most  obscure  in  the  whole  list  of  mottoes.  The 
following  explanation  has  been  suggested : — Canopus  is  the 
name  of  a  city  in  Egypt  (Gens  fortunata  Canopi,  Virg. 
Georg.  iv.  v.  237),  now  Aboukir,  a  place  celebrated  during  the 
Crusades.  The  word  also  signifies  a  fixed  star  of  the  first 
niiigiiitude,  in  the  constellation  of  Argus,  and  southern  hemi- 
splicre  (Sidus  ingens  et  clarum,  Plin.  Hist.  Nat.  vi.  22).  The 
motto  may  therefore  have  been  assumed  by  a  crusader,  im- 
porting that  to  have  fought  for  the  cross  in  Egypt  (in  Canopo), 
was  the  road  to  heaven  (ad  Canopum,  equivalent  to  adastra)." 
Admiral  Louis,  however,  having  died  on  board  the  ship 
Canopus,  another  meaning,  though  perhaps  somewhat  similar, 
is  intended.

placing  the  sign  and  words  on  the  imperial  standard.

Lamh  dearg  Eirin.  The  red  hand  of  Ireland.  O'Neill,  V. 
O'Neill,  B.  In  an  ancient  expedition  of  some  adventurers 
to  Ireland,  their  leader  declared  that  whoever  first  touched 
the  shfre  should  possess  the  territory  which  he  reached. 
O'Neil,  from  whom  descended  the  princes  of  Ulster,  bent 
upon  obtaining  the  reward,  and  seeing  another  boat  likely 
to  land,  cut  his  left  hand  off  and  threw  it  on  the  coast. 
Hence  the  traditionary  origin  ef  the  motto.  The  red.  hand 
was  adopted  by  James  I.,  as  the  badge  on  instituting  the 
order  of  I'aronet.  The  design  of  the  institution  being  the 
colonization  of  the  province  of  Ulster,  in  Ireland,  the  arms  of 
the  province  were  deemed  the  most  appropriate  insignia.

Mutas  inglorius  artes.     To  exercise,  unambitioxis  of  glory,   the 

silent  arts.    Halford,  Bt.     This  motto  is  an  elegant  quotation 

from  the  description  of  the  physician  lapis,  in  the  twelfth 

book  of  Virgil's  iEneid,  which  has  thus  been  rendered  by 

Dryden : 

"lapis  was  at  hand  to  prove  his  art. 
Whose  blooming  youth  so  fired  Apollo's  heart, 
That,  for  his  love,' he  proffer'd  to  bestow 
His  tuneful  harp,  and  his  uneiTing  bow  : 
The  pious  youth,  more  studious  how  to  save 
His  aged  sire,  now  sinking  to  the  grave, 
Preferr'd  the  powers  of  jilants,  and  silent  praise 
Of  healing  arts,  before  Phocbean  bays." 

The  medical  profession  was  by  no  means  in  honour  at  Rome. 
Every   senator  and  rich   Roman  had   his  family   jiliysician 
among  his  own  liondmen,  and  none  but  slaves  practised  the

art  until  Augustus  made  Antonius  Musa  a  freeman :  in  Greece 
it  was  different.  Tasso,  speaking  of  Erotimus,  when  attending

"  E  giS,  I'antico  Erotimo,  che  nacque 

In  riva  al  Po,  s'adopra  in  sua  salute ; 
II  qual  del'  lierbe,  e  delle  nobil'  acque 

Ben  conosceva  ogni  uso,  ogni  virtute. 
Caro  alle  Muse  ancor ;  ma  si  compiacque 

NeUa  gloria  minor  dell'  arti  mute  : 
Sol  curb  toiTe  a  morte  i  coiiii  frali, 
E  potea  far'  i  nomi  anco  immortal!. " 

Tasso,  Ger.  Lib.  canto  xi,  st.  70. 

"  Grey  Erotimus,  bom  beside  the  Po, 

Came  to  his  aid;  a  sage  who  knew  the  use 
And  secret  virtues  of  all  springs  that  flow — 

Of  all  green  herbs  the  hills  and  woods  produce  :  ^. .,

Earl  of  Comyn,  and  Baron  of  Tonsburgh,  in  Normandy,  and

bably lie  took  his  motto  ft-om  Caen,  an  important  seat  of  his 
jurisdiction;  his  grandson,  Robert  de  Burgh,  brought  the 
quaint  legend  with  him  when  he  came  to  fight  at  Hastings, 
and  to  settle  in  England.
